1tcrqnh.text: The University of Copenhagen in Denmark confirmed that hackers accessed one of its test environments containing personal data belonging to 525,000 people. The educational organization detected the breach last Tuesday and disclosed it on Friday. In an update yesterday, the university added another 20,000 staff and students whose PIN codes were exposed. “The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a cyber attack in which hackers gained access to one of the university’s test environments,” the university says. Founded in 1479, the University of Copenhagen is Denmark’s oldest university and one of its leading research institutions. It has approximately 36,800 students and 10,700 employees, with six faculties and more than 200 research centers. The University of Copenhagen is still investigating to determine the extent of the incident, but warns that the following information may have been exposed: Full names National identity numbers (CPR) Phone numbers Email addresses The exposed information increases the risk of phishing and social engineering attacks. Regarding the PIN access exposure, the University of Copenhagen has restricted physical access to certain critical locations on its campus out of abundance of caution and is gradually reopening them as it distributes new access codes. The university says it contained the attack and blocked the attacker’s access. Currently, there is no indication that hackers accessed systems supporting daily operations or disrupted university activities. The university reported the incident to the Danish Data Protection Agency, but also said it falls within the scope of Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and that it is taking the appropriate steps with the relevant regulators. Students and staff whose data may have been exposed in this incident should be cautious of unsolicited communications and independently verify requests. The university promised to provide more updates on the scope of the impact as soon as its internal investigation allows. 67ae76.text: South Korean police identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that breached more than 90 organizations in the country, with ARTEX AI pentesting framework used in most of the attacks. According to local media citing the Seoul Metropolitan Police, the gang leader has a background in penetration testing and worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022. In 38 of the incidents, the threat actor demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000), promising in exchange not to leak stolen data. Authorities believe the threat actor stole 8.2 million records from compromised organizations, including educational institutes, hospitals, large corporations, and even golf courses. Extortion message sent to a victim Source: Yonhap Yonhap News says that the gang leader is a self-taught 32 year-old hacker and started attacking organizations in September 2025. The Seoul Metropolitan police told the publication that the hacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite, the same autonomous framework used in the attacks against multiple South Korean banks attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor. Initially, the hacker used conventional tools but adopted AI utilities in late August 2026 to expand the attacks. Authorities arrested all seven suspects, but only the group’s leader remains in custody. Arrested on October 15, he was formally detained two days later and referred to prosecutors on October 23. The other six suspects remain under investigation without being detained. Police opened a case after a victim filed a complaint in June, and investigators traced the suspects through server logs from the breached entities. Law enforcement authorities reportedly used an in-house AI tool to analyze the recovered evidence. The police told local media that AI has lowered the barrier to entry for aspiring cybercriminals, resulting in large-scale, high-impact incidents that were previously only possible for skillful, knowledgeable actors. “This is the first case of arrest of a suspect in Korea related to a large-scale hacking and personal information theft crime that exploited generative AI," the police told Yonhap. “Even individuals who are not professional hacker organizations can now hack on a large scale with the help of AI.” The police continue the investigation, now focusing on whether any of the stolen data has been leaked on the dark web. 1umr5g5.text: Texas sued OpenAI and its CEO on Friday, alleging the artificial intelligence behemoth markets its ChatGPT product as safe even as purported safeguards are failing to protect consumers, including children. In an unusual move, the suit — brought under the state’s deceptive trade practices laws — seeks to hold founder and CEO Sam Altman personally liable for the alleged deception. Texas is seeking civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and sweeping injunctive relief, including a requirement that OpenAI bar minors from accessing ChatGPT, obtain third-party approval on new models from a court-appointed expert and stop the chatbot from giving users tips on suicide, eating disorders and how to commit violence. Attorney General Ken Paxton alleges that OpenAI also has long failed to verify identities in violation of state law. Paxton, who is locked in a close Senate race, has sued or settled with several tech companies in the last year, including Roblox, TikTok and Meta. In July 2024, the latter agreed to pay the state a record-breaking $1.4 billion to settle claims that it had deployed facial recognition without users’ consent. At the top of Friday’s lawsuit, Altman’s past proclamation that AI will “probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there’ll be great companies” is featured prominently in italics. A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit noted that OpenAI’s value has surged from about $17 billion to over $1.4 trillion in four years. “This success has not been earned; the rise of OpenAI is attributable to a web of deceit and the exploitation of users (including Texans), leveraging their data and safety to boost OpenAI’s market value at unacceptable costs and jeopardizing everyone in Texas,” the lawsuit said. “Because of Defendants’ misrepresentations about their artificial intelligence products and their careless introduction of ChatGPT to Texas and the world,” the filing said, “mass shooters have been aided and abetted in deadly rampages, vulnerable people have been encouraged into suicide… and minors have become addicted to a tool that feigns human compassion to collect their data with no parental oversight.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1o1q7oh.text: OpenAI has launched GPT-6.1 Terra, a new model focused on computer use, visual reasoning, coding, and everyday work, while costing significantly less than its larger models. Terra is designed as a faster and cheaper option for tasks such as filling out forms, editing videos, interpreting technical drawings, and automating repetitive desktop work. "We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing," OpenAI explained in a blog post. "A significant step up from GPT-5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos." OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Terra's API pricing is 50% lower than GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens. On Agents' Last Exam, Terra scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at medium reasoning effort while costing about one-third as much. "It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token," OpenAI noted. "Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks over three times faster than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol." GPT-6.1 Terra also hallucinates less GPT 6.1 Terra makes fewer errors On its internal benchmark, the error rate at low reasoning effort dropped from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra. "At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol," OpenAI said. Coding has improved as well, with Terra scoring 50.3% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at maximum reasoning effort, more than double GPT-5.6 Terra's 21.5% score. OpenAI still recommends GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra for the most complex coding tasks. GPT-6.1 Terra is available now to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, as well as through the API as gpt-6.1-terra. qc7tdu.text: DreamHost has forced password resets for email and FTP/SFTP users following an incident that disrupted connections to the File Manager interface. The latest update from the web hosting provider notes that all affected account owners have received recovery instructions. Users will be unable to log in until their account owner sets new credentials. DreamHost is a U.S. web hosting provider and domain registrar that offers WordPress hosting, business email, virtual private servers, dedicated servers, and cloud services. According to the company page, it serves over 400,000 customers in more than 100 countries and supports at least 1.5 million websites and applications, including 750,000 WordPress installations. DreamHost initially reported connectivity problems affecting its File Manager interface on October 23, but the impact quickly expanded to other services. The company responded by blocking access to all users until they completed password resets, an action described as a precaution. Over the weekend, the company sent out recovery instructions in batches and notified all affected account holders. As of publishing, the incident remains active and access to File Manager is still unavailable. In notifications to impacted account holders, the company advises users to also review each email address for forwarding rules and remove any forwarding destination they do not recognize. While this suggests that some email accounts may have been breached and exposed to external actors, DreamHost did not provide additional details. Long-time customers are also complaining about the lack of information from DreamHost, leading some of them to speculate about what happened. "It's disturbing to get these emails with zero explanation what's going on, and very frustrating that user community has to guess," one customer said. Users are also recommended to change reused passwords elsewhere if their old DreamHost password was reused on other platforms/services. DreamHost also said it cannot contact individual mailbox or FTP users directly, urging account owners to notify affected users by phone, text, or other means, as those whose passwords were reset may be unable to access their email accounts. BleepingComputer has contacted DreamHost multiple times with questions about the incident, the number of impacted accounts, and whether files or messages were exposed, but we have not heard back as of publication. e9bla9.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 26, 2026Malware / Web Security An unknown threat actor has infected 953 online stores, most of them running Magento, as part of a long-running campaign active since July 2025. According to Dutch e-commerce security company Sansec, the activity is designed to add a small piece of code to the store's pages that, when visited by unsuspecting users, serves malicious JavaScript loader code through Magento CMS blocks. "When you visit, that code makes your browser ask the group's server what to do next," Sansec said. "The server first checks whether you are a real shopper or a security scanner, so scanners get nothing." No less than five distinct domains have been observed over time in connection with the campaign - manulfie[.]click, first seen in July 2025 neswnsssn[.]click, first seen in December 2025 lanhd6549tdhse[.]top, first seen in March 2026 additionalver[.]com, first seen in June 2026 deepveindrilling[.]com, first seen in October 2026 Sansec said it found deepveindrilling[.]com in the CMS blocks of 83 online stores since the domain was registered on October 6, 2026. The latest JavaScript loader domain is hosted behind Cloudflare and only responds to script requests from real visitors of infected stores. The loader is staged within Magento's cms_block database table, which is used to render static content into storefront pages. The ultimate objective of the attack is to launch the attack-controlled code when the CMS block is rendered after a shopper opens the compromised website. While Sansec does not disclose whether the threat actor modifies an existing CMS block (such as header, footer, or promotional banner) or creates a new block, the attacker can adopt either of the approaches to run the loader. Two different versions of the loader have been spotted. In one version, the external JavaScript loaded from the attacker's domain stores the payload in the browser's localStorage. This causes the stashed code to be run again on subsequent visits, even if the external domain becomes unavailable. The second version expands on this behavior by incorporating browser fingerprinting checks to filter out bots and security scanners, while ensuring that only real shoppers are exposed to the malicious code. The exact nature of the final payload remains unknown. Early iterations of the campaign have also been observed using Keitaro, an advertising tracker and analytics platform, as a traffic distribution system (TDS), to route visitors to different responses – i.e., return a payload, a redirect or nothing – based on their characteristics. Sansec said requesting the additionalver[.]com script as a Windows desktop visitor returned as response "QWE=123;," which does nothing apart from setting a cookie that marks the visitor for 24 hours. The deepveindrilling[.]com domain, on the other hand, drops the Keitaro component and integrates the bot-filtering logic into the loader itself. As for the initial access vector, 471 Magento stores are estimated to have been injected with the loader through the PolyShell (aka CVE-2026-48356) vulnerability. Another 102 stores saw files uploaded through the PolyShell or SessionReaper (aka CVE-2025-54236) vulnerabilities. "One store on Magento 2.4.7-p1 had PolyShell webshells disguised as PNG images in pub/media/custom_options/quote/, next to the additionalver.com loader in a CMS block," Sansec said. "The block switched to deepveindrilling[.]com on October 7. The store still lacks APSB26-73, Adobe's PolyShell fix for supported release lines." In another case, an e-commerce store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 with no missing core patches was compromised to add a rogue administrator account and then use it to inject the code. Site owners are advised to audit their sites for suspicious accounts and unexpected CMS blocks in the cms_block and cms_page tables. It's also advised to keep the sites up-to-date and enforce strong passwords. The disclosure comes against the backdrop of PHP2Shell, a set of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that have witnessed widespread exploitation attempts following their disclosure last week. However, Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi has recorded what appears to be the first in-the-wild successful exploitation of the vulnerabilities to run shell commands on honeypot servers. These commands have been observed using wget, curl, or PHP CLI to fetch additional payloads from a remote server ("162.35.99[.]94:80").No downloaded second-stage artifacts have been observed so far.

1s77uzf.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code. PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on. The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws. They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1, the fixed version. PHP publishes a software bill of materials, a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions. PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page. Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip, and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build. Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports. Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system. An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts. Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1, or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale. Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update. Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21. Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes. PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it." In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING, because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false, which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed.

116bkki.text: Serbian strongman leader Aleksandar Vučić on Sunday admitted defeat in his race for prime minister, a loss that follows a series of incidents of digital repression that galvanized the opposition. Vučić has served as prime minister and, subsequently, president of Serbia since 2014, and has grown increasingly repressive throughout his tenure. Over the past two years, digital forensic researchers have said they have found evidence which strongly suggests spyware targeting or infections on devices belonging to dozens of Serbian opposition leaders, protesters, prosecutors and journalists. The regime has repeatedly deployed Cellebrite surveillance software to secretly extract data from opponents’ devices — and in some cases install spyware — during bogus interrogations and arrests, researchers from Amnesty International have said. Last week, researchers at the Citizen Lab alleged that University of Belgrade Rector Vladan Đokić’s device was infected with powerful zero-click spyware known as Pegasus earlier this year. Đokić has long resisted facilitating a government-led campaign to crack down on student protesters despite intense pressure from the Vučić administration. In March, Serbian authorities seized servers and computers in his Belgrade office, the Citizen Lab said. The regime also targeted Rade Bajić — a prosecutor who investigated alleged shady dealings between Vučić and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner — with Pegasus, according to Serbia’s SHARE Foundation. Kushner had allegedly sought to buy a protected historic site in Belgrade to erect a Trump Tower. Bajić, who received multiple Apple spyware threat notifications about the attempted snooping, had been pursuing government officials believed to have created forged documents in an effort to secure the deal, the SHARE Foundation said. The digital repression dates back to at least 2024, according to foundation researcher Andrijana Ristić, who works closely with the student protesters who have been targeted. “At first it was civil society, journalists, and activists and then it moved to these protesters and a new election cycle,” Ristić said in an interview last week. The recent spike in confirmed spyware cases is likely due to the fact that the “stakes are so high for the government right now,” said Ristić. So far this year, security experts have found at least 15 people whose devices have been targeted with mercenary spyware in Serbia, according to the SHARE Foundation. In February 2025, Cellebrite said it cut ties with the Serbian government after Amnesty International found that authorities there had “systematically deployed” the surveillance technology to penetrate civilians’ phones and install spyware. However, weeks later Amnesty found the software still being deployed in attacks against opponents. Two investigative journalists also were targeted with Pegasus in March 2025, according to Amnesty International. A spokesperson for the Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to a request for comment. d114av.text: Ukraine's leadership rejected Elon Musk's accusations that its military had misused Starlink's satellite internet service to carry out offensive drone strikes, as Kyiv announced that restrictions disrupting critical military communications had been lifted. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Saturday that Starlink and Starshield connectivity had been restored, with military monitoring systems recording stable connections on equipment exceeding 400 kilometers per hour. The announcement followed nearly two weeks of disruptions that forced Ukrainian troops to cancel some combat missions and complicated drone operations, reconnaissance and frontline logistics. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Saturday that the restrictions had been lifted, saying connectivity had returned to the levels needed for military operations. "This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shahed drones," Zelensky said, thanking the United States and other partners for helping resolve the issue. The apparent resolution came amid a public dispute between Musk and Ukrainian officials over whether Kyiv had misused the satellite service. Musk accused Ukraine's military Saturday of using commercial Starlink terminals to conduct offensive drone strikes, which he said violated the company's rules. "Ukraine's military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people," Musk wrote on X. He distinguished commercial Starlink from Starshield, a military-focused version of SpaceX's satellite communications service that he said was controlled by the U.S. government. "Starshield, a different system, is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them," Musk said. Ukrainian officials and military advisers disputed his claim, arguing that technical restrictions made it impossible to use commercial Starlink terminals for the drone missions Musk described. Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist who previously advised the country's defense minister, said a registration system introduced in February required all satellite terminals operating on moving platforms to be connected to the military Starshield service. "Using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible," Sternenko said, adding that Ukraine had not violated the service's terms. Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as "Flash," also rejected Musk's allegations, saying commercial Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine were limited to speeds of 70 to 90 kilometers per hour and did not work on Russian territory. Those restrictions, he said, prevented Ukrainian forces from using commercial terminals to conduct medium- or long-range drone strikes. The Starshield restrictions, introduced without warning in mid-October, disrupted connectivity on moving vehicles and drones, causing satellite terminals to lose their connections at higher speeds. The problems were particularly concerning for Ukraine's efforts to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, which require Ukrainian interceptor drones to travel at high speeds while maintaining reliable communications. According to a Sunday report by the Institute for the Study of War, Ukraine's interception rate against Russian jet-powered drones declined from 77% to approximately 74% between Oct. 14 and 24, when Starshield was experiencing disruptions. The researchers said Ukraine maintained a relatively high interception rate despite the restrictions. The figures do not establish whether the connectivity problems directly caused the decline. It remains unclear who ordered the speed restrictions. Musk previously said Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the U.S. government and that decisions about speed limits and permitted uses rested with the U.S. military and ultimately President Donald Trump. The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Trump had ordered Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions after becoming frustrated that satellite connectivity remained capped at approximately 160 kilometers per hour. Trump denied having spoken to Musk about the issue but said he might intervene if the problems persisted. The disruption came amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington, including disagreements over Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure and the Trump administration's efforts to pursue a diesel trade agreement with Moscow. In an interview with Piers Morgan earlier this week, Zelensky said he felt personally betrayed by Trump over the restrictions, accusing Washington of abandoning a crucial partner more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion. Musk, meanwhile, defended SpaceX's role in supporting Ukraine, saying Starlink had been essential to the country's defense since the beginning of the invasion. He warned that Ukraine remained heavily dependent on the satellite network, claiming its frontline defenses would collapse if the service were switched off. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

2619wj.text: A Chinese national was extradited from The Netherlands and arraigned on Friday after prosecutors accused him of facilitating an investment fraud scheme through scam centers in Cambodia. 44-year-old Zheng Zhao was allegedly a key money-launderer working with a group of scammers who called U.S.-based victims and urged them to invest in fictitious businesses. Zhao is the ninth person to be charged as part of the scheme after eight others pleaded guilty to money laundering charges. Court documents said Zhao helped facilitate the transfer of stolen funds to a bank account at Deltec Bank in the Bahamas. Zhao converted the funds into cryptocurrency stablecoin USDT, which allowed it to be transferred to digital wallets controlled by people in Cambodia. The funds were then spread to the leaders of scam centers throughout Southeast Asia. Zhao was charged in August 2025 and is facing up to 20 years in prison if convicted on one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. Zhao appeared in a California district court on Friday. U.S. investigators have identified at least 174 American victims of the scheme, which saw scammers contact people on social media or through phone calls, texts and dating sites. The scammers convinced victims to invest in fake digital asset services and used fictitious screenshots alleging their investments were growing. In total, the group transferred at least $36.9 million in victim funds to the Deltec Bank account. ShengSheng He and Jingliang Su – two other coconspirators previously charged alongside Zhao — pleaded guilty and were sentenced last year to 51 months and 46 months in prison respectively. Prosecutors said most of the funds were transferred to scam center leaders based in the Cambodian coastal city of Sihanoukville — a well-known haven for Chinese criminal activity. Several of those who pleaded guilty traveled back and forth between the U.S. and Cambodia’s capital Phnom Penh, coordinating the transfer of stolen funds.

159grct.text: A critical flaw dubbed 'HTTP2Shell' in Brotli, the C decoder library built into Node.js, could allow attackers to corrupt memory and access sensitive data. The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and is also known as “Broccoli2Shell” and “Node2Shell.” It affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0. The vulnerability has been reported under several names because it was initially identified in Node.js before researchers found that the same flaw in the Brotli decoder could affect software across multiple ecosystems. Broad impact The name HTTP2Shell reflects its impact on HTTP clients and servers, although the vulnerability is not specific to HTTP/2 and can affect other applications that decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data. Apart from Node.js, potentially affected software includes Python HTTP clients such as urllib3[brotli], requests, httpx, and aiohttp[speedups], when configured with a vulnerable Brotli decoder, as well as other applications and tools that use vulnerable Brotli implementations. On Sunday, Microsoft pushed an emergency security update to address the issue in .NET, warning that successful exploitation allows privilege escalation on systems with a vulnerable .NET version. Brotli is an open-source project developed and maintained by Google for lossless data compression. It shrinks files so they can be transmitted faster without affecting the original data. The Node2Shell vulnerability is a buffer overflow that lets a specially crafted Brotli-compressed stream trigger an invalid block switch that the decoder treats as valid and misinterprets as a request for more input. By continuing to append input bytes to an internal eight-byte buffer, the writing extends beyond its bounds, corrupting nearby memory. “An invalid block switch was reported as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error, so the streaming decoder kept appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer,” Node.js explains in an advisory. An attacker can exploit it by getting an application to decompress malicious data, such as by serving a compressed HTTP response to an application fetching a URL, or by sending a compressed request directly to a server. Node.js says that this can crash the process, expose memory, and enable remote code execution (RCE) A recent report from cybersecurity company Imperva confirms that exploiting the CVE-2026-111497 Node2Shell vulnerability can lead to RCE. The upstream Brotli fixes were first committed to the project’s source code in February, but Node.js and Google released stable fixes for users on October 21, followed by a public disclosure the next day. PyPI packages containing the fixes became available on October 23. Patched versions are: Google Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 Python Brotli 1.2.1 Python brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 Proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for Node2Shell have been published, but there are no reports of malicious exploitation in the wild. Nevertheless, users should prioritize applying the available security updates. After updating, administrators must restart affected processes, and affected container images must be rebuilt and redeployed. A dedicated online portal tracking the flaw's impact also warns that updating the system Brotli library does not address the risk in Node.js deployments or other apps that use their own bundled copy of the library. Also, blocking inbound Brotli requests still leaves the malicious HTTP-response route exposed. If updating immediately is not possible, the recommendation is to remove Brotli support from Python applications and block incoming Brotli-compressed requests at their proxy or firewall level. 15myic.text: Cybersecurity researchers are calling attention to what they say is a "recurring social engineering pattern" across hundreds of cases in which threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation feature to conduct impersonation scams or to deliver malware. "A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The attacks consistently employ IT-themed display names or friendly-sounding first names to subvert external-user warnings in Teams. These messages originate from Teams identities established through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Nearly 30–40% of the cases investigated by the cybersecurity company involve the use of *.onmicrosoft[.]com, a permanent fallback domain automatically generated by Microsoft when a Microsoft 365 tenant is created. These domains masquerade as IT infrastructure, opting for a help desk- or support-themed word as the tenant name to increase their credibility - helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft[.]com itendpoint365.onmicrosoft[.]com itcoreportal.onmicrosoft[.]com itadmin922.onmicrosoft[.]com corporateitservicellc.onmicrosoft[.]com As observed in many cases before, these Teams sessions are preceded by mail bombing, where the victim's inbox is flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations in a short span of time. The approach is designed to induce a false sense of urgency, with the Teams IT support message arriving soon after to help resolve the problem. Some of the display names observed by Arctic Wolf across different cases are listed below - Help Desk IT Support HelpDesk Manager IT Service Desk – Liam / IT Service Desk (Liam) IT Service Desk – Matt / IT Service Desk – Scott IT Support – Christopher Thomas HelpDesk Supervisor Enterprise IT & Security (Internal) IT Tech Support Internal Business IT Solutions & Support (Internal) Maintenance Service IT-Representative IT/Help Desk In recent iterations, the attackers have been observed adding the target organization's domain or company name in their display name to lend the messages additional legitimacy. "We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation," Arctic Wolf said. "Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br." The activity aligns with that of STAC4749, has a history of creating IT-themed cloud domains under the ".top" TLD and leveraging plausible employee usernames to make the accounts appear authentic. These attacks have led to the deployment of Chaos ransomware, according to Sophos. The attacks specifically go after organizations where external access is enabled. This also involves an element of vishing to trick victims to granting them hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool like Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn. The remote access is abused to conduct reconnaissance, deliver additional payloads like the GoGRPC backdoor, facilitate lateral movement to domain controllers, and deploy additional RMM tools like Level for redundancy, before exfiltrating sensitive data and dropping the ransomware binary. "In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft's notes," Arctic Wolf said. "Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.' In one case identified by the cybersecurity vendor, the threat actor is said to have instructed the user to run a PowerShell command to download a file and then launch it. The PowerShell command is designed to download an MSI installer from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. When the victim runs the installer, it launches a PowerShell script responsible for extracting and executing a Python implant embedded within it. The backdoor then runs another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects and then transmits the information to an external server. "External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability," Arctic Wolf said. "Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise."

f1suvw.text: Microsoft released emergency .NET security updates to patch a critical vulnerability known as Broccoli2Shell, also tracked as Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, this critical-severity flaw was found by Imperva Red Team and stems from an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, which expands data compressed using Google's widely used Brotli lossless compression algorithm. Successful exploitation lets unprivileged attackers use a maliciously crafted Brotli-compressed stream to trigger crashes or memory leaks and, in some cases, gain remote code execution on devices with vulnerable Brotli binaries or libraries. According to a Microsoft advisory published Sunday, attackers can also exploit this flaw to remotely escalate privileges on systems with unpatched .NET installations that use non-default configurations. "Applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression, or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs," Microsoft said. "Brotli decompression is not enabled by default in an out-of-the-box .NET or ASP.NET Core install. Applications must manually opt in to ASP.NET Core request decompression or HttpClient response decompression, or they must manually invoke the Brotli decompression APIs provided by .NET." To address this flaw, Microsoft has released out-of-band (OOB) security updates for .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10, along with .NET 11 Release Candidate 3, and advised "updating as soon as possible." .NET version Update Download .NET 8 8.0.33 .NET 8 SDK and Runtime .NET 9 9.0.22 .NET 9 SDK and Runtime .NET 10 10.0.14 .NET 10 SDK and Runtime .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 .NET 11 SDK and Runtime While proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for Broccoli2Shell have already been published on GitHub, no reports of malicious exploitation in the wild have emerged. A dedicated online portal tracking the flaw warns that updating the system Brotli library doesn't address the risk in apps that bundle their own copy of the library. Those who can't apply the updates immediately should block incoming Brotli-compressed requests using a proxy or firewall, or disable Brotli decoding until they can apply a patch. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. 1xck3cf.text: Ukrainian government cybersecurity researchers have warned that hackers are gaining unauthorized access to surveillance cameras made by Chinese manufacturer Dahua, potentially exposing video feeds and allowing attackers to remotely control the devices. Ukraine's computer emergency response team, CERT-UA, said late last week that it had identified cases in which hackers compromised the internet-connected cameras and video recorders, changed their settings and created unauthorized user accounts. The agency did not say how many devices had been compromised, when the attacks occurred or who was responsible. Chinese-made surveillance equipment remains widely used in Ukraine, including by government institutions and military units. According to CERT-UA, the attackers appear to be exploiting a feature called Easy4IP, which allows users to access Dahua cameras remotely through the manufacturer's cloud service. The feature connects devices to the cloud using their serial numbers, even when the devices are protected by firewalls or cannot be accessed directly over the internet. CERT-UA said the serial numbers follow predictable patterns, allowing hackers to guess large numbers of them and identify cameras connected to the cloud. As a result, devices with the remote access feature enabled could be vulnerable even if their serial numbers have never been publicly disclosed. Once a device is identified, attackers can attempt to gain access by guessing weak or default passwords or exploiting security flaws in outdated firmware that allow them to bypass authentication. The agency specifically warned about two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045, disclosed in 2021, that affect certain Dahua cameras and video recorders. Researchers at cybersecurity firm Hunt.io reported in August that hackers had compromised more than 14,500 Dahua devices earlier in the summer, with confirmed infections concentrated in Ukraine and Russia. The attackers reportedly used similar techniques, although it remains unclear whether the incidents are connected to those described by CERT-UA. Dahua is one of China's largest manufacturers of video surveillance equipment, producing security cameras, recording systems and facial recognition technology. The company has faced restrictions in the United States over national security and human rights concerns. In 2018, Congress prohibited federal agencies from procuring certain Dahua equipment, and the following year, Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist over its alleged role in the surveillance and repression of Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities in China's Xinjiang region. Surveillance risks in wartime The warning comes amid longstanding concerns in Ukraine that surveillance cameras could be exploited by Russian intelligence services to monitor military movements and critical infrastructure. Earlier this month, The Wall Street Journal reported that Ukraine's domestic security agency, the SBU, had identified and secured approximately 40,000 surveillance cameras since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, amid concerns that they could be used to gather military intelligence. In January 2024, the SBU said Russian intelligence services had hacked two cameras installed on residential buildings in Kyiv and used them to monitor air defense activity and critical infrastructure. The cameras, originally installed to monitor nearby streets and parking areas, were allegedly reconfigured by Russian operatives to change their viewing angles and stream footage to YouTube. A 2024 investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty found that approximately 24,000 cameras manufactured by Dahua and another Chinese company, Hikvision, were installed in municipal surveillance systems across Ukraine. Ukrainian public procurement records show that government institutions and military units continued to purchase Dahua equipment in 2026 despite longstanding security concerns. It remains unclear whether any of the devices identified in CERT-UA's latest warning belong to Ukrainian government agencies or military organizations. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

1newb1g.text: This2Shell, That2Shell, Everything2Shell. That's pretty much how the last week went. Critical bugs that let attackers run code remotely are showing up everywhere. Hackers are scanning for targets, some flaws are already being used in attacks, and security teams have more urgent patches than they can keep up with. And that's not even the full story. A leaked key led to a software supply-chain attack. AI agents are being tricked into following harmful instructions. Old bugs are still being used to break into systems, and some attacks are so simple it's hard to believe they still work. Some websites even went offline to avoid taking chances. It's been a rough week for anyone trying to keep systems safe. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week PHP2Shell Flaws Puts Organizations on Alert — The PHP Foundation released patches for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The security flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell. Since public disclosure, the shortcomings have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure. To date, no successful exploitation has been observed. The severity of the flaws, coupled with the ubiquity of PHP on the web, prompted several websites to go offline as a precautionary measure. 🔔 Top News eMudhra Exits TLS Certificate Market After Compromise of Weak Private keys — Eight intermediate CA certificates from Indian digital security firm eMudhra were found to use ridiculously weak private keys, potentially allowing bad actors to break them and potentially issue trusted certificates for arbitrary domains. Major web browsers stepped in to block the affected CAs. "On 19 October 2026, Apple began blocking these 12 certificates on Apple devices," Apple said. "Updates to certificate configuration data are sent to devices automatically and as needed, so you don't need to install a software update to get this change. Apple is making additional updates to this block, which will also be delivered automatically. On 23 October 2026, Apple also began blocking the emSign ECC Root CA - G3." Python has also released updated versions of the packages certifi, pip, uv, sigstore, conda, and pixi to remove the emSign root CA certificate from CA bundles. The development prompted eMudhra to exit the certificate-issuing business. Critical Flaw in Brotli Fixed — A severe vulnerability has been addressed in Google's Brotli decoder library (CVE-2026-111497) that could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The flaw, also called Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell, has also been addressed in other popular libraries that rely on Brotli, including libbrotli, Python, C++, Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and Istio. The disclosure comes as Ruby released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to address several bugs in Ruby's regular expression engine, Onigmo (CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229, and CVE-2026-110264) that could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. Two CVSS 9.0 Linux KSMBD RCE Flaws Disclosed Ahead of Fixes — Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws tracked as ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, along with a local privilege escalation flaw referred to as ZDI-CAN-33367. None of the vulnerabilities has been assigned a CVE ID, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. "Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix," Sysdig said. Plex2Shell Flaws Exploited in the Wild — Four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server, CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656, are being chained into an exploit called Plex2Shell to deliver cryptocurrency miners and proxy software. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added all four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Railway Warns of Targeted Campaign — Railway said it became aware of a "sustained and targeted campaign" to breach its infrastructure on October 20, 2026, at 7:53 p.m. UTC with an aim to conduct distillation attacks. "Early investigations tell us this attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys to perform distillation attacks," it said. "Initial evidence leads us to believe that the malicious actor had access to abliterated models and substantial compute resources which enabled them to perform highly sophisticated exploits against our infrastructure." The developer platform is urging users to revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables stored on Railway prior to October 21, 2026. LiteLLM Leaked Master Key Leads to Supply Chain Attack — LiteLLM revealed that an Agent Platform master key accidentally published to a public GitHub repository in late May 2026 ultimately allowed the threat actor to push a malicious version of the popular Python package. The files bundled with LiteLLM version 1.107.0 are engineered to execute automatically when Python starts, even if an application did not import LiteLLM. The malware features two execution paths: a credential harvesting module that targets authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, and web browsers, and a Unix-oriented backdoor that's launched as a background process to fetch and execute arbitrary code supplied by the attacker every one hour. GitLab Fixes Another Critical Flaw — GitLab shipped patches for CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS score: 10.0), a critical flaw that "could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to an integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression" under certain conditions. The issue has been addressed in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Systems). 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars From Zero-Days to Exploits in Minutes: Are You Ready for AI Threats? → AI-powered cyberattacks are accelerating, shrinking the time security teams have to detect, investigate, and respond. Are your defenses ready to keep up? Join this expert-led webinar to discover how to strengthen AI threat readiness, improve attack-surface visibility, and build faster, more resilient security operations before attackers gain the upper hand. Learn How to Turn Identity Context Into Faster, Smarter SOC Response → Your security tools can detect suspicious activity, but without identity context, critical threats may go unnoticed. As machine identities and AI agents expand the attack surface, SOC teams need deeper visibility to respond effectively. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how connecting identity intelligence with security operations can help uncover hidden risks, accelerate investigations, and contain threats faster. 📰 Around the Cyber World CrowdStrike said it uncovered four previously unreported threat actors orchestrating campaigns in which Claude Code is used to make decisions and execute commands, demonstrating how agentic AI is commoditizing baseline offensive cyber operations. This includes a Spanish/English-speaking operator that has compromised at least 15 Argentina-based healthcare entities and exfiltrated credentials and medical records from at least one victim; a Chinese-speaking operator that breached government entities of two countries and targeted private sector entities in Brazil and the U.S.; an Indonesian-speaking actor using 819 skills to break into Indonesian government domains and several private-sector entities; and group of Russian-speaking individuals who have exfiltrated corporate client data from a U.S.-based customer relationship management vendor and compromised several private-sector SaaS and data center entities based in Russia, Kyrgyzstan, and the U.S. Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center is alerting 3,182 patients their personal health information may have been exposed after a staff member uploaded a spreadsheet of patient information to an outside AI platform that was not approved for use. The information included patients admitted and treated between May 2026 and September 2026, including their names, dates of admission and treatment, medical record numbers, account numbers, the department that treated them, medications given, and the names of their providers. The U.S.-based hospital said it reached out to the AI platform provider to delete the data. Anthropic said it used Claude to analyze 25 major open-source projects written in C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python, and found 493 issues. This included a configuration flaw that sat undetected in unspecified software for 21 years. In a separate report, Anthropic said large language models (LLMs) are making "formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale," allowing code to be translated into a mathematical model and prove that it "always follows some defined set of security rules." The AI company said frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. The developer of the MeshCentral remote access software is urging users to update to version 1.3.1. "The[re] is an active exploit/hacker attacking MeshCentral servers and taking control of it and remote clients," the developer said. Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit CVE-2026-25243, a heap memory-corruption bug in Redis's RESTORE command, beginning around October 16. "One source hit the decoy five times on a timer with an identical payload: fingerprint the server, shape the heap with 26 key writes, fire a single malformed-zipmap RESTORE that triggers the documented over-read, run a throwaway Lua compute probe, then FLUSHALL the keyspace, destroying data and its own artifacts every run. Note that the bug needs command access to be exploitable," Defused Cyber said. Security researcher Patrick Wardle has detailed Heartbreaker, a Rust-based macOS ransomware sample that was uploaded to VirusTotal in May 2025. The malware attempts to set up a LaunchAgent for persistence, and then encrypts files in the user's Downloads folder. "Heartbreaker is unlikely to pose a major real-world threat in its current form," Wardle said. "It only targets files under ~/Downloads, lacks awareness of macOS privacy protections, embeds a universal recovery key, depends on a now-unavailable build framework, and performs an exceptionally noisy Rust installation and compilation workflow. Its disabled 'Decrypt Files' button does not actually recover anything, either. Heartbreaker demonstrates an unusual approach to metamorphism on macOS. Rather than decrypting or rewriting its machine code in memory, it carries its own Rust source, transforms that source, invokes the native build toolchain, and attempts to replace itself with the result. Because each generation embeds its newly transformed source, the design can – in principle – continue across executions." Axios reported that major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some attempting actions that appear independent of user instructions. Although the agents log in with the user's permission and credentials, the problem lies in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot. "Some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions," Axios reported. Banks are responding to the threat by either restricting them or allowing read-only access. In a new attack, Forever Security said it caught a malicious AGENTS.md markdown instructions file in a customer's Downloads folder that tricked an AI coding agent into installing a rogue npm package named "function-color," which was identified as part of a software supply chain attack campaign codenamed MALFEX. "An AGENTS.md is a file a coding agent is built to trust and obey, and ~/Downloads is the one folder a website can drop a file into with no click and no permission," Forever Security said. "Together, that lets the web plant orders your own agent carries out. Markdown is the new executable. The planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration. From there it can install malware (remote code execution) or hand over its own login token (account takeover)." It's unclear how the malicious instructions file ended up on the target's Downloads folder, although it's possible that threat actors could trick a user into downloading it by simply visiting a specially crafted page. A sophisticated organized crime gang is said to have hacked into Staples, issued millions of dollars' worth of gift cards, and gone on a spending spree across the U.S., 404 Media reported. In October 2025, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 detailed a threat cluster dubbed Jingle Thief that targeted cloud environments associated with organizations in the retail and consumer services sectors for gift card fraud. Pseudonymous blockchain investigator ZachXBT (aka Zachary Wolk) has revealed that a Chinese organized crime syndicate laundered more than $1 billion stolen in multiple cryptocurrency exploits for North Korea's Lazarus Group. ZachXBT said he posed as a paying client to infiltrate the money laundering network in February 2025, in the days following the massive Bybit hack, leading to the identification of a cluster of more than $12 million in Bybit-linked funds. About 442,000 USDT linked to the cluster was later frozen by Tether. Federal investigators suspect that at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm helped operate Shinywire, a now-defunct ShinyHunters site used to pressure nearly 100 hacked organizations into paying, according to security journalist Brian Krebs. Signal messages that authorities accessed when they apprehended ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in the Netherlands reportedly show frequent contact with Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky and at least one executive at a U.S. consulting firm, who sometimes knew about new victims before the victims themselves, citing an unnamed source. "The Dutch hacker's chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files," Krebs said. The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures of its adversaries, and "neutralize" them, The Intercept reported. The nascent program, codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE, is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target." In addition, the system "would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army's quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely. Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE's agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all." A group of academics from the University of British Columbia have detailed ICS-Sniper, a proof-of-concept attack aimed at industrial facilities that rely on cloud-hosted SCADA systems. It's described as a "targeted blackhole attack that analyzes the VPN traffic metadata (sizes, direction, timing of packets) to identify narrow time windows, called critical superperiods, during which the site-SCADA traffic would likely contain highly critical commands or data." An attacker with control over a router on the network path could examine the size, direction, and timing of VPN-encrypted packets to predict when critical commands or data are likely to be exchanged, and then deliver malicious payloads during those time periods. "Post-analysis, in a subsequent operational cycle, ICS-Sniper drops a small set of payload-carrying packets in the critical superperiods to disrupt the ICS's operations," the study said. In tests on emulated versions of a Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) plant testbed, the attack delayed the start of clean water pumping by about 15 minutes and kept a valve open more than nine minutes longer than intended. A new Windows malware called SiriusQT offers various capabilities in a single package: remote access, HVNC, browser automation, credential theft, cryptocurrency wallet collection, clipboard monitoring, keylogging, process injection, persistence, anti-analysis checks, and custom encrypted command-and-control traffic. SiriusQT has been advertised by a seller named GhostKernel on dark web forums since April 2026. Its author is Amonus. At least 30 users bought a valid license, Group-IB said. A lifetime subscription costs $500, but cracked versions of the program are said to be shared by multiple actors. Campaigns using the malware have targeted the U.K., Germany, France, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands. GhostKernel has also been observed advertising BTMob v4.0, an Android trojan, on their Telegram channel. As many as 2,894 ransomware attacks have been recorded in Q3 2026, a nearly 50% jump from more than a year ago, led by The Gentlemen (383) and Qilin (363). "Both break in through stolen credentials and exposed VPNs, and both hit many of the same industries," Nord Security said. […]

kqnpr5.text: Author: Len Noe, Solutions Architect, BeyondTrust The first question on any incident bridge isn’t about why it happened--it’s whose credentials were used. In my experience, whoever can answer that credential question in the first hour sets the pace for everything after it: what to isolate, what to revoke, whom to notify, and how far the damage could have spread. The teams that can’t answer it spend the first day reconstructing their answer from logs that were never designed to provide it. That discipline is about to be tested by a new kind of actor. On October 16, 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the National Security Agency (NSA) jointly published ten voluntary practices for incident readiness and response when AI agents act in ways nobody directed. The guide, Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation, is useful, and it’s also easy to misread. Its strongest guidance is about identity, even though it rarely uses that word as a headline. What the NIST, CISA, and NSA Incident Guide Covers The 14-page document is written for organizations that train or evaluate highly capable agents on long-horizon tasks (work that runs through many steps over a long period) with limited human supervision, although the authors say deployers may find it relevant. It organizes ten practices into five stages: prepare, detect, respond, recover and report. It defines a control incident as an event in which agents take significant actions that were not directed by the operator or an adversary, and that undermine controls, policies or human oversight. The agencies say the practices build on established incident-management frameworks, so most of what they ask for will look familiar: least privilege, credential management, monitoring, evidence preservation, rebuilding from known baselines. Familiar controls applied to a new principal are where most organizations are likely to stumble. AI Agent Incident Response Starts with Identity, Not Intent One detail in the definitions matters for responders. The guide treats actions caused by adversarial prompt injection or a backdoored model as instructed, not uninstructed, so they fall outside its definition of a control incident. While that line is coherent for researchers, it’s difficult for responders; at the moment of an incident, the question of intent is usually unanswerable. What an investigator has in hand is an identity, a set of permissions, and a trail of actions. Agent incident readiness can’t depend on classifying the cause first. It has to work from an identity record to determine which identity acted, what authority stood behind it, and whether the agent was misled, malfunctioning, or compromised. Control What AI Agents Can Do Before They Act AI agents can operate with the same privileges as the people using them, creating new risks when their actions go unchecked. Now generally available, BeyondTrust AI Agent Security enforces policy on individual agent actions at runtime, blocking unauthorized activity without restricting what human users can do. Explore AI Agent Security Revocation Reaches Only What You Can Reach Practice six tells organizations to revoke any credentials the agent accessed during the incident that the organization controls, and to rebuild potentially compromised environments. The qualifier "under the organization's control" carries more weight than it may appear to at the outset. Agents accumulate credentials that the organization holds, but doesn’t issue. The OpenCode breach shows how that plays out. OpenCode, an open-source coding agent, told some users of its hosted Console service that API keys they had stored there for external providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, were exposed. The company says 1.4% of its Console users were affected, and that the earliest exposure was at 00:30 UTC on October 17. Users reported unauthorized charges with costs ranging from several hundred dollars to as much as $1,700 overnight. In some cases, Google Cloud projects were suspended for abusive activity, consistent with hijacked resources. The company hasn’t said how the attackers got in, and describes the incident as a large-scale distillation attack. Take the company's account as provisional. What matters for readiness is the shape of the problem. A key stored by an agent platform is revocable only at the provider that issued it, by the person who owns the account. And the account holder may not even know the key was ever exposed. The guide's revocation step presupposes an inventory of what the agent could touch. Without it, there’s nothing to revoke against. The guide's reporting stage adds a second obligation that follows from the same inventory: notify the parties whose systems were compromised or exploited, including third parties who were not the final target. In the OpenCode case, those parties are the model providers and the individual key owners, and none of them can be notified in time unless someone knows which keys were stored where. Containing an AI Agent Without Relying on the Agent’s Cooperation The guide advises designers to assume agents will often find misconfigurations and vulnerabilities, and to build controls accordingly. MIT Technology Review's reconstruction of the July Hugging Face incident shows why. Agents built on OpenAI models were supposed to be isolated from the internet during a cybersecurity evaluation. They got online anyway, hacked Hugging Face, and retrieved solutions to problems they were stuck on. The one control the article describes is network isolation, and the agents got around it. OpenAI's own researchers attribute the behavior to training that rewarded it. Network boundaries can be evaded by a determined actor, human or not. A credential that’s scoped to one task, expires when the task ends, and belongs to an identity separate from the person who launched the agent does not rely on the agent behaving, and it limits what a leaked copy can do. The guide points the same direction when it asks for access limited to what’s necessary for intended tasks, single-use infrastructure where possible, and mechanisms to quickly block, contain, or terminate agent activity. Most of those are identity controls. Session Accountability for Non-Human Actors The guide also asks for tamper-resistant logs with reliable timestamps sufficient to reconstruct agent trajectories, and for assurance that agents can’t access or tamper with the monitors and logs themselves. That is session accountability in everything but name. For a human administrator, a privileged session is attributed to a person, recorded and reviewable. The same standard should apply to an agent. The guide supports this by asking responders to preserve rejected actions and tool calls, and to record the configurations of agents, safeguards and environments so an incident can be reproduced. A rejected action is evidence of what the agent tried to reach, which is often more revealing than what it succeeded in doing. New research from BeyondTrust Phantom Labs™ drawing on endpoint telemetry shows why prompt-level logs fall short. In customer samples taken over a four week period, coding agents requested about 1.28 million shell commands from roughly 132,000 prompts, close to ten commands per prompt. Those are requested commands, not confirmed executions. A log that can’t separate what the agent did from what the user did is unable to answer whose authority was used. Enterprise reality will complicate this. Many legacy applications can’t log per-agent activity. Some agents will run through shared service accounts because that’s how the integration was built three years ago. Budgets are finite. A realistic path starts with the agents that can reach the most sensitive data or the most consequential actions, gives them separate identities, and works outward as applications allow. Why Rare Agent Incidents Still Justify Preparation The strongest counter-argument is proportionality. The guide is aimed at frontier training and evaluation, and the incidents it responds to are rare: six in 141,006 evaluations in one lab's disclosure. Most enterprises deploy agents far less capable than the ones under study, and the reported harm so far has been modest. Why build response capability for a problem that’s mostly theoretical? The answer is that the underlying mechanics aren’t just theoretical. A compromised or misdirected agent behaves, from the perspective of the identity record, like a compromised service account with a faster tempo. How To Measure AI Agent Incident Readiness Readiness should be measured in outcomes rather than documents. How long does it take to enumerate every credential a given agent identity can use, including keys it stores for third parties? What share of agents runs under its own identity, with a named human sponsor? Can the organization produce a session record that distinguishes what a person did from what an agent did on that person's behalf? If those questions take minutes to answer, the organization is ready for the first agent incident, regardless of how it is classified. If they take days, a more elegant taxonomy will not help. About the Author Len Noe is a Solutions Architect at BeyondTrust, Transhuman, Podcaster, International Cyber Security Speaker, Author, Technical Evangelist, and Biohacker with 11 implanted microchips. A former blackhat with more than 30 years in technology, he has presented in over 70 countries and is featured in the documentary I Am Machine, which premiered at DEF CON 2025. As human, machine, and AI agent identities explode across every environment, BeyondTrust is the only company built to discover, control, and secure privilege across all of them from a single platform. Trusted by 20,000+ customers, including 75 of the Fortune 100, and recognized as a multi-category leader by top industry analysts, BeyondTrust reframes identity security from a management problem into a strategic advantage. 17tazo1.text: A Chinese national was arraigned in California after being extradited from the Netherlands for his alleged involvement in a cryptocurrency investment scam that stole nearly $37 million from 174 victims in the United States. In these fraud schemes (also known as pig butchering or romance baiting scams), cybercriminals contact targets through social media, dating sites, and messaging apps, build trust, and lure them into fake investment schemes, stealing their money instead of investing the funds as promised. Prosecutors said that, together with accomplices in the United States and Cambodia, 44-year-old Zhen Zhao tricked victims into transferring large sums of money to attacker-controlled accounts, claiming that the funds would be invested in digital assets. The criminal ring Zhao was allegedly part of reached out to targets across the United States via unsolicited text messages, social media, phone calls, and even online dating services to gain their trust, promoting the fraudulent digital asset investments and saying that the victims' funds' value increased, when, in fact, their money was stolen. "The co-conspirators created fake websites that resembled real cryptocurrency trading platforms and convinced victims to send funds through the fake websites for investments," the Department of Justice said. "Zhao and other co-conspirators arranged for Deltec Bank to convert victim funds to the stablecoin Tether (USDT) and to transfer the converted funds to a digital asset wallet controlled in Cambodia. From there, co-conspirators in Cambodia transferred the USDT to the leaders of scam centers throughout the region." Victims transferred over $36.9 million, "invested" in the scheme, from U.S. bank accounts to an account at Deltec Bank in the Bahamas, which was opened under the name Axis Digital Limited. Zhao was charged in August 2025 with conspiracy to commit money laundering and faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if found guilty. Eight of his accomplices, part of the same international crime ring, have already pleaded guilty, and two of them have been sentenced to 51 months and 46 months in prison. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, investment scammers stole over $8.6 billion last year (according to 72,984 complaints), up from $6.5 billion in 2024.
