iaza16.text: Two critical flaws in Wasmtime, a WebAssembly runtime that can be built into other software, could allow a malicious WebAssembly module to escape the sandbox intended to contain it, the project's maintainers say. An attacker would first need a vulnerable Wasmtime build to compile a module they control, and one of the flaws affects only ARM64 systems. Fixed versions were released on October 19 and 20, and the maintainers have not reported any attacks. Wasmtime runs WebAssembly code outside web browsers. Both bugs are in Cranelift, the compiler it uses by default to turn WebAssembly into machine code. Wasmtime's maintainers at the Bytecode Alliance rated each flaw 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale in advisories published on October 19. CVE-2026-115889 affects Wasmtime across all processor architectures. CVE-2026-115893 affects only ARM64, also called aarch64. The sandbox is meant to keep a module inside set limits. A module can only use its own memory and the host functions it is given, and its code can only jump to checked locations. Because both flaws need a module the attacker controls, the risk is highest for services that compile modules written by other people. Fastly, for example, says its Compute platform runs customer code using Wasmtime. The advisories do not name any affected services or specify what an attacker could access after escaping the sandbox. Neither flaw was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as of October 26. Which Versions Are Affected The two flaws were fixed at different times, so whether your version is affected depends on your release line and, for one flaw, your processor architecture. Wasmtime version CVE-2026-115889 (any architecture) CVE-2026-115893 (ARM64 only) What to do Before 36.0.19 (includes 24.x) Affected Affected Update to 36.0.19, or move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 36.0.19 Fixed Fixed None needed for these flaws 37.0.0 through 42.x Affected Affected Move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 43.0.0 through 47.x Not affected Affected Move to 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 48.0.0 through 48.0.6 Not affected Affected Update to 48.0.7 48.0.7 Not affected Fixed None needed for these flaws 49.0.0 through 49.0.3 Not affected Affected Update to 49.0.4 49.0.4, and 50.0.0 or later Not affected Fixed None needed for these flaws Wasmtime supports long-term support (LTS) releases, which are numbered in multiples of 12, for two years. Other releases get two months. Security fixes are guaranteed for supported releases. Only the 36, 48, 49, and 50 release lines are still supported. Every other line, including the 24.x LTS line whose support ended on August 20, 2026, got no fix. ARM64 hosts that updated to 36.0.7, 42.0.2, or 43.0.1 in April to fix an earlier Cranelift sandbox escape on ARM64 are still affected by CVE-2026-115893. What to Do Update to the fixed release for your line: 36.0.19, 48.0.7, or 49.0.4. Wasmtime 50.0.0, released on October 20, is fixed for both flaws. Hosts on an unsupported line need to move to one of these releases. Wasmtime can be built into other programs as a library, so updating the command-line tool does not fix them. Each program that includes Wasmtime needs to be rebuilt with a fixed version. Neither advisory lists a workaround. Until a host is updated, the risk comes from any module an outsider can supply. Both flaws are listed in RustSec, the database the cargo-audit tool uses to check Cargo.lock files, as RUSTSEC-2026-0380 and RUSTSEC-2026-0379. As of October 26, GitHub's advisory database had a reviewed entry for CVE-2026-115889 but none for CVE-2026-115893. GitHub says only reviewed entries trigger Dependabot alerts, so Dependabot users should not expect an alert for the ARM64 flaw. Spin, an open-source tool for building serverless WebAssembly apps that runs on Wasmtime, moved to Wasmtime 50.0.0 in version 4.2.4 on October 21. How the Two Flaws Work CVE-2026-115889 comes from how Cranelift stored the numbers it uses to track values inside a function. Before version 43, it packed these numbers into 24-bit fields, and in release builds, a number too large for its field overflowed without any error. Cranelift could then refer to the wrong value, producing incorrect machine code. A very large WebAssembly function, or one crafted to use many values, can use this to force type confusion and escape the sandbox, according to the advisory. Wasmtime's main development line had already removed the problem. A change merged on February 18 widened the fields to 32 bits and shipped in Wasmtime 43.0.0 on March 20. Its description presented it as a way to compile larger functions and did not mention security. The 36.x LTS line got the same change on October 19. The advisory does not say when the security impact was recognized. CVE-2026-115893 involves br_table, a WebAssembly instruction that jumps to one of many places in the code based on an index. An index outside the table goes to a default target. On ARM64, Cranelift sent these out-of-range indexes to the default with a branch that can only reach about 1 MiB. A br_table with more than about 256,000 targets made the jump table too big for that reach, so the branch silently pointed to the wrong place. Any Wasmtime engine on ARM64 with default settings "can be forced to jump to arbitrary code by a user-controlled Wasm module," the advisory says. The bug has been present since Wasmtime first supported ARM64 in 2020. The fix sends out-of-range indexes through the jump table itself, so no long branch is needed. Fixed versions also refuse to compile a br_table with more than 65,520 targets.

1nzpm62.text: Every SOC struggles with a pile of alerts. Very few of those alerts explain how an attack started or how it progressed. Network data, like that from a network detection and response (NDR) platform, connects individual alerts into one timeline, and it feeds the defensive systems that can tie all events together into one coordinated view. SOC teams often first see the shape of an intrusion through a series of smaller alerts that are triggered (e.g., when a signature matches a known malware hash, a threshold flags an unusual spike in failed logins, or an endpoint agent detects suspicious activity). When viewed through the SIEM dashboard, an attack often begins as a series of distinct events with related or overlapping timestamps. Artificial intelligence has accelerated modern attacks, enabling attackers to automate reconnaissance, craft targeted payloads, and execute scripts in seconds. Yet, speed does not obfuscate the need for stealth. To evade detection, adversaries deliberately draw out operations, hide inside standard admin tooling, and work in the quiet intervals between alarms. Adversaries might spend days or weeks inside an enterprise environment before an action generates a high-priority security alert. When an alert finally surfaces, it doesn’t necessarily mark the start of a compromise. It may, in fact, be one event in a much longer sequence. Analysts who investigate only the triggering event may miss the chained activity that explains how the intrusion developed. The anatomy of silent progression Between initial access and a high-severity alert, adversary activity can blend into ordinary business operations. Adversaries understand the operational limits of security teams, and they exploit them; if every DNS query, LDAP request, SMB connection, or authentication attempt generated an investigation, SOC queues would quickly become (even more) unmanageable. Tradecraft purposely takes advantage of that reality. Adversaries can spread reconnaissance across hours or distributed sources. Instead of launching an obvious scan, they may use a compromised account to query a domain controller over LDAP at a modest pace to map users, groups, and systems. A handful of Kerberos service ticket requests can yield credentials to crack offline, well outside the SOC’s view. Valid credentials then open the door to SMB or RDP, the same services administrators rely on every day, and the attacker moves from host to host. Files may be gathered on one internal system and compressed. Later, that system may reach an external destination over HTTPS or DNS at regular intervals, with just enough variation in timing to resemble normal traffic as it exfiltrates data. Each step borrows something the business already depends on. While individual actions may not necessarily look suspicious, their significance often emerges from relationships and sequences. For instance, a host that communicates with a new system once may be unremarkable. A host that queries several internal services, authenticates to a peer, establishes an SMB session, and then connects to an external destination presents a different investigative picture. The activity becomes more meaningful when viewed across time. When siloed tools see only slices of this type of transaction, they might miss the bigger picture. Context only becomes readily apparent when activities and signals are combined and correlated via network observation. What’s more, attackers increasingly use AI to automate reconnaissance and move faster. Defenders need to apply AI to the same problem, but it needs detailed network evidence from an NDR to search. The evidence between the alerts SecOps teams don’t have to turn detection thresholds down and drown analysts in more alerts just to spot adversary activity. Doing so would be untenable anyway. A SOC can’t investigate every DNS query, authentication request, or connection as though it were an incident. In addition, many teams operate with tools that show an alert fired yet offer sparse detail on how the activity behind it unfolded. To prevent blindspots, SOC teams can retain the underlying network telemetry so an analyst can go back and review what happened when an alert, outage, or other signal gives them a reason to look. However, that requires more than knowing when two systems exchanged traffic. Protocol-aware network data from an NDR platform can show the kind of interaction that took place, who or what participated, when it happened, and how that relationship evolved over time. For instance, if a workstation triggers an endpoint alert at 2:14 p.m. the alert may show an analyst what happened on the endpoint at that moment. Network evidence from an NDR can extend the timeline and answer a few crucial questions: Was the workstation querying an unusual domain earlier that day? Did it authenticate to another system or establish SMB connections to internal peers? Did those systems communicate with additional hosts? Did the workstation later establish an encrypted session with an external destination? Each individual event may have perfectly legitimate explanations. It’s only in combination, though, that the sequence provides a different level of context. For an investigator, that context helps establish whether the endpoint event was an isolated problem or one discrete stage in a broader progression. For an AI-assisted investigation, the context derived from NDR provides the evidence needed to search for related activity across hosts, users, protocols, and time rather than treating each alert as a separate event. Why this matters for the AI SOC AI in the SOC changes the economics of an investigation. While a human analyst has to decide which systems, users, sessions, and time periods deserve attention, an AI-assisted SOC can search across that same breadth of evidence much faster, bringing relevant data into one view in minutes rather than hours. Correlation and analysis can happen asynchronously, allowing analysts to review and query a broader set of data much sooner. When AI handles the synthesis, the process of identifying patterns is faster, still. When an attacker is patient, methodically timing actions across longer periods, evidence might be spread across hundreds of seemingly ordinary transactions. Since a human analyst can’t reasonably manually investigate each piece of evidence, the more practical approach is to construct an automated workflow in an NDR platform to identify context and look for relationships, then give the analyst the evidence so they can make a judgement call. The outcome is more activity examined, across more systems, over a longer period. The benefits are: Time savings: manual work is significantly reduced Clearer insights: more context can be surfaced by advanced algorithms searching across thousands of data points Better decisions: analysts can focus on making strategic risk decisions instead of picking apart pieces of alerts The same process can help with operational issues. If an application goes down, for example, network telemetry will show which services were communicating, where communications began to fail, which dependencies were affected, and what changed around the event. If the cause turns out to be malicious, the investigation already has a record of the activity. Beyond individual alerts Alerts give analysts a place to start an investigation. They do not necessarily explain what happened before it, what happened after it, what’s happening simultaneously, or whether other activity in the environment is related. Issues that appear routine in isolation may look very different when data is correlated and context is added. Network telemetry provides the surrounding evidence needed to build critical context. Protocol-aware data from the NDR preserves the details of network interactions, including both ends of a communication, the protocols and services involved, timestamps for those interactions, and how interactions change over time. It’s the telemetry that gives automated investigation workflows a broader body of evidence to work from when triaging a high-priority alert. With evidence available for automated analysis, AI agents can correlate activity over time, connect communications between systems, and surface sequences that would otherwise remain separate innocuous-looking events. The ability to apply context across disparate communications and sequences is what allows SOC teams to find the riskiest activity. Without this evidence, individual alerts and sequences may continue to present as harmless. Attackers have already identified the opportunity; now it’s time for defenders to apply the same principles and keep up. About Corelight: Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. Learn more about Corelight at https://corelight.com/cp/elitedefense

12wg4pf.text: Kali Linux has released version 2026.3, its third release this year, featuring six new hacking tools, desktop environment improvements, refreshed build scripts, and more. This Linux distribution is available as an installable OS or as a live environment and supports a wide range of hardware, including Raspberry Pi devices and Android phones via Kali NetHunter. Kali is designed for ethical hackers and cybersecurity professionals who want to perform red-teaming, penetration testing, security assessments, and network research. New tool added to Kali Linux 2026.3 In this release, the Kali Team has updated 126 packages, added new libraries, and upgraded the kernel from 6.19 to 7.1.5. It has also added 6 new tools, including: dalfox - Powerful open-source XSS scanner and utility focused on automation katana - Next-generation crawling and spidering framework qsreplace - Accept URLs on stdin, replace all query string values with a user-supplied value rustscan - Modern port scanner sdrangel - Qt-based SDR front-end for various devices snaffler-ng - SMB share credential and sensitive data scanner Desktop environment updates Kali Linux 2026.3 also brings desktop environment updates, including KDE Plasma 6.7 and new icons. KDE Plasma 6.7 includes performance and integrated Intel GPU power-usage improvements, plus workflow optimizations. These changes include per-screen virtual desktops that let you create separate workspaces on the same desktop for web browsers, terminals, and documentation. "Moving around those desktops is also quicker from the Overview, while support for additional Wayland protocols and portals continues to improve the experience on modern Linux setups," the Kali devs explained. "Network connections can now be duplicated, which can save some time when working with several similar network configurations, and System Monitor has received further refinements." KDE Plasma 6.7 (Kali Linux) ​Build-scripts refresh This version also refreshes the build scripts used to generate official Kali images, with support for Docker and Podman containers and more consistency across platforms. "We've brought consistency to our build-scripts across platforms. Each one now has the same features, command-line arguments, structure and layout (where possible), and the same look and feel," the Kali Linux 2026.3 announcement explains. "Would you rather build inside a container? That is now supported, with both Docker and Podman! Each refreshed build-script comes with build-in-container.sh, which detects which container engine you have, creates the build container, and then runs the build from within it." While not all build scripts have been refreshed before Kali Linux 2026.3 was released, the team aims to have them all ready for Kali 2026.4 and wants to automate builds and workflows in the next stage of this process. How to get Kali Linux 2026.3 To start using Kali Linux 2026.3, you can upgrade your existing installation, select a platform, or directly download ISO images for new installs and live distributions. To switch, you can use the following commands to upgrade to the latest version: echo "deb http://http.kali.org/kali kali-rolling main contrib non-free non-free-firmware" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list sudo apt update && sudo apt -y full-upgrade cp -vrbi /etc/skel/. ~/ [ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && sudo reboot -f If you're using Kali on Windows Subsystem for Linux, you should upgrade to WSL 2 for better support of graphical applications. To check the WSL version on your system, run wsl -l -v in a Windows Command Prompt. After upgrading to Kali Linux 2026.3, you can check whether the process was successful using the following command: grep VERSION /etc/os-release. The complete changelog for the Kali Linux 2026.3 release is available on Kali's website. yx760k.text: A rentable Android spyware kit called uCreator takes over Telegram and WeChat accounts by hiding its code inside working copies of the two apps, researcher Ovi found. It only reaches people who install one of these tampered copies, spread outside the official app stores, or who run WeChat inside the kit makers' own container app. The kit's Telegram part matches Baohuo, a backdoor that Doctor Web reported in October 2025. Doctor Web found Baohuo in tampered copies of Telegram X, an Android app from Telegram. At the time, the company estimated that more than 58,000 devices were infected. The Hacker News compared the two reports. Doctor Web's technical description of Baohuo lists the same code namespace, com.ucreator.tgjar, the same command-and-control (C2) server, and matching command names as Ovi's analysis. Ovi's analysis, published October 21, 2026, does not mention Doctor Web's findings, and Doctor Web did not name the kit. It is not clear whether the kit's makers or one of their customers ran the campaign Doctor Web tracked. Who Is Exposed The tampered apps spread through sideloading, where a person installs an app file directly instead of from an app store, and through social engineering, Ovi found. He could not confirm how every victim was infected. A second route is the kit makers' own container app, called 洋葱盒子 ("Onion Box"), which runs other apps inside itself. Some of the tampered Telegram X copies use the same package name as the real app on Google Play, so the name alone does not give them away. Doctor Web found that Baohuo copies had been spreading since mid-2024 through in-app ads that led to fake app store sites. Those sites promoted Telegram X as a dating and video chat app. The sites' banners were available only in Portuguese, for users in Brazil, and in Indonesian. Even so, Doctor Web's 2025 map of infected devices by country put India first, at 22.8%, ahead of Brazil at 20.5% and Indonesia at 9.6%. Baohuo copies also turned up in the third-party stores APKPure, ApkSum and AndroidP. On APKPure, one was listed under the official developer's name, although its digital signature was different. Ovi got access to one of the kit's command servers. It held data on victims apparently located in China and the United States, but not enough for a reliable count. He calls his report "an analysis of technical capability, not a measurement of victim impact." The apparent targets, still unconfirmed, are users of mobile wallets and messaging apps in China and Southeast Asia, including WeCom, QQ, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, GCash and MoMo. He found code supporting about 20 apps, but has published code only for Telegram and WeChat. The kit's hooking engine is the part that lets its code intercept an app's functions. Ovi checked it on a Pixel 10 Pro running Android 17. It could not find an internal Android function it relies on, because newer Android versions changed that function. Another tool, Frida, could still hook apps the same way on that phone. Ovi therefore describes this as extra work for the kit's makers, not proof that Android 17 blocks the attack. The newest sample, dated July 29, 2026, still carried the old engine. He recovered samples built for Android 16 but did not report testing that version. He has not tested phones from Chinese makers. How It Takes Over a Telegram Account Inside a tampered Telegram app, the kit's code starts with the app and runs with the app's own identity and permissions, Ovi found. That gives it the same access as the signed-in app. Each tampered app also runs a local command server inside itself. The code for each target app is downloaded after installation, which makes the installer file harder to analyze on its own. Attackers can send any database query to the app's message store and get chat history back. Telegram's two-step verification (2FA) password is entered in the app, which uses it to generate a login proof on the phone. The kit hooks that step and copies the password in readable form before the app hashes it. With the password, the code can reset the account's logged-in sessions, change the linked phone number, or delete the account. Other parts of the code are designed to lock out the owner while keeping the attacker's session alive. The code can also hide the attacker's session from the device list that the tampered app shows the user. Doctor Web's description of Baohuo covers the same device-hiding. The backdoor also sends the account's phone number, name and password to its server every three minutes. Neither Ovi nor Doctor Web says whether a hidden session still appears on the user's other, untampered Telegram apps. Neither gives steps for securing an account taken over this way. Ovi says the code shows what the kit can do, not that attackers have used every step from start to finish. Earlier Android malware has also run legitimate apps with attacker code inside them. FjordPhantom did this to banking apps through virtualization in 2023, and so did the GodFather banking trojan in 2025. Ovi argues the kit is different because it is sold as a product. Customers can steer it remotely against any app its makers write a module for. The WeChat Part and the Leaked Back End For WeChat, the kit can also use app virtualization, running the unchanged app inside its own container, Ovi found. A command copies out the account's login identity. The app's data is then zipped and uploaded, and a bundled login script is used to clone the account. This part goes after the account itself, not its chat history. Ovi and another researcher, Jurre, also found the back-end code behind the kit on a self-hosted GitLab server. It was the one part of the setup not limited to approved IP addresses. The code shows a cloud console that merchants and resellers rent. Every command carries the customer's ID, so each customer aims its own share of the phone fleet at victims it picks. Commands go to phones in the kit's phone farm, a set of phones the operation controls, and to victims' phones. There, the kit captures login authorizations, adds friends in bulk, collects contact and profile data, and backs up whole accounts. A scheduler sets time windows, random daily limits, and per-account budgets, so the activity looks human and gets past the platforms' risk checks. The code calls this "account cultivation," in Ovi's translation. About three dozen developers, all working on China time, appear in the code's history, and some were still adding changes in October 2026. The leaked back end covers personal WeChat and WeCom accounts. Ovi says it did not appear to cover Telegram, and only one of several GitLab servers was exposed. Who Is Behind It Ovi ties parts of the operation to three companies in Hunan province, China. One is linked to the kit's brand website and a server certificate, another to a government website filing for a command server, and the third to the signature on the kit's Windows control program. He says a shared owner is "plausible, but remains unproven." The makers' own name for the product is YingGai, and the product line appears in records dating back to September 2021. The samples Ovi studied date from 2024 to July 2026. Ovi assumes the kit is used for financially motivated crime, given its focus on wallets and one-time passcodes. Doctor Web described Baohuo as "a tool for boosting the number of subscribers in Telegram channels." Indicators of Compromise The kit leaves two traces on a phone that Ovi calls reliable. One is a code file, TgJarPine.dex, in the assets of some tampered Telegram copies. The other is the original app copy that LSPatch, an off-the-shelf patching tool, leaves at cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk. Because that second trace comes from LSPatch itself, it can also appear in apps patched with the tool for other reasons. When The Hacker News checked DNS records on October 23, 2026, several of the kit's server and download domains no longer resolved. The domain for its version-upload server still pointed to 121.37.194[.]194. ox0ka9.text: Two critical RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively tracked as PHP2Shell, have been successfully exploited in the wild. The malicious activity was caught by Adel Karimi, detection and response lead at Perplexity, whose honeypots recorded evidence of confirmed remote code execution against an Apache mod_php installation running PHP 8.4.26. "This is now confirmed RCE with usable memory disclosure, not just a crash followed by a suspicious process. The response delivered an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, and a function address derived from that dump using the public exploit's offsets appears in the subsequent execution payload," Karimi shared. "The client acknowledged the full response; the shell command then ran about 1.6 ms after the execution request's final captured byte." Karimi's findings were also confirmed by Expel threat researcher Marcus Hutchins, who has been tracking a stream of alleged successful PHP2Shell exploitation reports. "This is by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild php2shell exploitation I've seen so far. Deep technical breakdown of a successful exploitation attempt against an Apache mod_php installation running PHP 8.4.26," Hutchins said. ​The PHP security team patched the PHP2Shell flaws on Wednesday, October 21, one day after asking admins to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they became available. While details on the PHP2Shell security flaws (including the CVE IDs and mitigation advice provided to some critical infrastructure providers) leaked online and some proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits were published before the patches went live, the PHP security team said that none were functional. Additionally, multiple cybersecurity companies (including Cloudflare, Hadrian, watchTowr, Previdian, and Patchstack) detected exploitation attempts before public disclosure, but flagged them all as unsuccessful. Security researchers at Amazon Threat Intelligence also spotted attackers targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities four days before security patches were released. However, until Karimi's findings, the malicious activity was "limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and use of non-working exploits, with no known compromises," according to Dataminr's Threat Research and Cyber Engineering (TRACE) team. On Friday, the PHP security team also shared mitigation measures for a new RCE vulnerability (tracked as CVE-2026-115560) that has no patch and can only be exploited when targeting systems "with an unusual combination of configuration and application code." Until a security patch is released, the PHP devs advised admins to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 to block potential attacks, a mitigation already recommended before patches for the PHP2Shell security updates were released. PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a web development language used by roughly 70% of all websites on the Internet, with more than 5.1 million PHP hosts exposed online and roughly 3.8 million with at least one port open to attacks, according to recent VirusTotal estimates. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. Get the report

136bw3p.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a Microsoft 365 campaign that has been observed leveraging an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) relay to capture sign-in sessions and then replay the stolen tokens to break into email accounts at 79 organizations. Huntress, which observed the activity between July 14 and September 22, 2026, said it detected 497 successful Microsoft 365 sign-in events across the victim organizations from over 200,000 login attempts, with the attackers ultimately compromising 97 accounts and registering 48 rogue Entra devices. "Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range," Huntress researchers Andrea Hatcher, Susannah Matt, Matt Poto, and Andrew Schwartz said. The attack has been found to employ an AitM login page, which sits between the victims and legitimate Microsoft infrastructure to capture the entered credentials and MFA codes and relay the information to the real login page. The end goal is to collect the access token issued by Microsoft following the sign-in process so that it doesn't have to bypass MFA a second time. The "proof of login" token is subsequently replayed by the attacker from their own devices within minutes to conduct automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. The approach has been codenamed token spraying, as it involves the attacker replaying many stolen tokens at scale across several organizations in a manner that's analogous to password spraying. Upon gaining successful access, the attackers moved to add their own authenticator app as a form of persistence to complete MFA challenges for new sign-ins and overcome scenarios where the stolen session token expires or gets revoked by the victim. In no less than 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were removed and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in. In one case observed on July 21, 2026, the threat actors activated a new authenticator app named "iPhone 13" less than 51 minutes after the session was hijacked. "Rogue devices served the same purpose," the researchers said. "The threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it." Furthermore, the attackers have also been spotted setting up hidden email rules in victims' inboxes with names such as ".," "sss," "ss," "iT," ",.," "........," "s," and "d" to delete incoming mail with certain keywords referencing payroll, deposit, and bonus, or move them to obscure folders like RSS Feeds and Conversation History. In one compromised mailbox, the email rule marked all incoming messages as read and deleted them. The mailbox was then used to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients before Microsoft Entra ID Protection rated the account high risk. Huntress said the tokens originate from multiple sources, including AitM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process. The campaign was first observed from a Romanian IP address "193.26.115[.]221," which, according to VirusTotal, is used by a remote access trojan called AsyncRAT. The IP address is associated with a German hosting provider named 1337 Services GmbH. Data from GreyNoise currently lists 29 IP addresses matching the hosting provider, out of which 10 have been flagged as malicious and five are marked suspicious. Notably, the entity is linked to StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh, which allows paying customers to rent virtual servers. The domains linked to both StarkRDP and rdp[.]sh were taken down, alongside websites for Nulled, Cracked, and Sellix, as part of an international law enforcement operation dubbed Talent in January 2025. As of writing, the two platforms are operational, with the former now rebranded as exy[.]sh. "StarkRDP has always been operating by the law and is not involved in any of these alleged crimes, and the legal process will confirm this," the StarkRDP Telegram account said in a post dated January 30, according to independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs. "The only things that were seized is [sic] the website server and our domain. Unfortunately, no one can tell who took it and with whom we can talk about it. Therefore, we will restart operation soon, under a different name, to close the chapter [of] 'StarkRDP.'" Organizations who suspect a token replay compromise are recommended to revoke sessions and reset the password, audit Entra devices, review MFA methods, check for unexpected inbox rules or new enterprise applications, and restrict device-code workflow with Conditional Access policies. "Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented," Huntress researchers said. "Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally."

24ki3c.text: An automated campaign is using stolen GitHub tokens to plant workflows that print a repository's secrets into its GitHub Actions logs, which the attackers then download before deleting the runs. The attacks have succeeded in private repositories and GitHub Enterprise environments, according to an analysis by cloud security company Wiz. A GitHub safeguard that pauses suspicious workflow runs stopped every public-repository run Wiz checked, but it does not cover private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. Every secret the repository could read should be rotated, and the token that pushed the branch revoked. Wiz has tracked the campaign since September 15 and calls it Gheist, after the user agent gheist that the attackers' tool sends with GitHub API requests. Wiz has recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, from personal projects to the private repositories of enterprise organizations. Wiz's analysis does not say how many organizations had secrets exposed. In private repositories and on GitHub Enterprise Server, GitHub audit logs show runs on the planted branches finishing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. AWS CloudTrail logs show the organization's own workflows also running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, a sign that GitHub Actions ran there without approval. In enterprise organizations, the tool cycled through tokens from several users and automation accounts within minutes and cloned private repositories before planting the workflow. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager. Wiz's analysis does not say where those credentials came from or who used them. As of October 24, the campaign was still running and changing. About two-thirds of the accounts involved were no longer available on GitHub. Wiz reported the activity to GitHub and says their disappearance likely reflects a response. Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can read every secret configured in it, according to GitHub's documentation. A stolen token with that access is enough. For each repository a token can reach, the tool creates a ci-sync- branch and commits one file, .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and includes the token owner's name; pushing it starts the workflow. The workflow prints the job's environment and every secret the job can read, encoded in base32. GitHub masks secrets in logs, but its documentation says this is not guaranteed once a value has been encoded or otherwise changed. Wiz says the base32 text no longer matches the original secret, so it prints in full. The workflow sets an empty permissions block. That limits the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attackers do not need, and does not stop the job from reading secrets. One version of the tool also runs a job for each deployment environment in the repository, so secrets limited to those environments print too. These are often production credentials, according to Wiz. The tool then downloads the log through GitHub's API and deletes the run seconds later. Because the secrets leave through GitHub itself, there is no attacker server or outbound connection to block. Since July 28, GitHub has held workflow runs it identifies as potentially malicious until a collaborator with write access approves them. GitHub says the hold "currently applies to public repositories on github.com only" and that GitHub Enterprise Server does not have it at this time. Every public Gheist run Wiz checked, across all versions of the tool, was still waiting for approval, so its payload never ran. The hold only catches runs that GitHub flags. A new variant of GhostAction, a separate campaign, ran in public repositories until GitHub began blocking it on October 9, according to research from security company GitGuardian. Wiz says Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files. Around October 19, one version of the tool began pushing a second job meant for self-hosted runners, the machines organizations run themselves to process GitHub Actions jobs. It appears to target only repositories that have such a runner registered. The job is written to search the runner machine for credentials, including 31 types of tokens: private keys, process environments, AWS instance role credentials, runner credential files, and the Kubernetes service account token. Wiz describes the job as buggy, and its analysis reports no successful run. The sources Wiz could trace for the stolen tokens include infostealer logs and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain attacks, such as the March compromise of the Trivy vulnerability scanner. Other attackers also use the same accounts. On October 6, 391 accounts, many of them also used by Gheist, renamed about 1,461 repositories to appear to be cracked software and spread malware. The renaming wiped 610 of the planted branches. Some victims also appear to be infected with PolinRider, malware that researchers have linked to North Korea. On October 19 and 20, three of them re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader added to a vite.config.js file. Megalodon, a campaign that pushed secret-stealing workflows into thousands of GitHub repositories in May, had also hit 57 of the accounts. How to Check Your Repositories Wiz recommends these checks: Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message ci: sync config. In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of finishing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist. If your workflows sign in to a cloud provider with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. This works even if you do not collect GitHub logs. On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs. OIDC lets workflows sign in with short-lived tokens instead of stored cloud keys. By default, a token's subject includes the branch name only when the job does not use a deployment environment, according to GitHub's OIDC documentation. The published indicators are: User agent: gheist Branch: ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$ Commit message: ci: sync config, adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml String: toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120 String: ===== gdmp-pivot: File: .gdmp_pat File: .gdmp_patg File: .gdmp_sweep Git blob SHA (plain workflow): f3da2b8b357dcda02fd455d314be2a95007516a6 Git blob SHA (timeout version): d09535857a741bbb976bdc084a9a021713133291 Git blob SHA (separator version): 1dc5af9cce950aad1eb1546ecce8565b117540c4 Git blob SHA (self-hosted job version): c665b778b2d822453293003e7ca0bbb2cb08e39d Versions of the workflow that list a repository's deployment environments vary by repository, so they have no fixed hash. What to Do If You Find a ci-sync Branch Wiz advises these steps for an affected repository: Rotate every repository, organization, and environment secret the repository could use. Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers. If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the machine and its cloud instance role as compromised. Do not approve held sync-check runs, and do not run code from ci-sync branches. To make a stolen token less useful, Wiz also recommends these steps: Require reviewers on environments that hold production secrets. Limit OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments. Use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens. Run self-hosted runners as short-lived machines without Docker socket access or open access to cloud metadata. A job cannot read an environment's secrets until a required reviewer approves it, according to GitHub's documentation.

bsat5o.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Endpoint Security A malicious instruction file sitting in a developer's Downloads folder tried to make their AI coding agent install a known-malicious npm package, security firm Forever Security said in a report published last week. The company caught the attempt on a real customer's machine and stopped the agent before any code ran. It could not determine how the file got into the folder. The file was AGENTS.md, a plain-text instructions file that a coding agent, such as OpenAI's Codex, reads when it starts in a folder and follows as directions. It was dressed up as ordinary engineering notes. One section told the agent to add a server to its own configuration and install a package called function-color from npm. That package is part of a malware campaign that other researchers have documented separately: function-color pulls in a downloader called function-flag, which fetches and runs a Windows payload. Researchers at CloudSEK and Checkmarx, who analyzed the campaign, named it MALFEX. Two things, each harmless on its own, make this work, Forever said. An agent is built to trust and obey the instructions file in the folder it opens. And a web page can save a file to the Downloads folder on its own, without a click or a permission prompt, choosing the name and contents. Put together, a web page can drop a file the agent will treat as orders into a folder the agent trusts. Researchers did not establish that this is how the file was caught. To test whether the full path was possible, it built its own proof-of-concept page: visit it, and an AGENTS.md downloads silently into Downloads. Whether a real attacker used that route against the customer is not known. The firm then reproduced the attack on two coding agents to show that it was not specific to a single product. Against Codex, it ran the real attacker file inside an isolated virtual machine. The file, framed as routine project setup, told Codex to register a server in ~/.codex/config.toml and run a command that installed the package. Because that config file applies to every Codex session on the machine, the change would load the attacker's server in any folder afterward, not just Downloads. Codex ran the malware in more than 90% of attempts, Forever said. Against Claude Code, the working attack looked different and succeeded less often. A planted CLAUDE.md, framed as internal gateway setup, tried to make Claude write an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL into a project settings file, pointing its API traffic at a server Forever controlled. That one change leaks the session's login token, which is account takeover on its own, and lets the server reply as if it were the model and hand back commands the agent runs. Claude needs a person to approve a write like that and often refuses one that looks wrong; the long engineering-doc framing got the write approved about half the time, researchers said. There is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, in Forever's view, because an agent following the instructions file in its folder is doing what it was built to do. The company compared it to a browser rendering a phishing page: the browser worked as designed, and the attack lies in the page. "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch," Forever said. What to do Forever's advice is practical and needs no product: Do not start Codex, Claude Code, or any agent in ~/Downloads. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own. Look for instructions files you did not write. A stray AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, in Downloads or in a repository you just cloned, is the whole attack. Read it before you let an agent near it. Check the agent's own config. In ~/.codex/config.toml, watch for a server block or a changed base URL you did not add. In a project's .claude/settings.json, watch for an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or other API endpoint you did not set. Leave approval prompts and sandboxes on, and be wary of anything that tells the agent to switch them off. If you find a planted file, assume the login token leaked and rotate it. A stolen token is a live session, not just one caught request. In its own telemetry, Forever said that about half of its customers run a coding agent in their Downloads folder, and roughly a quarter of agent sessions open a browser. Those are the conditions the attack needs: an agent starts where the web can write, and, in many cases, an agent does the browsing itself, so no person is watching when a file arrives.

m7px2y.text: A single hacked device on a Tailscale network can be used to gain root access to other servers it can reach, according to a security researcher who published the findings this week. The attack requires two things: Tailscale SSH set up to allow port forwarding, and an attacker who already controls one device that the network's access rules permit to connect to the target. The findings were published on October 25 in a report called Tailworm by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs. Windisch tested Tailscale version 1.104.2 and headscale version 0.29.5, the self-hosted server some networks use to run Tailscale instead of the company's hosted service, over three days in a lab. The report describes tests on that software, not attacks against real networks. As of publication, Tailscale had issued no security bulletin, no CVE identifier, and no fixed version. Tailscale has responded in public. Mike Shaver, the company's vice president of engineering, wrote on Reddit that Tailscale had received the report, had already been looking at the same areas with outside security specialists, and had found issues it is working to fix. Shaver said the company is still working out which setups are affected, and that it is "not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH." Tailscale SSH does not work like a normal SSH server. Rather than checking a connecting user's password or key, it identifies the device, and a single access rule decides whether that device may open an SSH session to a target. Because of this, the attack needs no stolen passwords or keys. It needs a foothold on one device first, which the report says an attacker can get the usual ways: a vulnerable web application, a poisoned software package, phishing, or stolen login details. Tailscale does not create that first foothold. How much an administrator can do about it depends on where the network is run. On Tailscale's hosted service, forwarding can be switched off per rule. On headscale version 0.29.5, forwarding cannot be turned off at all. The report says every SSH grant there should therefore be treated as giving root on the target. In the lab, Windisch showed the problem in stages. Using standard SSH port forwarding, an ordinary session caused the root-level Tailscale process to connect to a system socket that only root should access, and the test gained root and read the system password file almost immediately, without administrator rights. A second method replaced a root-owned socket with the attacker's, allowing direct root command execution against certain services. A third method defeated a safety check meant to limit which files forwarding can access by racing the system between when it checks a file path and when it uses it. That chain went further in the lab, the report says: it captured a key used to enroll new devices and used the key to join an attacker's own machine to the network as a trusted server. That last step worked from start to finish only on networks where Tailscale's Tailnet Lock feature was not enabled. On networks that do, the needed secrets were captured in transit, but the final step was not completed. Windisch describes the overall result as "wormable." In the lab, one compromised device could spread to every device that the access rules allow, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step. In the report's words, "the mesh converts one ordinary foothold into fleet-wide privileged access at machine speed." That spread was measured in a lab, not seen on real networks. The report names two things that held it back: access rules written as single source-to-destination pairs, which stopped the spread on their own, and device keys tied to hardware such as a TPM or Secure Enclave. Some researchers who read the report have publicly questioned the "wormable" description, while others have called the root-access finding serious. The SSH problem is one of 11 findings in the report, which also covers Tailscale's app connectors, its serve feature, the DERP relay used between devices, and headscale. Windisch told The Hacker News that the SSH privilege escalation "is worrying," but that the app connector finding "may be more impactful to some organizations." The app connector finding, in an experimental feature called conn25, lets a permitted user send traffic to destinations the security team never approved, including a cloud provider's metadata service, which can hand out server credentials. All of the findings rest on Windisch's report alone. No other researcher has publicly reproduced them, and Tailscale has not confirmed the specific technical claims. Windisch said the proof-of-concept code behind the findings is not public, and that she provided it only to Tailscale's security contact. Windisch has described the disclosure as "reported but not coordinated," writing as much on Ycombinator HN, and at least one commenter there called publishing without first reporting to Tailscale irresponsible.In response to questions from The Hacker News, Windisch said she had in fact given Tailscale a copy of the report and the proof-of-concept code before the public post, sending them to the company's security contact on the Saturday beforehand. She said she had also raised concerns about Tailscale's architecture with the company's chief executive earlier, and had publicly posted a file hash and advised users to disable Tailscale SSH. The report is the latest in a run of problems in the same part of Tailscale. Earlier in 2026, the company fixed several Tailscale SSH and server socket-handling flaws, including one where SSH Unix socket forwarding could reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9. What to Do Now Because there is no patch, the available steps are changes to how Tailscale SSH and related features are set up. The report and Tailscale's own advice overlap on most of them. Review your Tailscale SSH access rules. Write them as single source-to-destination pairs that name one device and one target, and remove broad rules that grant access by identity or tag. The report calls per-pair rules the one control that stopped the spread in testing. Turn off SSH port forwarding where you can. On Tailscale's hosted service this is a per-rule setting. On headscale version 0.29.5 it cannot be turned off, so treat every SSH grant there as giving root on the target. Remove app connector permissions from devices that do not need them. Remove any tailscale serve forward that points at a Unix socket. Turn on node-key expiry, so a stolen device key does not stay valid forever. If a device is compromised, delete it at the control plane. Reimaging the machine does not revoke keys an attacker may have already copied off it. Tailscale also suggests enabling SSH check mode, which adds a login step before a session starts, and enabling automatic updates. Check mode does not fix the privilege escalation. It only adds another barrier in front of it.

13y5lfe.text: Threat actors have been observed using agentic artificial intelligence (AI) platforms for post-exploitation activity following the abuse of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. "In one case, the attackers targeted a government entity in Europe and within two hours of the initial exploitation they had successfully accessed password hashes and multi-factor authentication secrets," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "They also established an NT LAN Manager (NTLM)-relay tunnel into Active Directory and attempted Domain Admin privilege escalation." The network security company said it also observed the unknown attacker enumerating the compromised endpoint, with commands and behavioral markers suggesting the work of an agentic attacker. These include commands to facilitate - Reconnaissance of the authentication database with stolen credentials, targeting password hashes and two-factor authentication (2FA) secrets. Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance via curl-based anonymous LDAP queries to the domain controller (DC) in an attempt to look for the administrator account. Reconnaissance of the host to hunt for DNS/AD integration, internal hosts, privileged groups, and interactive users. "Each command batch is wrapped in section-header delimiters, such as ==SHELLUSER== and ==PASSWD==," it added. "These delimiters produce machine-parseable output for an AI model to read." Suspected N. Korea Campaign Targets PHP2Shell The disclosure comes as CYFIRMA said it uncovered a suspected North Korea-linked campaign employing PHP2Shell to actively probe global PHP infrastructure from 21 compromised nodes. "The scanning is deliberately low-volume and paced," Kumar Ritesh, CEO and founder of CYFIRMA, told The Hacker News. "Nodes are rotated and abandoned at the first sign of blocking or rate-limiting, so threshold-based alerting is unlikely to catch it." The targets comprise a set of 216 unpatched or partially mitigated hosts located across the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, Taiwan, India, Singapore, the U.A.E., Saudi Arabia, and the E.U. The hosts span government, financial institutions, logistics, airports and aviation, manufacturing, and online transaction platforms. "The campaign has moved from reconnaissance into active, low-and-slow scanning of a filtered target set," CYFIRMA said. "Organizations in the prioritised sectors and geographies should assume they are in scope for deliberate targeting." The activity, coordinated via a closed I2P channel, has been attributed with moderate confidence to a Korean-speaking operator assessed to be affiliated with the Lazarus Group ecosystem. According to CYFIRMA, the two handles (전창혁 2 aka Jeon Chang-hyuk 2) and (최아린 aka Choi A-rin) active in the I2P channel have previously been observed running covert operations for the threat actors. "Korean-speaking operators have used [the channel] to share target lists, exploit-hosting infrastructure, and tasking and prioritisation consistent with DPRK objectives," Ritesh said. "The captured conversation uses vocabulary and spelling specific to North Korean (Munhwaŏ) rather than the South Korean standard." Other primary indicators that link the campaign to the Lazarus cluster are below - Command-and-control (C2) infrastructure that Lazarus has previously used to exploit web assets. Lazarus Group's documented history of compromising PHP and WordPress servers for C2 and planting of PHP and ASP web shells, as observed in the SyncHole watering hole campaign. Prioritizing government agencies and banks, specifically online transaction platforms, which is in line with Lazarus Group's track record of breaching financial institutions for financial and cryptocurrency theft. "Exploitation is the next step," CYFIRMA said. "The operators said they would shortlist the most promising targets the same day and then choose which public exploits to adapt." Other Exploit Efforts and Mitigations In an October 25, 2026, post shared on X, Defused Cyber said it's also seeing PHP2Shell probes targeting its Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect honeypots. The activity originates from 204.76.203[.]7, a known mass-exploit IP address. "The requests carry a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS marker ('p2s-rider') and a dummy file upload with no payload, which points to someone checking for the vulnerable upload-progress behavior and likely building a target list of Palo Alto devices," the threat intelligence company said. Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. The security flaws have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure. "An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses," Datadog said. "The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit." "When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table." ReliaQuest, in an update published on October 22, 2026, said it reproduced CVE-2026-109618 in a controlled lab and observed a sequence of errors that could help defenders identify exploitation. "This testing identified a specific sequence of artifacts across PHP error, Apache access, Apache error, and system logs that may help defenders detect exploitation," it said. "Defenders should focus on the sequence: a POST request returns a 500 error, PHP reports memory exhaustion and heap corruption, and the Apache worker handling the request crashes." The PHP Foundation has since warned of a third remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560), which can only "occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code." The issue is expected to be addressed as part of the regular release cycle. "An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start()," the Foundation said. "Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled." Xint has released a scanner to check if a host is exposed to PHP2Shell, stating remote code execution is possible in any PHP script regardless of the application and in applications where decoding occurs, such as with session_start() and unserialize(). Bitsight's internet-wide scans show that there are nearly 37 million internet-facing systems running PHP or PHP-related software, with most of the exposures in the U.S., Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Japan. "PHP runs a very large portion of the web, from content management systems and online shops to bespoke internal tools," Bitsight said. "A flaw in the runtime can't be repaired by changing application code, and a web application firewall or plugin update won’t remove it. Only updating PHP on the host itself closes the gap."

rdmtqt.text: Researchers found a malicious AGENTS markdown instruction file in a customer’s Downloads folder that tricked an AI coding agent into installing a rogue npm package. They reproduced the attack against OpenAI Codex and demonstrated a related technique against Claude Code to leak OAuth tokens and hijack the account using only the malicious instructions. Markdown files such as AGENTS.md are plain-text files that contain project-specific instructions for AI coding agents, such as the tools to use, how to run tests, and the coding conventions to follow. Agents following malicious instructions Researchers at Forever Security, a company that monitors for risks introduced by AI agents and autonomous software, discovered the tactic on a customer’s computer, where a coding agent attempted to install the malicious npm package ‘function-color.’ The investigation traced the AI agent’s attempt to install a malicious npm package to an AGENTS.md file in the customer’s ~/Downloads folder, which also served as the agent’s working directory. Agents automatically load applicable files from their working directory and use the contained instructions to guide their actions. While these files aren’t executables, malicious instructions contained in them can lead to AI agents running commands, installing packages, or changing settings using the tools and permissions available to it. "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch. An agent that follows the AGENTS.md in its folder is doing exactly what it was built to do," the researchers say. The researchers' test confirmed that an attacker could use such a file to manipulate OpenAI Codex and Claude Code into executing code or stealing credentials. Although the researchers could not determine how the malicious instructions file landed into the target's ~/Downloads location, they explained to BleepingComputer that simply visiting a malicious page could drop a payload without any user interaction. In a report this week, Forever Security says that "~/Downloads is special. It is the one folder the web can write to on its own," and that "a web page can download a file named AGENTS.md into your Downloads folder, silently." The researchers created a proof-of-concept (PoC) to demonstrate how the attack could land a malicious file into the ~/Downloads location without the user noticing. When BleepingComputer verified the PoC page, it downloaded an AGENTS.md file containing harmless content, namely the strings "sensitive data here" and "line 2." By default, many popular browsers, including Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, save files downloaded from the web to the user's ~/Downloads directory without prompting them to choose a save location for each download. BleepingComputer’s tests in other browsers, such as Brave, prompted the user to approve the download, which should be enough to alert the user that a file was downloaded. However, Chrome, Edge, and Firefox display download notifications by default, alerting users when a file has been saved locally. After dropping the file into Downloads, the attack would require the target to launch their AI agent in that same directory so it could load the instruction file and digest its malicious instructions. Forever researcher Gal Weizman told BleepingComputer that this is common practice, as people often use AI agents to organize that folder or to act on a newly downloaded file. Weizman says that internal statistics show that hundreds of customers run AI agents, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor CLI, from their ~/Downloads folders. Claude Code alone launched more than 1,300 sessions from that location, the researcher told BleepingComputer. Tests show attack feasible The researchers tested their reconstructed attack chain against Codex using a harmless payload that simply opened the calculator app, recording a 90% success rate. In a separate test, they used a malicious CLAUDE.md file to redirect Claude Code’s API traffic to a server they controlled. This exposed the agent’s OAuth token, allowing the server to impersonate the model and return tool calls that executed code in roughly 50% of tests. The researchers say that the risk is a combination of intended browser and agent behavior, which puts the precaution and defense responsibility directly on the user. Users should avoid setting ~/Downloads as an AI coding agent's working directory because the location may contain untrusted files that the agent could interpret as instructions. OpenAI and Anthropic recommend running their AI coding agents from the project directory they are intended to work on. Keeping the working directory scoped to the relevant project helps provide the agent with appropriate context and limits its working scope, reducing the risk of it processing untrusted files in unrelated locations. The common recommendation from OpenAI and Anthropic is to start an AI coding agent in the root of the specific project it should work on, rather than in your home directory or a broad parent directory. Keep its working area as narrow as practical, and expand access only when needed. The key idea is that the working directory defines the agent's default project context and, depending on the tool, helps establish its filesystem access boundary. Users should review unfamiliar AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and similar instruction files before allowing an AI coding agent to follow them, keep approval prompts and sandbox protections enabled, and test potentially untrusted code in an isolated environment before running it on their main system. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. 1pbleii.text: OpenAI has announced plans to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access, as it resumes reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of its most advanced AI models. "Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the artificial intelligence (AI) company said. "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access." OpenAI said models' growing capabilities can have the side effect of them getting much better at devising ways around environmental restrictions to escape containment and perform unintended actions. This can involve the model exploiting a software flaw or misconfiguration to reach the live internet, or finding unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. Late last month, the Frontier Lab made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models after one of its agents during reinforcement learning (RL) training contacted an external chatbot by exploiting a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to obtain limited internet access. OpenAI said it also kicked off a "high-compute red-teaming campaign" to test the resilience of its research and evaluation environments in the face of increasingly powerful models, leading to the discovery of previously unknown software vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution in Google Brotli (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS score: 9.2), a widely used compression library. Patches for the vulnerability, also called Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell, have since been released for libbrotli, Python, C++, Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and Istio. The red-teaming agents OpenAI dispatched to test its security safeguards also uncovered virtual machine escapes, novel paths to access the internet through vulnerabilities in metrics, logging, and authentication management services, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents, bypassing isolation boundaries. "In one test that assumed compromise of a host machine, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL," it said. "In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs." In another experiment, after prompting the AI agents in separate microVMs to exchange synthetic secrets without relying on network connections or shared writable files, OpenAI said the digital bots found a way to communicate using the processor's cache via a timing-based side-channel. Particularly, one agent is said to have encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. A second agent measured the time it took to reload that data, leveraging the difference between fast and slow cache reads to recover the message. "Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection," OpenAI said. The AI giant said the discoveries prompted it to strengthen its own safety and monitoring mechanisms and deem them sufficient enough to restart frontier RL training and internal inference, while continuing to invest in several key areas - Improving virtual machine security Probing cloud infrastructure for weaknesses Scanning source code and cloud configurations Testing monitoring and stopping systems Red-teaming sandbox and isolation guarantees "After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1," OpenAI said. "We've reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely." Earlier this month, Anthropic said it was cutting off live internet access for all its internal evaluations until further notice after discovering new incidents in which its AI models exhibited misaligned behavior and targeted real websites. The disclosure comes as concerns have been raised over the ability of AI agents to detect and exploit software flaws, even in the guardrails designed to restrict them. In a report published this week, third-party AI ​safety evaluators METR ⁠and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed before July 21, 2026, and during the time frame when the company's agents broke into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. "We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," researchers David Rein and Adam Kaufman said. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored." OpenAI is believed to have addressed all of the vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards stack, although the safety organizations said they had not verified the fixes. Anthropic's Mythos 5 Pursues an Unsanctioned Supply Chain Attack The developments also coincide with a report from the U.K. AI Security Institute (AISI), which has found Anthropic's Mythos 5 model to be consistently taking unsanctioned actions even when presented with evidence that doing so would be out-of-scope and cause real harm (e.g., submitting a malicious code change). The evaluation also revealed that the Mythos 5's chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning process failed to consider the impact of harmful actions, with the model often producing invalid justifications that implied the target was simulated when asked if the human maintainer was real, but never generating incorrect justifications implying that it was real. "Most models tested take a range of unsanctioned actions during simulated cybersecurity evaluations, Mythos 5 most frequently," AISI said. "Taken together, these observations could indicate that models are engaging in 'motivated reasoning': producing inferences and reasoning biased towards conclusions that justify continuing a particular approach to task completion." In the most severe case, the model has been found to attempt a supply chain attack by submitting malicious code and creating five sock-puppet accounts to vouch for the changes and pressure a software maintainer into accepting it. Responding to the findings, Anthropic has attributed the alignment failures to recklessness, biased reasoning, and an urge to "continue on its current trajectory" to a degree that disregards potential harm. The OpenAI rival also noted that its newer models, including an internal research model, are less susceptible to this behavior. "Nevertheless, this incident serves as further evidence that current AI models are capable of surprisingly misaligned behavior in evaluation settings," it said. "We've built new evaluations that we run on new production models automatically, and we are specifically studying biased reasoning to better understand where it comes from in our training and how it affects our models."

2phbgt.text: A new UEFI bootkit named BlackX, deployed in an espionage campaign in early 2026, exploited the old Baton Drop vulnerability to bypass Secure Boot and load a malicious driver designed to interfere with security solutions from Kaspersky and Avast. The operation has been attributed with medium confidence to APT41, a Chinese state-sponsored threat group also known as Brass Typhoon, Wicked Panda, and Barium. It was discovered in early 2026 and targeted diplomatic agencies in Central Asia, particularly in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. Kaspersky researchers analyzed the BlackX bootkit and found similarities with BlackLotus, which has been circulating on hacker forums since October 2022 and leveraged the Baton Drop vulnerability (CVE-2022-21894) to bypass Secure Boot protection. ESET confirmed in March 2023 that BlackLotus exploited Baton Drop, and at the time it could compromise even fully patched Windows 11 systems. According to Kaspersky researchers, BlackX's implementation of the exploit is "remarkably similar" to the one used by BlackLotus, allowing the attacker to enroll custom Machine Owner Keys (MOKs) and load arbitrary EFI files to bypass Secure Boot protections. However, BlackX differs from BlackLotus and deploys a different kernel driver and follow-on payloads. Kaspersky suggests that BlackX was either derived from reverse-engineering BlackLotus or from its source code. Although the source code for BlackLotus was leaked in July 2023, the release was incomplete. Kaspersky researchers found that some BlackLotus samples they analyzed contained code missing from the public repository but present in the BlackX bootkit. Since the BlackX operator could not have obtained this code from the leaked repo, the researchers believe the attacker either reverse-engineered BlackLotus or purchased its source code. BlackX capabilities BlackX injects a malicious Windows kernel driver signed with a now-revoked certificate issued to an organization named Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio. The driver disables security-related processes and registry callbacks, and tampers with Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers to obstruct monitoring. The researchers note that some tampering procedures are configured to run only if Kaspersky or Avast products are detected on the target host, adding that the mechanism is useless against the company's solutions. The driver also protects the bootkit’s files by intercepting user requests to open them and launching the Windows Calculator instead. Its purpose is also to deploy the following espionage payloads on infected machines: A RAT that uses Google Drive, OneDrive, or Yandex.Disk for command-and-control (C2) to execute .NET payloads and upload and download files. OxiDLLRunner, an OLLVM-obfuscated DLL sideloaded by googleupdate.exe. It decrypts v8_context_snapshot.bin to launch shellcode and a Rust payload, which retrieves DLL plugins from archivetj[.]com and executes their ‘create_plugin’ functions in separate threads. Insufficient fix Kaspersky says that all BlackX victims used a fully patched Windows release. However, the bootkit was still successful because admins did not manually activate the additional Secure Boot revocations. “The patch for the Baton Drop vulnerability is designed to revoke the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components,” Kaspersky explains. “However, this revocation does not happen automatically upon patch installation - the user has to trigger it manually.” The researchers say this is a gap in the update process, since it’s extremely uncommon for administrators to take any manual action after applying a security update. They believe that the attacker used this mitigation gap to their advantage and "decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit." Instructions to fully patch Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894) are available here. The researchers warn that the October 19, 2026 expiration date of the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate does not stop the vulnerable binaries from loading on Windows systems unless admins add the certificate to a blocklist.
