ub0wvs.text: A memory-corruption flaw in Google's Brotli decoder sits in many programs that unpack Brotli-compressed data, among them Bun, the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages, and Envoy proxies set up to decompress Brotli. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw allows crafted compressed data to overwrite past the end of a buffer and corrupt a program's memory, potentially causing a crash, a memory leak, or the execution of attacker-controlled code. Imperva researchers have shown that code can run on one unpatched Node.js build. The same has not been demonstrated on the other software, and no real-world attacks have been reported. The flaw was first disclosed on October 21, when Node.js and Google shipped fixes, and more have followed product by product since. Because the bug is in Google's decoder and each program ships its own copy of it, every one has to update that copy on its own. Brotli is a compression format from Google, used across the web to shrink pages and other traffic. The bug is in the C code that unpacks a Brotli stream, so it travels into anything that reuses that code, from language runtimes to proxies to Python packages. Which Software Is Affected Product Affected Fixed in Exposed when Google Brotli (C library) 1.0.3 to 1.2.0 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 code decodes untrusted Brotli Node.js 22.x, 24.x, 26.x before the fix; 20.x and older (end of life) 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 fetch() of a br response, or Express or body-parser br bodies Bun 1.4.3 and earlier 1.4.4 fetch() of a br response, or node:zlib Envoy 1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.11 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12 only if the Brotli decompressor is configured Istio 1.31.0 to 1.31.1, 1.30.0 to 1.30.5, 1.29.0 to 1.29.8 1.31.2, 1.30.6, 1.29.9 only if Brotli decompression is enabled Python Brotli 1.2.0 and earlier 1.2.1 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br Python brotlicffi 1.2.0.x and earlier 1.2.1.0 installed, and an HTTP client decodes br cdxgen standalone binaries and images, 13.4.0 and 12.8.8 and earlier 13.5.0, 12.8.9 standalone binary or image scanning untrusted input A program is exposed only if it decodes Brotli data that someone else controls. For Node.js and Bun, that happens when the built-in fetch() reads a response sent with Content-Encoding: br, or when request-body code such as Express 5 and body-parser 2 unpacks a Brotli upload. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode request bodies on its own. Envoy and Istio are affected only when Brotli decompression is enabled, for example, through an Envoy filter. Where it is off, the flaw cannot be reached. In Python, the risk comes from the Brotli or brotlicffi package being installed at all. Once either is present, HTTP clients such as requests, urllib3, httpx, and aiohttp decode Brotli responses on their own, so an application can be exposed without ever importing Brotli in its own code. A web application firewall helps only so far. Vercel, which added firewall rules on the day of disclosure, said those rules do not cover "responses your functions fetch from other servers." For that path, only updating the runtime or library closes the hole. How far the flaw can be pushed depends on the software. Imperva's Red Team, which calls its work Node2Shell, ran attacker-supplied code on an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build for Linux on ARM64, delivering it both as a fetched response and as an Express request body. The exploit took several tries, has not been released, and was not tested on other builds. OpenAI, whose Codex Security team reported the flaw, describes it as enabling unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli and lists Node.js, Bun, and Envoy as affected software. In its account, the flaw works both ways: an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as "curl --compressed") could be taken over by a malicious server. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. CISA's October 23 assessment recorded exploitation as "none" and automation as "no," and Red Hat said there is no reliable public proof-of-concept for running code. Severity ratings differ by who is scoring. Google, which assigned the CVE, rates it 9.2, or critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Node.js calls it high, and Red Hat rates it 8.1, or important. The fix has an unusual history. The change that closes the flaw was added to Brotli's source code on February 27, but no new Brotli release carried it until October 21. OpenAI said the root cause "was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli." Node.js credits Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI's Codex Security for reporting the flaw, and maintainers Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel for the fix. What to Do Now Update to a fixed version from the table above, then restart the service and rebuild any container image, because a running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts. Where you cannot update yet, stop decoding untrusted Brotli. OpenAI's disclosure page and the security firm Aikido both recommend: Reject incoming requests with Content-Encoding: br before any proxy or parser decodes the body. Turn off automatic Brotli decoding in HTTP clients, and reject Brotli responses before they are decoded. In Python, uninstall the Brotli and brotlicffi packages so clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Dropping br from the Accept-Encoding header does not help on its own, because a server can send Brotli whatever the client asks for. For Node.js, no workaround has been published, so updating the runtime is the only fix. System packages are being fixed at different times. Debian fixed its brotli package for Debian 13 (trixie) on October 23 in version 1.1.0-2+deb13u1. Amazon Linux 2023 still listed its brotli and Node.js 24 packages as pending a fix as of October 22. Dependency scanners may not flag the Python packages yet. The CVE record names Google's Brotli repository, not the PyPI packages, and GitHub's advisory still lists no affected package, which is what Dependabot reads. Advisory entries for the two Python packages, PYSEC-2026-4322 and PYSEC-2026-4323, were added on October 23, so check the installed versions manually as well.

lrnc7u.text: LiteLLM on Friday revealed that an Agent Platform master key accidentally published to a public GitHub repository in late May 2026 ultimately allowed the threat actor to push a malicious version of the popular Python package. "On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents," LiteLLM's Oliver Jensen and Mateo Wang said. "The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key." LiteLLM said the unknown attacker (operating from "69.48.229[.]143") used this unrevoked key on October 10, 2026, to gain access to the Agent Platform and extracted a GitHub CLI OAuth token the service was configured with to allow self-hosted cloud agents to file pull requests to GitHub repositories. The token, per the developers of the open-source large language model (LLM) gateway, was "not scoped down" and associated with its GitHub organization owner's account. Gaining access to the token allowed the attacker to possess owner-level access to all repositories across the organization and perform additional credential exfiltration. The sequence of actions performed by the threat actor following this step is as follows - October 10, 2026, between 10:11 and 10:12 p.m. UTC: Author commits into throwaway branches on internal repositories to run workflows (BerriAI/litellm and BerriAI/litellm-auto) designed to acquire GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges via an attacker-controlled webhook[.]site endpoint. The two runs are deleted minutes later. October 21, 2026, between 10:08 and 11:08 a.m. UTC: Override branch protection and alter the release pipeline with the source set to the lookalike repository "Berri-AI/litellm" rather than "BerriAI/litellm." October 21, 2026, between 11:39 and 11:40 a.m. UTC: LiteLLM version 1.107.0 gets published to PyPI on October 21, 2026, 11:46 a.m. UTC: Docker Hub and GHCR images are published. October 21, 2026, between 11:53 and 11:54 a.m. UTC: Production and staging run records are deleted. October 21, 2026, 12:06 p.m. UTC: Supply chain attack reported by Upwind researcher Lidor Machluf. October 21, 2026, 1:23 p.m. UTC: PyPI quarantines LiteLLM version 1.107.0. October 21, 2025, 2:20 p.m. UTC: Docker Hub tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable are removed or repointed to verified clean images. "In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office," LiteLLM said. Leaked master key in May 2026 "This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it." In addition, the project maintainers noted that the threat actor could have very well loosened this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves given that they were already in possession of a token belonging to an organization owner. It's suspected that this was not done to evade detection. LiteLLM also said the workflows are designed to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, specifically focusing on upstream inference API tokens. In response to the incident, the company said it's working to revoke each and every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform. More Details About the Workflows Emerge Socket, which published its own investigation into the malicious workflows, said it recovered two malicious commits that each added a workflow at ".github/workflows/cache.yml." The first commit was made on October 10, 2026, at 10:11:45 p.m. UTC. It was followed by a second commit on October 12. "Neither commit was pushed to a branch that still exists," Socket security researcher Karlo Zanki said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Both were pushed to short-lived branches named ci-tmp-<hex> that were created, used, and deleted within minutes, which is why the activity leaves almost nothing behind in the repository's ordinary history." According to the application security firm's analysis of the repository's activity log records, both commits rely on a legitimate commit as the branch base to make the push look seemingly harmless - Create a throwaway branch named "ci-tmp-<hex>" (namely, ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-4d8517) from a recent legitimate commit on the repository. Push a commit adding ".github/workflows/cache.yml" with the same subject, "ci: bump cache config." The workflow is configured to be run every time a commit or tag is pushed (i.e., "on: [push]"), causing it to be triggered. Delete the branch. Both workflows, as highlighted by LiteLLM, are equipped to harvest GitHub tokens and API keys for the organization's Linear workspace, LiteLLM deployment, and Together AI, along with the identifier and signing key of a GitHub App. The October 12 run extends the collection to more secrets, including API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Tavily, and GitGuardian's secret-scanning tenant. It also captures Playwright storage state, PostgreSQL database information (connection string, account name, password), Redis endpoint address, port, and authentication password. The data gathered from the two workflows is exfiltrated to two different webhook[.]site endpoints - webhook[.]site/65a42464-3cfa-4b02-a18c-17a6d7b86f37 webhook[.]site/4da03473-a3e7-4dc2-a087-9c564b4208e1 "A GitHub token and a GitHub App private key are credentials for the platform hosting the repository, not for a third-party service," Zanki said. "GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY is a credential for the secret-scanning platform itself, which gives an attacker visibility into, and potentially control over, the alerts that would surface this activity. "E2E_LINEAR_STORAGE_STATE_B64 is serialized browser session state used by Playwright for end-to-end tests; a valid storage state permits authenticated access to the associated Linear account without a password and without satisfying multi-factor authentication." The findings rule out LiteLLM's initial hypothesis that the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens were stolen from the logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment. "The investigation was a process in which we continually learned additional information, meaning some of our assumptions and beliefs were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete," Jensen acknowledged. What the Malicious Version of the Package Does Multiple reports have revealed that the files bundled with LiteLLM version 1.107.0 are engineered to execute automatically when Python starts, even if an application did not import LiteLLM. The malware features two execution paths: a credential harvesting module that targets authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, and web browsers, and a Unix-oriented backdoor that's launched as a background process to fetch and execute arbitrary code supplied by the attacker every one hour. Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow The stealer also collects system information, SSH files, Git and GitLab credentials and tokens, environment variables, and tokens associated with npm, PyPI, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo. The data is then compressed and sent to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" using an HTTP POST request. The domain was registered on October 13, 2026. "Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported," the Microsoft Security Research team said. "Because the startup files resided outside the LiteLLM application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind."

1si9f12.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 24, 2026Privacy / Artificial Intelligence Google has updated its privacy policy to spell out that using personalized artificial intelligence (AI) features in Search or Gemini could allow the company to serve targeted ads to users based on their activity on other connected Google services. "You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service," reads a policy update effective October 16, 2026. "For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads." Google also notes in its revised policy that "We don't show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads." News of the policy update was first reported by Android Authority. Personal Intelligence, unveiled by Google in Gemini in January 2026, allows users to connect other services like Gmail, Google Photos, and YouTube as a way to provide tailored answers in combination with their chat history preferences. The feature is currently rolling out as a beta to eligible users over the age of 18 globally, except in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the U.K., and Nigeria. It's worth noting that the policy states it doesn't use content from Gmail, Drive, or Photos to personalize ads by default. However, that changes should users opt to share photos or emails with AI Mode and other Search tools via the Personal Intelligence feature. In other words, if users interact with AI Mode or Gemini while Personal Intelligence is enabled, the data that informs those answers (i.e., content from Gmail or Photos) could be used as a signal to serve targeted ads. The privacy policy aims to make it clear that feeding personal data into its AI tools could contribute to ad personalization. Users should be mindful of the privacy trade-off when connecting their apps to enable AI features. Those who prefer to opt out can do so by selecting the apps they want to disconnect from Personal Intelligence or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings ("www.google[.]com/search-personalization"). In January 2026, OpenAI began showing ads to logged-in adult U.S. users in both the free and ChatGPT Go tiers, while emphasizing that users' data and conversations are protected and never sold to advertisers. It has also said the ads do not influence responses from the chatbot, and that users are in control of the experience. Earlier this week, the AI company said it's expanded advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, ​bringing the total to 89. This includes 14 more ​Latin American countries and several markets across Europe, Africa, and Asia. "We keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data," OpenAI stressed. "Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT's answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides."

16uxixg.text: Between November 2025 and March 2026, the Dutch security firm Eye Security pushed more than 2 million updates to computers it did not own to switch off a background updater that it said could have allowed an outsider to take over the machine. The updater belongs to Time4Popcorn, an abandoned copy of Popcorn Time, a free app that streamed pirated films and TV over BitTorrent. Popcorn Time was popular about a decade ago, and the original shut down in 2014, but several copies kept running under the same name. A separate, legal project that took the Popcorn Time name in early 2025 is unrelated to it. Eye Security, which monitors client networks for threats, found the updater during a routine threat hunt: a program called Updater.exe on one client's laptop kept trying to reach a web address that was no longer registered. The firm registered the address itself to see what would connect, and about 50 requests a second poured in. It later laid out the operation, which it named Operation IXIM, in a write-up and a talk at Hack.lu on October 22. Over six months, those requests carried more than 3.8 million different hardware IDs. The IDs proved an unreliable way to count machines, because some Windows PCs shared one and some Macs changed theirs, so Eye revised its estimate to 2.5 to 3 million Windows computers and 250,000 to 350,000 Macs. The updater ran in the background on Windows and Mac from the moment the computer started. It checked for new versions over an unencrypted connection and installed whatever it was sent, at the highest privilege level, called SYSTEM on Windows and root on Mac, without checking who sent it. Because the web addresses it called had been abandoned, Eye said, anyone who registered the right one could have served their own program to every machine still calling it. On a machine with that access, an attacker could install ransomware, steal saved passwords, or pull the computer into a botnet, Eye said. Mapping a sample of the connecting addresses, the firm said it saw home users around the world, as well as machines on government, military, and corporate networks, though it added that it is "hard to draw conclusions" from that. Eye had disclosed the flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-30612, in June. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency rates it 9.8 out of 10. It affects three versions of the Time4Popcorn software: Windows, up to and including 6.2.1.18 Mac, up to and including 6.2.1.17 Android, up to and including 3.5.0.173 Turning the Updater Against Itself With no company left to fix the software and no patch coming, Eye decided to use the updater against itself. After taking legal advice, it served the machines an update that does one thing: it stops and disables the updater, deleting no files and collecting nothing. Eye compared the step to Operation Ladybird in 2021, when Dutch police pushed an update to computers infected with the Emotet botnet to disable the malware on them. The difference, Eye said, is that Emotet's victims never chose to be infected, while Popcorn Time's users installed the app themselves. Still, the firm said, "none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years." Soon after the updates began, someone uploaded Eye's update to VirusTotal, and antivirus engines started flagging it as malware, a fair description of a program that disables a Windows service. Because every product that blocked it left the vulnerable updater running, Eye reworked the update until only one scanner continued to flag it. By December 2025, Eye had updated more than 1 million systems and cut the traffic to its web addresses by about 90 percent. By March 1, it was sending about 5,000 updates a day, a 98 percent reduction. Judging the remaining numbers too small to interest a botnet operator, Eye stopped, having sent more than 2 million update downloads in all. In late March, Eye handed the 15 web addresses it controlled to the Shadowserver Foundation, a non-profit that takes abandoned and malicious domains out of circulation, so a trusted party would hold them rather than Eye. Public registration records for one of them, popcorntimeupd[.]xyz, now point to Shadowserver's sinkhole servers, with a transfer dated March 20, 2026. Other addresses the updater calls were never Eye's to take and remain with outside owners, the firm said, so machines that reach those are still exposed. Eye found no sign that anyone else was serving code through the addresses: the ones already registered by other people were parked or up for sale, not pushing updates to the machines calling them. The flaw is not listed in CISA's catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 23, 2026. What Popcorn Time Users Should Do Switching off the updater does not make the app safe. Eye said Popcorn Time runs on a 2014 browser engine with its security sandbox turned off, loads content over unencrypted connections, and pulls in code from other abandoned web addresses. Eye registered those abandoned addresses too, which it said would have let it run its own code on every machine that opened the app. It did not, but it built a working proof of concept, so the risk is real. The update only changed the updater, so the rest of the app remains dangerous for anyone who keeps using Popcorn Time. Eye's advice is to uninstall Popcorn Time. The updater can also be turned off by hand: on Windows with two commands that stop and disable its "Update service," and on a Mac with one that unloads the PT.updd helper. Removing the app is the safer step, because disabling the updater leaves the rest of it in place. Windows: sc.exe stop "Update service" Windows: sc.exe config "Update service" start= disabled Mac: launchctl unload -w /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist On Android, the updater is built into the app and cannot be turned off on its own, and it installs only if the user taps to accept, so Eye did not send updates to Android devices. Removing the app is the only fix there. To check a network, defenders can look for the two updater files, Updater.exe on Windows and PT.updd on Mac, and for traffic to the web addresses in Eye's write-up, which lists all 20 domains and the file hashes.

1smfce.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 24, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added two vulnerabilities impacting Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing reports of active exploitation in the wild. The critical-severity vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server (aka richdocumentscode) when used within the NextCloud platform that could allow remote code execution via "proxy.php" when the CODE local document server isn't running. (Fixed in September 2026 in version 26.4.303) CVE-2026-114625 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An SQL injection vulnerability in on-premise versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator that could allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality. (Fixed in October 2026 in versions 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12) As reported by The Hacker News, threat actors have been observed exploiting CVE-2026-110447 to backdoor Nextcloud servers with a web shell so as to conduct reconnaissance and search for credential stores, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. As for CVE-2026-114625, successful exploitation requires an attacker to have network access to the VCO web interface and a valid authenticated session on the VCO portal. The minimum user role required is Enterprise Read Only. Although Arista has acknowledged that the vulnerability is "known to be actively exploited," it has not attributed the activity to a particular threat actor or provided technical details on how the vulnerability is being exploited and what actions the attackers took after privilege escalation. The company also has not disclosed the number of affected organizations. However, it has shared two IP addresses geolocated to Japan as responsible for driving the activity - 74.82.197[.]86 38.54.50[.]151 CVE-2026-114625 is the third vulnerability in the same product to have been weaponized in the wild since July 2026, following CVE-2026-16812 (CVSS score: 10.0) and CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS score: 10.0). In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by October 26, 2026, to secure their networks.

36ungx.text: Researchers remotely disabled a vulnerable updater in the abandoned Time4Popcorn app, a fork of the Popcorn Time BitTorrent client, closing a security flaw that could have allowed attackers to execute malicious code with elevated privileges on millions of computers. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612, affects Windows and macOS updaters that contacted the app's abandoned domain (popcorntimeupd.xyz) over unencrypted HTTP and accepted executables without verifying digital signatures. Anyone controlling the update domain could manipulate HTTP traffic and execute code as SYSTEM on Windows and as root on macOS. The Popcorn Time app featured a Netflix-style interface that integrated BitTorrent downloads, allowing users to consume illegal content right directly inside the app. The project was abandoned for legal reasons but later relaunched as a legitimate content-streaming app. However, forks such as Time4Popcorn emerged under the Popcorn Time name, quickly attracting millions of users. Researchers at Eye Security discovered the security risk after registering the popcorntimeupd.xyz domain and observed up to 3 million Windows and 350,000 macOS client connections to Time4Popcorn. Location of Time4Popcorn ​​​​users Source: Eye Security Connections came from residential ISPs and corporate, government, and military networks. However, none of the users appeared to be actively using the app, suggesting it had been installed and forgotten. “If we were able to send an update, we could potentially get code execution on millions of systems,” Eye Securit notes, adding that “the impact would be severe if this were to fall into the wrong hands.” Following this discovery, the researchers registered 14 more domains associated with the service. Securing the systems Between November 2025 and March 2026, Eye used the vulnerable update mechanism to deliver remediation code that stopped and disabled the updater. Their payload collected no host data or telemetry, and deleted no files on the users’ computers, keeping their actions within a fully legal context. Eye explains that it had to modify its payload during testing to evade antivirus products that flagged it for disabling a service. After deploying the remediation, Eye recorded 2 million update downloads, and by March 1 this year, requests to its update domain dropped by 98%. Following the successful completion of the remediation operation, domain ownership was passed to the non-profit security organization The Shadowserver Foundation. Despite this success, the researchers warned that the risk is not fully eliminated for users of the app. First, Android users remain exposed as installing an update would require user interaction, and researchers could not disable the updater remotely for the mobile platform. Second, the Time4Popcorn app uses a severely outdated Chrome engine from 2014, with no sandbox protections, which could be exploited in attacks. The best course of action would be for users to remove the software entirely from their systems. fc0k0a.text: Microsoft says Teams will begin using AI-powered phishing detection in early November 2026 to detect malicious behavior in messages. The rollout is part of a targeted release phase expected to end by mid-November, with the new security feature likely reaching general availability worldwide between early and mid-December. Microsoft first revealed in a Microsoft 365 Roadmap entry last week that the AI-powered phishing detection will use conversation context (without retaining message content) to identify phishing and suspicious behavior in higher-risk messaging scenarios, such as external first-contact chats. "Microsoft Teams is introducing AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection to help identify phishing, social engineering, impersonation attempts, and deceptive intent," the company said in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update on Wednesday. "The capability analyzes conversation context to identify suspicious behavior that may not include traditional indicators such as malicious links or files." Microsoft says IT admins won't need to take any action to enable this new security protection feature, which will focus on external first-contact chats for most users. Teams AI-powered phishing detection (Microsoft) ​It also added that while the new Teams feature will analyze conversation context to discover suspicious behavior, it will not retain customer data for further AI training or other uses. "This capability is used only for security protection and not for productivity, summarization, advertising, user monitoring, or other non-security purposes," Microsoft said. "Customer message content is not retained by the detection system for model training or other secondary uses." This is part of a broader list of Teams security changes, with Microsoft announcing in December that admins could lock external users via the Defender portal starting in January to thwart cybercrime groups (including ransomware gangs) from abusing Teams in social engineering attacks that target victims' employees. It also began rolling out a new Teams meeting protection policy in August that lets admins block all identified external bots automatically from joining meetings. Last month, Microsoft also revealed that Teams will blur QR codes sent by external senders to better protect against fraud and phishing attempts, and that it will let users report suspicious guest invitations directly in Teams to help security teams block phishing attempts and other attacks abusing guest invitations. More recently, in early October, the company announced plans to introduce support for third-party deepfake detection solutions and impersonation protection in Teams meetings. 1gpxdv.text: Diplomatic organizations in Central Asia have been targeted by a sophisticated new Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) bootkit called BlackX. The activity, which singled out diplomatic entities in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan in early 2026, is suspected to be orchestrated by a China-linked state-sponsored hacking group known as APT41, Kaspersky said in a technical report published this week. The primary objective behind deploying the malware is to undermine Microsoft Windows startup defenses, along with third-party security solutions, while maintaining long-term, covert access to compromised devices. Notably, BlackX is assessed to be an updated version of BlackLotus, a notorious bootkit that was first observed being advertised on cybercrime forums in late 2022, before its existence was officially confirmed by ESET in March 2023. BlackLotus is designed to exploit a now-patched Secure Boot bypass vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS score: 4.4), also known as Baton Drop, to load malicious code before the operating system starts. However, successful exploitation hinges on an attacker having administrator privileges or physical access to a target host. "It is critical to note that a threat actor's use of this bootkit is primarily a persistence and defense evasion mechanism," Microsoft noted at the time. "It is not a first-stage payload or an initial access vector and can only be deployed to a device to which a threat actor has already gained either privileged access or physical access." That said, completely addressing the threat requires additional actions beyond installing the latest update, including running manual steps to apply Microsoft's Secure Boot revocation mitigations, such as adding the "Windows Production PCA 2011" certificate to the Secure Boot UEFI Forbidden List (DBX). The Russian cybersecurity company has found that attackers are capitalizing on the fact that organizations have not carried out these manual steps, enabling them to still use the Baton Drop vulnerability even on systems that have the "patch" applied. "On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted," researchers Georgy Kucherin, Vladimir Nestor, and Vasily Berdnikov said. "It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit." Attackers have been observed deploying BlackX after breaching victim networks through an unspecified method and gaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, the threat actor drops the following files - inst.exe, an installer executable PVMDIJGKAX2, an encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation The installer is then launched via the command line as "C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1," where "Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1" is the RC4 key used for decryption. The binary then drops additional files to both system and UEFI partitions to exploit CVE-2022-21894 in a manner that's "remarkably similar" to the one used in BlackLotus. The end goal remains the same: install Machine Owner Keys (MOK) to load arbitrary EFI files on the infected hosts and interfere with Secure Boot. What's interesting here is that the source code of BlackLotus has never entered the public domain, indicating that the threat actors behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the original bootkit or purchased its source code from another party. "Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors," Kaspersky said. The UEFI payload delivered following the exploitation of the vulnerability is engineered to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. The driver has been signed with a certificate belonging to a company named Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio. The certificate has since been revoked by the issuer. Like in the case of the bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) attack, the driver attempts to tamper with the functioning of endpoint security software installed on the machine. In an interesting twist, some of the unauthorized modifications are allowed to run only if security programs associated with Kaspersky or Avast are present. However, Kaspersky's analysis has found these routines to be ineffective. Not just content with trying to render security solutions ineffective, the driver also drops a user-mode payload for cyber espionage. Two such payloads have been observed - A remote access trojan that can deliver additional .NET payloads, while using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk for command-and-control (C2) to blend in with regular enterprise workflows. It's also equipped to harvest system information and upload files of interest. A malicious DLL dubbed OxiDLLRunner that's sideloaded by the legitimate "googleupdate.exe" binary, which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts and launches a Rust payload that communicates with "archivetj[.]com" to receive and execute more DLL plugins. BlackX's connections to APT41 stem from an ESET report in June 2026, which documented FishMonger's use of a Windows backdoor called SprySOCKS in attacks targeting government entities in Honduras, Taiwan, Thailand, and Pakistan between 2023 and 2024. FishMonger, also tracked as Aquatic Panda and Earth Lusca, is assessed to be operating under the APT41 umbrella. The Slovakian cybersecurity company said it also found "limited indications" that some versions of the backdoor may feature a UEFI bootkit component likely exploiting CVE‑2023‑24932, another security feature bypass vulnerability linked to BlackLotus. An interesting overlap is the presence of the "xdd" string in BlackX and the kernel implant used by FishMonger, raising the possibility that the UEFI bootkit used in those attacks is none other than BlackX. The second clue that points to China-aligned hackers is the use of DLL sideloading to deploy the payloads – a pattern that's extremely common among threat actors of Chinese origin. "By adapting a commercial crimeware tool, the group could bypass procedures intended to protect the Windows boot processes," Kucherin said. "This hybrid approach proves that sophisticated adversaries do not need to reinvent the wheel to establish persistent, invisible control over high-value networks."

zu3c0.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security Ruby has released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to fix three bugs in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into the language. The bugs lie behind four critical security flaws that GitLab patched over the past month. GitLab found that a specially crafted pattern could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles it, potentially leading to code execution on its own servers. Ruby says any application that builds a regular expression from text an attacker controls is affected, not just GitLab. Which Applications Are Affected In its advisory, Ruby said an application is affected only if it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls. That happens when a program passes such a string to Regexp.new, Regexp.union or Regexp.compile, or places it inside a pattern through interpolation, as in /#{input}/. Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected. Ruby fixed the bugs in 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13. The 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 releases are the first in their series to carry any of the three fixes. Ruby 4.0: upgrade to 4.0.9 Ruby 3.4: upgrade to 3.4.12 Ruby 3.3: upgrade to 3.3.13 An earlier release from the same week, 4.0.8, does not include the fix for one of the flaws, CVE-2026-110264, so 4.0 users should install 4.0.9. Ruby 3.2 and earlier will not get a fix. Ruby 3.2 reached end of life on April 1, 2026, and 3.2.11 was its final release. Ruby recommends moving to 3.4 or 4.0. If you cannot upgrade yet, the advisory says to stop compiling regular expressions from untrusted input. Two defenses that look like they would help do not. Setting Regexp.timeout does not stop these bugs. Capping the length of a pattern is also unreliable because short patterns can trigger bugs. How the Bugs Reached GitLab GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as the patterns in a CI/CD configuration. It found that crafted patterns could corrupt memory as Ruby compiled them, and it issued four CVEs between September 23 and October 21, fixing each by shipping a patched Ruby. The first two, disclosed on September 23, each need a logged-in account and were rated 9.9 out of 10. The two from October, CVE-2026-97229 on the 12th and CVE-2026-110264 on the 21st, need no account and were rated 10.0, the maximum. CVE-2026-110264 reaches every GitLab version from 7.0 onward. A researcher using the handle joaxcar reported all four through GitLab's bug bounty program. As of October 23, none of the four was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. No Ruby CVE, for Now Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for these fixes, "at least for now," it said, and told users to track the issues by GitLab's four CVE numbers instead. That leaves a gap for anyone who scans by CVE. GitLab's CVE records name only GitLab as the affected product, so a scanner that checks those records against installed Ruby versions has nothing to match. Ruby has treated this kind of bug as a vulnerability before, assigning CVE numbers to fixes in 2022 and 2024, even though it has long been unsafe to build a regular expression from untrusted input. Its documentation still describes untrusted patterns only as a denial-of-service risk. Ruby said it will update its advisory if it requests any CVE identifiers. For GitLab Administrators Self-managed GitLab instances need the release that fixes CVE-2026-110264. GitLab shipped it on October 21 and backported it as far as version 18.11.13. 19.5.1 19.4.3 19.3.6 19.2.9 19.1.9 19.0.10 18.11.13 GitLab.com already runs the patched version, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on recent internal releases need no action, GitLab said. Because GitLab bundles its own copy of Ruby and patched it there, installing one of these fixed versions applies the fix. GitLab also published detection rules that self-managed administrators can use to look for signs of exploitation attempts.

1m29kec.text: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven intrusion ecosystem run by affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups. Central to the operation is an "Autonomous Red Team Kill Chain Framework" referred to as Phantom. The threat actor is assessed to be Russian-speaking and functions both as an intrusion and data-extortion operator, as well as an infrastructure provider supporting different partners across the ransomware ecosystem. "The operators exploited edge and remote-access systems at scale, including FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel, and VPN gateways," SOCRadar said. "They used AI-managed knowledge bases to track victims, stolen credentials, and campaign progress." A notable aspect that defines the campaign is its "AI-executed, human-approved operating structure" in which a human operator provides a victim-specific prompt and reviews every step, while the intrusions themselves are executed through OpenCode with OpenRouter-hosted commercial models. An examination of the exposed directory at 45.227.254[.]43 has revealed the activity logged 8,257 messages across 133 sessions. Should the models refuse to act on the prompts, the operator has been found to rewrite requests as an authorized red team assessment instead of simply switching models. Initial access is achieved by exploiting public-facing edge devices at scale, following which the attackers move laterally, establish persistence, exfiltrate data, and escalate toward ransomware deployment. Operator records indicate that the attacks involve the exploitation of the following flaws - CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal) (Actively exploited) CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient authentication bypass) (Actively exploited) CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM authentication bypass) (Actively exploited) CVE-2026-15409 (SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF) (Staged for targeting, no confirmed compromise) CVE-2026-63030 (WordPress wp2shell) (Developed) CVE-2026-42208 (LiteLLM SQL injection) (Developed or referenced) CVE-2026-9082 (Drupal SQL injection) (Developed or referenced) "Once inside, the operators followed a recurring lifecycle: enumerate the domain, escalate to domain admin where possible, harvest credentials with stealer tooling, prioritize finance, HR, legal and executive files, and collect them over reverse-SOCKS tunnels," SOCRadar said. "Credential reuse was the main force multiplier; in one case, a single reused password unlocked the VPN, servers, RMM, backup and security management platforms at once. Security products were impaired with a BYOVD killer and loader-level evasion, although the operators' own logs record mixed results against enterprise EDRs." Supporting the threat actor in their goals is a diverse toolkit comprising bespoke frameworks, modified open-source tools, and compiled binaries - Phantom, an AI-powered offensive security and penetration testing framework that's deployed in live operations via OpenCode and employs an agent that communicates with an external server to retrieve tasks, execute commands, and return outputs. It supports 18 skill modules to facilitate reconnaissance, binary reverse engineering, exploit research, steganography, telemetry assessment, and EDR fingerprinting, among others. WormGPT-MCP, a set of 32 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connecting the AI system to 32 different modules that span functions ranging from reconnaissance to extortion. Ghost C2, a collection of three generations of polymorphic implants that communicate with a remote server over Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS, and execute tasking and maintain persistent beacons on compromised endpoints. RevSocks, a reverse SOCKS5 framework used to pivot inside victim networks and stage data for exfiltration. Other tools include a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent dubbed QuickLine, a Quick Heal/Seqrite EDR killer that abuses the Zemana driver ("zam64.sys") as part of a BYOVD attack, and exfiltration programs such as rks3 and BackupAgent. Analysis of dozens of AI-authored extortion records shows that the threat actors adopt a data-centric approach. It involves examining the stolen financials to determine the amount a victim can pay without having to involve a bank or an insurer, and then sending masked proof samples and ramping up pressure through scripted vishing calls and threatening to notify customers, partners, and regulators. The stolen data is eventually published on the data leak site if the victim fails to pay within a 24-72 hour deadline. That said, the final outcomes of these ransom demands are unknown as no cryptocurrency wallet or payment record has been recovered. A total of 62 organizations are estimated to have been targeted by the operation, out of which four of them ended up being listed on the data leak sites for INC and The Gentlemen ransomware. The U.S. accounts for more than 50% of the targets. The attacks also primarily targeted industrial, manufacturing, and energy sectors, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations. "Across this exposed infrastructure, the actors engaged in widespread exploitation of exposed internet services, specifically targeting FortiClient EMS gateways, Ivanti/Citrix/SonicWall/OpenVPN gateways, SimpleHelp remote management servers, and cPanel hosting controls," SOCRadar said. "Concurrently, they orchestrated operations via the Phantom framework, established RevSocks reverse-SOCKS proxies for network pivoting, deployed Ghost C2 variants, and utilized AI-managed knowledge bases to meticulously log victim telemetry, compromised credentials, and active campaign statuses."

35qu9r.text: Microsoft says Windows Server 2016 will stop receiving security updates after it reaches the end of support in January 2027. Windows Server 2016 was released in September 2016 at Microsoft's annual Ignite conference and reached general availability one month later, on October 12, 2016 It reached the end of mainstream support in January 2022, and extended support will end in roughly three months, on January 12. "The January 2027 Windows security update will be the last update available for this version. After this date, devices running Windows Server 2016 will no longer receive monthly security updates containing protections from the latest security threats," Microsoft said in a message center update. "This end of updates in 2027 applies to all editions of Windows Server 2016: Datacenter, Essentials, MultiPoint Premium and Standard." On the same date, Microsoft will also stop support for all Windows Server 2016 Essentials features, including Remote Web Access and related Essentials-specific functionality. Admins advised to switch to Windows Server 2025 Before Windows Server 2016 reaches the end of support, Microsoft advised IT administrators to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, which started rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024. "To help keep your environment protected and supported, plan to upgrade to Windows Server 2025," the company added. Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server. According to Microsoft's lifecycle platform, it will reach the end of mainstream support in November 2029 and receive an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034. Those who want to test Windows Server 2025 before deployment can get a free 180-day Windows Server 2025 trial via the Microsoft Evaluation Center. More information about Windows servicing dates is available on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or via the Lifecycle Policy search tool. Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced that systems running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions stopped receiving security and non-security preview updates and advised customers to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 (also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update). Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. Get the report

n4mo4b.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale campaign that has targeted exposed network edge devices such as Fortinet FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect firewalls. "Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration," according to a joint investigation published by Group-IB and NyxLab. The widespread exploitation activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as k0t, who also goes by the aliases CryptoFeel, Member19, and QazWsxShop. The cybercriminal actor was first seen in the wild on October 22, 2025. The threat actor is assessed to share connections with ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely operating as an initial access broker or an affiliate. Analysis of the threat actor's dark web activity reveals a keen interest in purchasing vulnerability exploit code and tools or premium accounts for metadata search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye. The campaign's victims are global and belong to a broad range of sectors, given the indiscriminate targeting of exposed network devices. A significant chunk of compromises are said to have taken place between February and June 2026, which also overlaps with another credential harvesting campaign codenamed FortiBleed. Nearly 38% of victims are concentrated in the Asia Pacific region, followed by 31.9% in Latin America, 15.8% in Europe, and 12.7% in the Middle East and North Africa. The attack chain plays out as follows - Conduct reconnaissance through public scanning tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances, filter candidates by product, and put together target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices. Attempt to exploit these devices via known vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 (a path traversal flaw in FortiWeb) and CVE-2026-0257 (an authentication bypass flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Prisma Access) through bespoke Python scripts named "fortnew.py" and "exploit_2026_0257.py," or perform brute-force attacks using common username and password combinations, to obtain initial access. Establish a foothold on the targets via an OpenConnect VPN connection. Conduct post-exploitation actions and additional credential theft like enumeration of Active Directory, SMB, and installed antivirus solution. Establish persistence on the host via legitimate remote access tools like MeshCentral Agent, Atera, Teramind, and AnyDes, as well as an open-source, adversary-emulation framework known as AdaptixC2. Exfiltrate harvested data using Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives. The attacks are also characterized by the use of legitimate administrator and pentesting utilities like NetExec, SoftPerfect, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam, and Mimikatz to burrow deeper into victims' corporate environments. "k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations," Group-IB and NyxLab researchers said. "His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets." "The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign." k0t's links to Qilin and The Gentlemen stem from the fact that many victims of the campaign were also later listed by the ransomware groups on their data leak sites. However, the exact nature of the connection between the threat and these gangs is unclear. What's more, Group-IB and NyxLab said they found a "negligible overlap" in compromised data between this activity and FortBleed. More than 70,000 exposed credentials associated with network devices and LDAP dumps have been identified in connection with the campaign. "This aligns with reports that many operators are likely to be involved in the FortiBleed activity cluster, suggesting that this may be a separate dataset, operator subset, or related access operation within the broader FortiBleed-related activity," the researchers said. "Organisations are advised to act on ensuring that any vulnerabilities mentioned in this report are appropriately remedied."

10pw4j3.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security PHP has warned of another way an attacker could run code on a web server, two days after it shipped emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell flaws. The new issue, assigned CVE-2026-115560, affects only web applications configured in an unusual way, and PHP considers it an unlikely risk. The project is not issuing an emergency fix for it. Instead, it recommends turning off a feature called session upload progress until a fix is available in the next routine release. The warning came in a short informational advisory published on October 23. It follows the October 21 emergency release that fixed two critical PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which let an attacker without an account run code on a server. Those were patched in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The new issue is separate and is not fixed by those releases. Only a narrow setup is at risk. PHP says the problem can occur when a web application does all of the following: sets the session.serialize_handler option to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, then changes that option to php while running by calling ini_set(), and makes that change before it calls session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be turned on. An application that never changes the serialize handler while running can leave the feature on and is not exposed through this path. PHP says this setup is unlikely in practice. The action is one line. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next routine bugfix release. This is the same setting it already listed as a mitigation in the October 21 advisory for CVE-2026-109619. Anyone who applied it then and left it in place needs to do nothing more for the new issue. Session upload progress is turned on by default and lets an application track the progress of a file upload. Because the setup is uncommon, PHP is handling the fix as part of its regular release cycle rather than as an emergency, and it will publish a full advisory for CVE-2026-115560 with the next release. PHP has not stated which versions are affected, which releases will contain the fix, or a severity score. It also has not said whether the new issue shares a root cause with CVE-2026-109619. No exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 has been reported; the attacks reported since October 21 target the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws. Separately, attempts to exploit the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws have surged. Amazon said its honeypots logged an exploit attempt against CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on October 17, four days before the flaws were disclosed, and Cloudflare said attempts rose from tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the October 21 disclosure to millions by early October 22.Attackers have tried to use the flaws to install a Mirai botnet variant, according to Sophos and Arctic Wolf. Those attempts have so far failed: Previdian, Wordfence and others report scanning and probing but no confirmed code execution, and researchers say a reliable exploit is proving harder to build than expected. That activity targets the two flaws patched on October 21, not CVE-2026-115560, which has not been reported under attack.

1tjtc5m.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 23, 2026Malware / Cyber Espionage The Russian state-sponsored hacking group Sandworm teamed up with another threat actor to carry out a destructive wiping attack targeting a Ukrainian logistics company last year. According to ESET, the attack involved UAC-0099 (aka Earth Sirrush) obtaining initial access to the target on July 16, 2025, via a spear-phishing email bearing a malware-laced attachment that led to the deployment of the MATCHWOK backdoor via a downloader called MATCHBOIL. The activity ultimately culminated with the threat actor handing off access to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17, 2025, more than two months after it obtained a foothold. What makes the attack stand out is UAC-0099's use of a previously undocumented backdoor called MythicRatatoskr that communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. The backdoor was deployed a day after MATCHWOK was executed. There are indications that development on the backdoor started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025. Its functionality is fairly straightforward in that it sends victim metadata to the C2 server, poll for new commands, transmit command output, take screenshots, and upload/download files. It can also alter the current working directory, enumerate directory contents, change the C2 server URL, execute a shell command via "cmd.exe," and spawn a reverse SOCKS5 proxy. In addition, some artifacts include a 10-minute startup delay in a likely effort to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network and evade detection. "To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor, and it may signal a broader trend of adversaries adopting experimental peer-to-peer networks to increase the resilience and stealth of their infrastructure," ESET researchers Anton Cherepanov and Peter Strýček said. MythicRatatoskr is said to have been used to deploy a SOCKS5 server to route connections through the compromised network. The attack culminated with Sandworm carrying out a data-wiping attack by dropping the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy. It's worth noting that the Sandworm-linked NikoWiper malware is also derived from SDelete. Yggdrasil map with the C&C serve While the attack investigated by ESET compromised a Windows system, source code references to "crond" within MythicRatatoskr suggest there possibly exists an equivalent Linux version of the malware. The assessment that UAC-0099 is likely collaborating with Sandworm is not new. In its APT Activity Report Q2 2025–Q3 2025, ESET said it observed UAC-0099 conducting initial access operations and subsequently transferring "validated targets" to Sandworm for further post-exploitation. These attacks targeted government, energy, logistics, and grain sectors in Ukraine, the Slovak cybersecurity company noted at the time. This sort of cooperation between Russia-aligned actors is also not new. Last year, ESET said it identified evidence that Gamaredon and Turla were working together to target and co-compromise Ukrainian entities, with one intrusion leveraging Gamaredon's PteroGraphin to deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor. Furthermore, a Gamaredon-linked downloader called Pterodo has been used to retrieve and execute InvisiMole, a modular spyware program put to use against targets in Ukraine and Russia. "This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyber espionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact," ESET said.

1se2rnk.text: Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open. The flaw, CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first. Ghostscript can read a name chosen by an attacker as instructions rather than as a file, and point it to a second file that carries commands to run. Pillow's maintainers fixed it in version 13.0.0, released on October 16. Pillow turns up almost everywhere Python handles images: web upload forms, avatar and thumbnail tools, document and PDF pipelines, and most machine-learning projects pull it in. OX Security, the firm whose report drew attention to the flaws, estimates the library is downloaded about 436 million times a month. Version 13.0.0 is a large security release, with fixes across four severity levels, from low to critical, two of which are rated critical by the maintainers. None of the flaws is known to be under attack. The weakness is the filename, not the picture. "The flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document," the advisory says, meaning a harmless EPS file can still cause damage when an attacker sets its name. That makes upload endpoints that keep or build a stored file's name from user input the realistic target. The flaw only reaches Ghostscript on hosts that have the gs program installed, which Pillow needs to open EPS at all. It affects Pillow from version 2.6.0 up to 12.3.0. The maintainers rate it moderate, because the attacker has to control the filename. The CVE record assigned by GitHub rates it 9.2 out of 10 and marks it as the same condition. Two of the fixes sit in the maintainers' top "critical" tier. One is a separate memory bug, described in the release notes as stale image data reused after a mode change. The other covers two overflow flaws in Pillow's JPEG decoding. One of those JPEG flaws, in the FlashPix (FPX) format, was shown to run an attacker's command from a single call to Image.open() on a crafted file, as long as the optional olefile package is installed. Pillow recognizes these files by their content, not their extension, so a server that opens untrusted uploads can be hit with no user action. The other, CVE-2026-112403, overflows a memory buffer when a program makes a thumbnail of a crafted lossless JPEG. Its advisory reports a crash, not code execution. The bug was "found by Anthropic using Claude to study the security of open-source software, validated manually by Ada Logics," the advisory says, part of a wider effort by the company that has turned up hundreds of flaws in open-source libraries. A third flaw, CVE-2026-112393, has been in Pillow since 2013. It overflows a memory buffer when a program saves a compressed TIFF image to memory rather than to a file on disk, the common pattern for a service that re-encodes an upload and hands it back. The advisory says the reporters crashed the process with it, and turned it into code execution only with the help of a second, separate flaw that leaked memory addresses. Saving to a real file on disk is not affected. The CVE records, assigned by GitHub, score the EPS, TIFF, and JPEG-thumbnail flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. Each depends on conditions the score does not carry, and the maintainers' own ratings for the batch run from moderate to critical. In the CVE records, CISA's analysts mark no known exploitation for the EPS flaw and a public proof of concept for the TIFF one. What to do Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0, which fixes all of these, and rebuild any containers, wheels, or base images that bundle an older copy. Pillow 13 drops Python 3.10, so installs still on 3.10 need Python 3.11 or newer as well. pip install -U "Pillow>=13.0.0" Until you can upgrade, Pillow's security guidance and the advisories point to steps that cut each path: EPS / Ghostscript: keep the gs program off any host that processes untrusted uploads, and never pass an attacker-controlled filename to Image.open() for EPS. JPEG thumbnails: avoid draft() and thumbnail() on untrusted JPEGs, or call load() first, or pass reducing_gap=None. TIFF: treat saving a TIFF to an in-memory buffer such as io.BytesIO as a sensitive path when the image came from a user.

1ukioqa.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Malicious Brotli data can make an application on an official build of Node.js run attacker-supplied code, security researchers at Imperva have demonstrated. Their "Node2Shell" proof of concept ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image for Linux arm64, with no debugger or custom build, by feeding crafted data to the bundled Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497). Node.js disclosed the flaw and released fixes on October 21, and applications that decode untrusted Brotli data should update. Imperva's test did not succeed on every attempt, and code execution took several tries in its Linux arm64 setup. The result covers that one build and application setup, with other architectures and the 22.x and 26.x lines not tested. On the fixed release, 24.22.1, the same data was rejected, and no code ran. The demonstration goes beyond the first public proof of concept, which achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard build, that proof of concept's author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved. No exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22. Which Applications Are Affected The flaw is in the Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles, so it affects applications on the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines, not only the one build Imperva tested. A service reaches that decoder from either side of an HTTP exchange: when it reads a Brotli-compressed response through Node.js's built-in fetch(), or when middleware decodes a Brotli-compressed request body. Express 5's body parsers, such as express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text() and express.raw(), now decode Brotli request bodies when applied to a route, alongside gzip and deflate. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode a Brotli request body just by receiving one, so the decoding needs that middleware or an explicit call. Imperva reproduced code execution through both the request-body and response paths, testing Express 5.0.0 to 5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0 to 2.3.0 at pinned versions, and did not test every release in between. How the Bug Works Imperva traced the cause to how the decoder handles an impossible point in a Brotli stream: the stream announces the block types it will use as decoding runs, and the test input reached a block change that the stream's own structure ruled out. The vulnerable decoder read that as a request for more input and kept going in an invalid state. In a separate test with a memory sanitizer, continuing from that state wrote past an intended buffer, the out-of-bounds write behind the flaw. Node.js fixed the flaw by importing an upstream Brotli patch that makes the decoder stop with a format error at that point instead of continuing. What to Do The fix is to move to a patched release. The update should reach container images and other artifacts that bundle a Node binary, which a package inventory can miss. End-of-life lines 20.x and earlier do not receive the fix and should be moved to a supported line. The advisory lists no workaround inside Node.js, so an application that cannot update at once has no fallback in the runtime. Imperva suggested limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths where that is practical, and said only the update removes the flaw. The company also added rules to its own web application firewall and tested them against the attacks it reproduced. Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace updating.

1nw9arq.text: AI agents paying for API calls with the x402 SDKs could sign a payment for their full balance of a supported token if a malicious API asked for it, security firm V12 said on October 22. The cause was the SDKs' default client, which set no spending limit until releases on August 18 added one. The risk was limited to agents who automatically signed payments and whose apps set no limits. The missing limit is one of 25 flaws V12 found in the x402 code, and one of three it rated critical and described in detail. The x402 Foundation, which maintains the SDKs, had already fixed all three critical flaws in the August 18 releases. One of the other two let a facilitator, the service that checks x402 payments, accept a Solana transaction that moved no tokens as a valid payment. Among the x402 SDKs, only the TypeScript one had this flaw. The other let a malicious server get an agent to sign a login message for a different website. V12 found the flaws by reviewing the code and running local tests. Neither V12 nor the x402 Foundation has publicly reported any attacks using them. The foundation has published no security advisory for the three flaws, and its changelogs list the fixes without calling them security fixes. As of October 23, npm audit returned no advisories for the last TypeScript releases before the fixes, and PyPI listed no vulnerabilities for the last Python release before them, The Hacker News found. A developer who relies on those checks gets no warning to upgrade. Coinbase created x402 and handed it to the x402 Foundation this year, a Linux Foundation project whose members include Visa and Mastercard. Coinbase holds the most senior seat on the foundation's technical steering committee. No Spending Limit in the Default Client x402 is an open standard that lets software, including AI agents, pay for an API call within the web request itself, without requiring a person to approve each payment. A server that wants payment answers with the HTTP status code 402 Payment Required and lists its payment options, each with an amount, a token, and a recipient. The client picks one, signs a payment, and sends the request again. The default client took the first option on the list, and before the fix, it set no limit on the amount. A hostile API could use that to turn a routine data request into a request for the wallet's full balance of a supported token, V12 said. An earlier small payment could reveal the wallet address, so the server could look up the balance first. With an automatic signer and no payment policy set by the app, the client could sign a payment for that amount. For a token that supports signed transfers, the attacker could then submit the signed payment and collect the funds. The August 18 releases added spend controls to the TypeScript, Python, and Go clients. By default, they now cap each payment at $1 and allow only US dollar stablecoins the SDK recognizes, such as USDC. Token Approvals Accepted as Solana Payments In x402, a merchant's server relies on a facilitator to check each payment and submit it to the blockchain. On Solana, the facilitator also pays the transaction fee. The TypeScript facilitator code for Solana checked that a payment called an allowed token program, then read it as a transfer without checking the instruction type. A token approval, which lets another account spend tokens later but moves none itself, differs from a transfer only in its first byte. In V12's local test, the facilitator accepted such an approval as a valid payment. The test did not send a live transaction. A merchant relying on the facilitator could therefore deliver a paid resource while receiving no tokens, V12 said, calling it "a complete payment bypass." The attacker needed a token account, but no balance, and the facilitator paid the transaction fee each time. The Python and Go SDKs already checked the instruction type. The August 18 releases added the same check to the TypeScript code. Every published @x402/svm release from 2.0.0 to 2.22.0 lacks the check, and every release from 2.23.0 on has it, The Hacker News found by searching the published packages. Logins Signed for Other Websites x402 also has a sign-in extension called Sign-In-With-X (SIWx). It lets an agent log in by signing a short message with its wallet, for example to prove an earlier payment instead of paying again. On Ethereum, the message names the website, the wallet address, and a one-time code. The automated client signed these messages without verifying that the website named in them was the one it had contacted. A malicious server could get a fresh login message from another site, pass it to the agent, and use the signature to log in to that site as the agent's wallet, V12 said. That would work wherever the other site accepted the relayed message, and the attacker would get whatever access the login allowed. The August 18 releases make the TypeScript, Python and Go clients refuse to sign unless the site in the message matches the site that sent the 402 response. The project also changed the SIWx specification, which now says a client must refuse to sign when the two do not match. TypeScript code that calls createSIWxPayload directly must now pass the URL of the 402 response, after any redirects. The @x402/fetch and @x402/axios wrappers pass it on their own. What to Update Upgrading to the latest releases also brings later fixes, including one for a separate payment bypass in @x402/core 2.27.0 in September. As of October 23, the latest versions are 2.28.0 for @x402/core, @x402/svm, @x402/extensions, @x402/fetch and @x402/axios, v2.28.0 for the Go module and 2.25.0 for the Python package. In TypeScript, clients get the spending fix by updating @x402/fetch or @x402/axios to 2.23.0 or later, which pulls in the matching @x402/core. Apps that use SIWx also need @x402/extensions 2.23.0 or later, which holds the login check. Facilitators that check Solana payments need @x402/svm 2.23.0 or later. After the upgrade, existing clients are capped at $1 per payment and limited to recognized stablecoins unless the app sets its own spend controls. Apps that pass spendControls: false turn all of these controls off. Teams that cannot upgrade yet can register a payment policy that drops any option above a set amount. The older clients support this with registerPolicy in TypeScript and Go and register_policy in Python, which also has a ready-made max_amount policy. V12 advises clients to check that a SIWx login message identifies the site they contacted before signing, to set budgets for each payment and in total, and to limit which tokens, networks, and recipients they will pay.

c3imod.text: Threat actors have been observed unsuccessfully attempting to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to rope infected systems into a Mirai botnet variant called Potassium, as it emerges that weaponizing the flaws may be harder than previously thought. The attacks aim to exploit CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), which can result in unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests. The vulnerabilities have been patched in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. "However, analysis of the sample revealed that it is an updated and significantly expanded version of the Mirai-derived botnet variant identified in early 2026," Sophos said. "The sample displays downloader and network disruption functionality." Specifically, it resolves a hard-coded, encrypted command-and-control (C2) address, establishes a TCP connection to 134.199.154[.]64, and sends an HTTP request. The malware then checks for an HTTP 200 response status and verifies that the resulting payload begins with the ELF magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, indicating that it expects a Linux ELF binary as a follow-on payload. "A resolver function supports IPv4 addresses and hostname resolution, with additional fallback resolution logic that includes hard-coded public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, and 1.0.0.1," Sophos added. "As with Mirai malware historically, this sample can execute DDoS attacks." The attacks have been found to originate from the following three IP addresses - 85.11.167[.]243 217.60.242[.]76 45.198.224[.]169 These attack sources have been found to contact 92.118.112[.]100 to retrieve a loader, which is responsible for deploying the Mirai botnet variant. Further analysis of the artifact within a network-contained sandbox has revealed that the botnet issues a DNS query for thunder.godofthunder[.]st, resolves it to 134.199.154[.]64, and establishes a C2 channel on TCP port 50792. The end goal is to launch sustained volumetric flood attacks against two adjacent hosts located within a single Ukrainian network - 45.88.138[.]0 45.88.138[.]44 The lack of a successful attack leveraging PHP2Shell in the wild suggests that threat actors are "struggling" to come up with reliable exploits, Sophos added. Potassium was first flagged by botnet tracking platform Synthient in March 2026.
