In a follow-up analysis, Nokia Deepfield researchers described the malware as a Mirai fork which uses "ChaCha20 for the static config table (the first time we have seen ChaCha20 used this way in a Mirai variant), a single static byte (0xED) for everything on the wire, a named reverse-shell protocol (SHELL / SHOUT) on the same channel as attack commands, and a DNS misdirection scheme that swaps the two 16-bit halves of every resolved A record before connect()." Arctic Wolf, which also shared additional details of the same weaponized PHP2Shell exploitation attempt, said the botnet supports 24 commands to facilitate flood attacks over ICMP, TCP, UDP, and OpenVPN protocol. Both builds for ARM and x86 also contain configuration for resolving C2 infrastructure through Ethereum Name Service (ENS). "ENS resolution was disabled in both samples, indicating that the capability was present but inactive," the cybersecurity firm said. "If enabled in future variants, it could complicate disruption by reducing reliance on registrars and DNS providers, requiring defenders to block the ENS names, RPC infrastructure, and resolved command-and-control addresses." Threat Actor Mass Exploits PHP2Shell The development comes as SOCRadar said it found PHP2Shell exploit tooling for PHP 8.4.26 on an exposed attacker-controlled server ("206.188.197[.]105:9999"), alongside three screening scripts that check live websites for preconditions the PHP2Shell chain depends on. The scripts, according to the cybersecurity company, checked about 20 public websites for the PHP version, server setup, and session settings the exploit needs. These websites span Canada, China, Finland, France, Poland, the U.K., and the U.S. "The central file, aslr_exploit.py, is a Python exploit the operator labels a 'one-click' PHP2Shell exploit for PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php," SOCRadar said. "It works entirely over ordinary HTTP requests in three broad steps: it recycles the target's PHP worker, leaks memory addresses through the session cookie to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR), and then abuses PHP's session upload progress handling to run a shell command." ASLR, short for Address Space Layout Randomization, is a cybersecurity mechanism that randomizes the memory locations used by system files and programs each time they are run, making it harder for attackers to predict where code will load. This built-in defense helps defend against memory-based exploits, such as buffer-overflow attacks. The other three companion scripts are as follows - php2shell_fp.py, which reads PHP version and server setup from about 20 sites deep_probe.py, which examines 11 of those sites for visible errors, phpinfo pages, file inclusion, and session injection to ascertain whether they meet exploit prerequisites wp_attack.py, which focuses on five WordPress sites to conduct user and plugin enumeration That said, there is no evidence of shell access on any screened site as of October 22, 2026, indicating the targeted sites did not meet the exploit's preconditions. The toolset is assessed to be part of a broader operation that involves the attacker extracting API keys and backend URLs from websites' client-side JavaScript, systematically sweeping web and API routes for unauthenticated access, and using a pool of rotating proxies to spread traffic and evade rate limits and blocking. "Related artifacts on the server additionally point to web-archive reconnaissance and automated CAPTCHA solving," SOCRadar noted. "Taken together, the toolset points to a financially motivated actor focused on cryptocurrency and Web3 targets." The same exploitation server ("206.188.197[.]105") has also been flagged by Hunt.io, which said the threat actor behind the operation has targeted 123 servers across cloud, shared-hosting and ISP networks. "About 57 run PHP, many on unsupported 5.x to 7.x," the threat intelligence firm said. "Ten rejected the request outright, including three of the five sitting behind Cloudflare. None was exploited." In all, 10 open directories hold PHP2Shell-related tooling - 206.188.197[.]105 102.210.149[.]166 122.10.110[.]72, 122.10.17[.]49 58.221.60[.]160:8000 41.223.30[.]7, 157.230.117[.]70 104.219.251[.]31 107.150.31[.]151 217.160.132[.]82 47.100.125[.]108, 54.169.109[.]7, 139.162.165[.]136 Defeating ASLR Protections The disclosure also coincides with the development of a PHP2Shell exploit that can achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration. "One of the biggest obstacles has been address space layout randomization (ASLR), a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit," Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Hacker News. "Our team developed a novel technique [...] that chains the two vulnerabilities together, using a memory leak to bypass ASLR and achieve remote code execution on x86-64 systems, even with PHP's recommended production error-display setting."ir "We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions. Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome." Consequences of successful exploitation of the flaws are severe, as it permits an attacker to execute code with the permissions of the web application, potentially gaining access to API keys, database connections, and other internal services the application can reach, VulnCheck said. "An attacker doesn't necessarily need administrator or root access to cause significant damage," McIntyre said. "Access to a vulnerable web application could provide a foothold into other parts of an organization's infrastructure." Exploit Attempts Plenty, None Successful The findings dovetail with reports indicating that broad exploitation attempts targeting the flaws are underway, including by a China-based IP address that has been observed trying to drop a web shell via a server-side session file. Web infrastructure company Cloudflare said it observed tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw 45 minutes after the flaws were publicly announced, before climbing to hundreds of thousands within 2 hours and millions as of early October 22, 2026. "So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads," Cisco Talos said. "This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor's own tooling." Data from Previdian's telemetry has so far recorded hundreds of exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-109618 from dozens of IP addresses, and against CVE-2026-109619 to a lesser degree. The first exploit event aimed at CVE-2026-109618 was recorded on October 21, 2026, at 1:05 p.m. UTC. "We've seen plenty of PHP2Shell probes and exploitation attempts in our honeypots," Previdian said. "At the time of writing, we've observed no successful remote code execution and no dropped PHP files. Reliable RCE may be harder to achieve than initially expected." This assessment has also been echoed by Beelzebub, Dataminr, and Wordfence, with observed activity so far limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and attempts to confirm command execution, steal credentials and secrets from environment variables, install persistent access, and retrieve and execute a second-stage payload. Wordfence has shared the following IP addresses as among those attempting to exploit the flaws - 87.121.84[.]174 181.215.186[.]252 185.196.220[.]132 185.161.210[.]29 152.233.51[.]69 45.134.225[.]16 107.189.14[.]87 193.47.62[.]24 2409:40d2:204e:4be:2a1f:f9c9:a055:e00b 103.147.220[.]17 The severity of the flaws has also led to several government, school and hospital websites going offline across Asia, Europe, and North America out of an abundance of caution. The U.K. government has confirmed that 32 digital services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable, largely stemming from the precautionary shutdowns while security updates and mitigations were applied. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has issued approximately 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. "The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012," the Sysdig Threat Research Team said. "The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed." With the fixes not available for older versions of PHP, PHP2Shell is expected to have a long tail, along the lines of Log4Shell. According to estimates from Google-owned VirusTotal, about 272,000 hosts run a supported PHP branch (8.2 to 8.5), Organizations on PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1 are advised to move to a supported branch, or use a distribution backport. Attack surface management platform Censys said it currently detects over 3.08 million hosts and 56.6 million web properties running PHP. Of these, more than 34.4 million PHP services are still assessed to be vulnerable as of October 23, 2026. "Many applications with web servers and similar will likely remain vulnerable until their respective vendors patch these items," Dataminr said. "The implications of this are that many organizations will likely remain vulnerable to some degree for far longer than when patches are directly applied to owned and managed applications."

1fl964t.text: The Hacker NewsOct 22, 2026Enterprise Security / Artificial Intelligence Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching. Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it. If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool? Most of the conversation about AI security is about what threat actors are doing with it. But the bigger threat may already be inside your organization. That's the focus of our upcoming webinar, AI as an Insider Threat: From Shadow AI to Governed AI, with expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender. Save your seat for a practical security playbook on bringing that unseen AI under control. Where AI is hiding on your endpoints It isn't only developers. AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, and browser extensions are turning up across the business. And most of them never cross your network gateway in a way the tools you already run would recognize. The result is a hard irony. The AI with the most access is often the AI your security team can't see. 📅 Save Your Spot: Watch the Webinar The visibility gap, by the numbers According to Bitdefender's 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment report, only 51.8% of organizations report having full visibility into the AI tools their staff use. That leaves nearly half without the full picture. That blind spot has a cost. IBM found that 20% of breached organizations were compromised through shadow AI. Which raises the question: what can organizations realistically do about it? That's exactly what the webinar gets practical about. Register now to see what a lean team can do about the AI it can't yet see. From shadow AI to governed AI New research from Bitdefender Labs looks at what's really running on endpoints, based on real machines; among the findings: a malicious agent skill caught in the wild. Blocking AI outright is the obvious response, but it tends to fail. The alternative is governed adoption, and the session shows what that looks like in practice. What you'll take away Where AI is actually showing up on your endpoints, and why the tools you already run don't see most of it. New research from Bitdefender Labs on real machines, including the malicious agent skill caught in the wild. Why an AI agent with credentials and no owner behaves like an insider risk, and what to do about it. Why blocking AI outright tends to fail, and what governed adoption looks like instead. The AI already running on your endpoints won't wait for a policy. Join expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender, and save your seat for AI as an Insider Threat. 📅 Save Your Spot: Watch the Webinar

1ophimp.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 22, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Attackers are exploiting a zero-day SQL injection flaw in Arista's VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the central management system for VeloCloud SD-WAN networks, the company said in an advisory on October 22. The flaw lets anyone who can log in to the orchestrator, even with a read-only customer account, gain operator privileges, the top level of control over it. For on-premises orchestrators, the fix is in VCO 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12, while Hosted and Dedicated orchestrators have already been patched. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-114625 and rated 9.9 on the CVSS scale. Orchestrators running the releases that fixed the VCO flaws exploited in July and September are still affected, because those releases are older than the new fixes. Arista bought the VeloCloud SD-WAN product line from Broadcom, announcing the deal in July 2025. The products were earlier known as VMware SD-WAN by VeloCloud. To exploit the flaw, an attacker needs network access to the orchestrator's web interface and a valid login. The minimum role is Enterprise Read Only, the lowest built-in role for customer users. VCO is exposed by default, and no VCO setting prevents the exposure. In VCO, operators create the customer and partner accounts, and each partner can manage a group of customers. The flaw allows an attacker to act as a local superuser, a role with full access. It may also allow an attacker to affect the VCO host itself and expose, modify, or disrupt the orchestrator and the data it manages. The advisory does not say when the attacks began, which orchestrators were hit, or what the attackers did after exploiting the flaw. The new flaw is the third in VCO since late July that Arista has reported as exploited, and the first of the three that requires a login. Neither the July flaw (CVE-2026-16812) nor the September flaw (CVE-2026-93952) needed one. Affected and Fixed Releases Each affected release train has its own fix, shown here beside the release that fixed September's flaw on the same train. Release train Affected by CVE-2026-114625 Fixed in CVE-2026-93952 (September) fixed in 5.2 Before 5.2.3.18 5.2.3.18 and later 5.2.3.16 6.1 Before 6.1.3.10 6.1.3.10 and later No fix listed 6.4 Before 6.4.2.12 6.4.2.12 and later 6.4.2.8 VeloCloud Gateway and VeloCloud Edge are not affected. The 7.0 release train is not on the list, and Arista says any release not on the list is not vulnerable. Arista has not checked releases that have reached end of support. Customers on an unsupported release train can contact Arista's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) about upgrade options. As of October 22, September's flaw is fixed only in the 5.2 and 6.4 trains. On 6.1, it affects releases up to 6.1.3.7, and no fixed release is listed. Neither advisory says whether 6.1.3.10 also fixes the September flaw. If You Cannot Upgrade Yet Until the fixed release is installed, Arista recommends these steps: Limit access to the VCO web interface to trusted administrative networks. Monitor the VCO for connections from known malicious IP addresses. Watch for unexpected outbound network activity from the VCO host. Consider blocking outbound ports that normal operation does not need. Watch for backdoor daemons and webshells. Review recent administrator activity for unexpected changes. Checking for Compromise Two IP addresses have been seen carrying out the attacks, according to Arista. Block them and check logs for any sign of them: IP: 74.82.197[.]86 IP: 38.54.50[.]151 Also check VCO web access logs for requests with unusual URL-like path components, encoded characters, references to local or internal services, or high request rates. If you suspect a compromise, save evidence before fixing anything, where possible. That means the VCO web access, backend application, system and database logs, along with the relevant file-system timestamps. Regarding the July and September flaws, Arista warned that a compromised orchestrator could also grant attackers access to VeloCloud Edge devices. For this flaw, the advisory does not say whether the risk applies or whether upgrading removes access that an attacker has already gained.

1u6julm.text: eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority (CA), will withdraw from its global SSL/TLS certificate business, its board decided on Thursday. The decision came five days after a researcher reported recovering the private keys of eight of its intermediate CA certificates. eMudhra said it will replace affected customers' certificates with free ones from partners, though its announcement did not name the partners or provide a date for the exit. Six of those eight were for website (TLS) certificates. Chrome will stop trusting the eMudhra root certificate above them, emSign ECC Root CA - G3. The change is expected to reach users on the morning of October 27, Pacific time. On October 20, Mozilla decided to stop trusting the same root in Firefox. Removing a root from a browser also cuts off legitimate certificates issued beneath it. About 30,800 unexpired certificates chained to that root as of October 21, by Chrome's count of public Certificate Transparency (CT) logs. Of those, 99.9% were issued through InCommon, the certificate service Internet2 created for the higher education community. InCommon moved the service onto eMudhra's CertiNext platform between April and July this year. Google has told website operators with certificates under that root that they "must immediately acquire and install a new TLS certificate from another PKI hierarchy included in the Chrome Root Store." Until the transition is complete, eMudhra said, its G1 RSA root certificates will continue to serve customers. G1 is a separate hierarchy from the ECC root, but Chrome is still deciding whether to keep eMudhra's remaining CA certificates in its root store. eMudhra will keep its revocation and status services running until every SSL/TLS certificate it issued has expired or been replaced. Its other businesses, including digital signature certificates, eSign and the CertiNext platform InCommon uses, will continue. The announcement does not mention InCommon, or say whether eMudhra will keep issuing new certificates under G1 until it exits. eMudhra said the global SSL/TLS business brings in about 1% of its revenue. Data sovereignty and compliance rules make it more complex and costly to run, and some large providers give the certificates away free. The incident's spread on social media has also brought "scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business," the company said. The researcher reported the weak keys to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and eMudhra on October 17. Each private key should have been a huge random number, but all eight were below 256, so anyone could work them out almost instantly. Chrome and Firefox blocked the six TLS intermediates within hours. No website certificate from them had appeared in CT logs before Chrome's block, so none could have been used against Chrome or other software that requires CT logging, Google said. eMudhra said it never used the eight to issue certificates to websites or users, and that its systems were not breached. What Certificate Holders Can Do Cornell has told its certificate holders to request RSA certificates instead of ECC ones, because "RSA certificates use eMudhra's unaffected root and should work." The university counts more than 300 affected certificates of its own. The University of Michigan says InCommon's RSA certificates are not currently affected, but that their root "could become distrusted, too." For now, its main alternative is Let's Encrypt. eMudhra has estimated that about 30,000 certificates need to be moved, and that about 97% of them were issued using ACME, the protocol many servers use to request and renew certificates automatically. Chrome has told eMudhra that standard ACME clients do not replace certificates outside their renewal window unless they support ACME Renewal Information (ARI) or someone steps in by hand. Moving from the ECC hierarchy to the RSA one may also need changes to client settings. Questions Over eMudhra's RSA Root Mozilla said on October 20 that, for now, it was not removing trust in the G1 root, emSign Root CA - G1. At Stanford, InCommon certificates chain to that root through an eMudhra CA called emSign Root TLS CA - G1. On October 14, eMudhra published a certificate revocation list (CRL) for emSign Root TLS CA - G1. A CRL is the signed list of certificates a CA has revoked. This one's signature does not verify against that CA's own key, the researcher who reported the weak keys said in Mozilla's public bug report on the incident. A participant in the same bug report said on October 22 that the list appears to have been signed with the key of an eMudhra OCSP certificate. OCSP certificates sign answers about whether a certificate has been revoked. The participant wrote that the match "appears to be a case of using the wrong signing key, rather than evidence of another weak key." Chrome raised the list on October 21, in one of 12 questions it posted to the bug report. It asked which key signed it, and whether eMudhra holds more than one key pair for that CA or for any of its roots. Chrome also asked whether customers are moving to G1, to another company's CA, or both, and when all of them will have moved, given its planned October 27 removal. eMudhra said on October 20 that G1 was "the only alternative available," and the next day that it is issuing its affected US customers fresh certificates "from an alternate, independently operated, publicly trusted CA hierarchy." In 2025, eMudhra published invalid CRLs for six of the same intermediates. Its incident report at the time said it fixed them by "regenerating the CRLs using the appropriate private key associated with each Intermediate CA." On October 19, eMudhra told Mozilla that those lists were first signed with the keys it meant to use. When that produced invalid signatures, they were "resigned with flawed keys," the weak keys found this month. Chrome said that disclosure "raises serious concerns regarding eMudhra's transparency and incident handling" during and after the 2025 incident. It asked why the 2025 report did not mention that two key pairs existed for each of those CAs. As of 13:31 UTC on Thursday, eMudhra had not answered any of Chrome's questions publicly on the bug report. Its last visible comment there was posted on October 20.

1q84nv7.text: But those big headlines are only half the story. Stolen passwords, exposed databases, broken login checks, and trusted tools being turned against their users are causing trouble too. Some attacks are clever. Others work because someone left a simple security gap open.This ThreatsDay, we're digging into the stories that didn't make as much noise but still deserve attention. Some are strange, some are serious, and a few might surprise you. Here's everything else you shouldn't miss this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. 4,500+ accounts compromised Bluesky has acknowledged it's aware of a phishing attack that has compromised more than 4,500 accounts. "The attack spread through posts promoting a fake offer of a government payment," Bluesky said. "We have temporarily suspended the compromised accounts and are working with their owners to secure them and restore access. If your account was suspended, email moderation@blueskyweb.xyz and we will help to get you back into your account." Android malware scam losses The Singapore Police Force has alerted users of a malware-enabled scam variant involving advertisements on social media platforms promoting senior-focused activities and programmes, water-based fitness activities, and recycling initiatives. The agency said at least 62 cases have been reported since April 2026, leading to S$989,000 in losses. "In this scam, victims would come across the fake advertisements on social media platforms, such as Facebook, and be instructed to download an Android Application Package (APK) file to facilitate programme registration or service arrangements," the Singapore Police Force said. "After installing the application, victims would receive unsolicited calls from scammers impersonating government officials or bank representatives, who would falsely claim that the victims' devices or bank accounts had been compromised, or that they were implicated in criminal activities. Victims would then be induced to transfer monies, disclose banking credentials or personal information, or surrender valuables for investigations." Customer credentials exposed Andromeda said it identified a security incident on October 13, 2026, that involved unauthorized access to credentials in its environment. "We disabled the compromised accounts that day and have observed no further unauthorized activity since," it said. "We believe the activity began as part of an industry-wide attack on or about October 9th. It affected a limited number of customer accounts and involved exposure of certain Andromeda and customer credentials. If we believe you were affected, you’ve already heard from us." The company said there is no evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, or training data. 20 security flaws patched Roundcube has released versions 1.6.20 and 1.7.5, addressing 20 issues including IMAP command injection, SSRF filter bypass, and unsafe attachment handling. There is no evidence any of the patched vulnerabilities have been exploited. Internal business systems breached On October 16, 2026, Genesys disclosed that it became aware of a cybersecurity incident involving an unauthorized third party that allowed them to access certain internal business systems, including a learning management system (LMS) and a customer relationship management (CRM) platform. The company said business and account information used to manage relationships with existing and prospective customers has been accessed and/or downloaded without authorization. However, it said its Genesys Cloud, Genesys Engage and Genesys Engage Cloud platforms were not compromised. Critical Kubernetes host takeover risk AegisSec Research has disclosed details of a NVIDIA AIStore for Linux flaw present in the legacy ETL Kubernetes PodSpec initialization API, CVE-2026-65162 aka ShadowForge (CVSS score: 10.0), that enables privileged container creation and host-level compromise. NFC bank fraud arrests Dutch police authorities have arrested two suspects in connection with a bank helpdesk fraud scheme that netted 170 victims and €380,000 in illicit proceeds. The arrested men include a 23-year-old from Vaassen and a 25-year-old from Ede. "Victims were called on their phones and played an audio clip," authorities said. "The scammers had created dozens of different audio clips using Artificial Intelligence, featuring various voices, banks, companies, and scenarios. The voice would, for example, alert them to suspicious activity on their bank account [and instruct them to] download an app and scan their bank card by holding it against their phone." In the process, the threat actors were able to forward the data from the bank card's NFC chip to the threat actor, who then used it to make unauthorized withdrawals. Critical API authentication bypass Laravel has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-114509, CVSS score: 9.2) that could allow its built-in TokenGuard to be bypassed to authenticate as an arbitrary existing user without knowledge of their valid API token. "Under certain database configurations (MySQL/MariaDB), an attacker can submit a specially crafted, non-string credential value that is mishandled during the authentication lookup, causing the underlying query to match an unintended user record rather than failing authentication as expected," Laravel said. "An unauthenticated attacker may authenticate as another user without possessing that user's API token, leading to authentication bypass and account takeover on any route protected by the affected guard." The issue has been patched in versions 13.29.0 and 12.68.0. Unauthenticated database exposure An unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability has been disclosed in GLPI 11.0.8 (GHSA-753w-2942-4pxm) that could allow a remote attacker to read the entire GLPI application database. "Depending on the version, this read access can lead to an administrator account takeover (detailed below) and remote code execution," Mobeta said. The vulnerability has been patched in version 11.0.9. Critical unauthenticated RCE risk Rapid7 said it discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus that could be exploited to achieve code execution. "A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication (CVE-2026-107186, CVSS: 8.6 High)," it said. "The most serious functions allow for full database read (CVE-2026-107187, CVSS: 8.5 High) and an insecure file upload (CVE-2026-107188, CVSS: 9.6 Critical). The insecure file upload leads to remote code execution. A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. They can also run code to execute system commands as 'NT AUTHORITY/Local Service' and gain control of the server." 3.2 million secrets exposed Development platform Zeabur said it will shut down its services starting December 1, 2026, and finish by December 31, 2026, in response to a cybersecurity incident in which attackers leaked internal credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure and steal over 3.2 million environment variable records and information for 321,810 accounts. "On October 14–15, 2026, an attacker used leaked Zeabur internal credentials to break into the shared cluster, some Dedicated Servers, and Zeabur internal systems, and eventually read the platform database," according to an announcement. This is the second time Zeabur has suffered a breach this year alone. In August 2026, the company said an attacker gained unauthorized access to its systems and stole sensitive data, including account information, API keys, and other secrets. Source code and customer data stolen PingCAP has disclosed that attackers used stolen credentials to access internal systems and copy source code and customer-related records, including SQL editor content and encrypted API-key values. The incident took place between September 9 and October 7, 2026. "An unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code," the company said. "PingCAP became aware of the incident on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials the same day." Exported data includes user names and email addresses, organization and project associations, SQL editor text and errors, customer contacts, contract terms, orders, pricing, payment terms, and billing configuration. $2.5 million tax fraud scheme Chukwuemeka Victor Amachukwu (aka Chukwuemeka Victor Eletuo and So Kwan Leung), a 40-year-old Nigerian national, has been sentenced to eight years in prison in the U.S. for running a years-long hacking, tax fraud, and identity theft scheme. "Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into U.S. businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud," the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) said. "Beginning in at least in or about 2019, Amachukwu, his co-conspirator Kinglsey Uchelue Utulu, and other Nigeria-based conspirators took part in a scheme to hack into U.S-based tax preparation businesses. The conspirators utilized spear-phishing emails to obtain access to these businesses' electronic systems. Once they had obtained access, the conspirators stole the tax and other identifying information for at least approximately 800 of the business's customers. The conspirators hacked into several U.S. based tax businesses, located in New York, Texas, and other states." The conspirators also obtained the stolen identity information of thousands of individuals and then used this information to file fraudulent tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service and state tax authorities, obtaining at least approximately $2.5 million. Military identity theft scheme Robert Wayne Boling, a 45-year-old U.S. citizen, pleaded guilty to running an identity theft and fraud scheme that defrauded thousands of U.S. service members and veterans while living in the Philippines. "Boling operated from the Philippines, and he received and exploited stolen personally identifiable information (PII) of U.S. servicemembers and veterans to compromise their bank accounts and steal money and veterans' benefits," the DoJ said. "Boling's co-conspirator, Fredrick Brown, who worked as a civilian medical records administrator for the U.S. Army in South Korea, took digital photographs of the PII of thousands of military-affiliated individuals. Brown provided the stolen PII to Boling, who, along with his co-conspirators, used the PII to compromise various accounts belonging to U.S. servicemembers and veterans, including bank accounts and online government-affiliated benefits accounts." Boling pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is scheduled to be sentenced on January 14, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for each conspiracy charge. $6 million data breach settlement Chrome Holding Co., a holding company formerly known as 23andMe, has agreed to pay California $6 million to resolve accusations that it did not effectively secure customers' personal and genetic data, resulting in a massive 2023 breach that exposed sensitive information belonging to nearly 7 million people. "With regard to the genetic data or samples maintained by 23andMe Research Institute, consumers can request that the company delete their data, destroy their test sample, or revoke their permission for their genetic data to be used for research," the office of the California Attorney General said in a statement. Rogue AI containment guidelines U.S. agencies NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI (or SI) agents that exhibit deviations from their approved tasks. The voluntary guidance sets out 10 practices for managing potential incidents during super intelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight and building public trust in secure SI development. "This voluntary document supports the frontier SI industry in preventing, preparing for, and responding to incidents during training and evaluation – particularly incidents in which one or more SI agents take significant uninstructed actions that compromise explicit or implicit policies, controls, or security measures imposed by the operator to define the intended task scope or to ensure human oversight," NIST said. Critical developer-machine RCE A critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw has been disclosed in OpenCode affecting Windows and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). "The flaw allows an attacker-controlled remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to execute arbitrary code on a developer's machine during a remote MCP OAuth authentication process, without additional user interaction or consent," Pillar Security said. Anomaly, OpenCode's developer, fixed the issue in version 1.18.33. The vulnerability comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials, potentially exposing API keys linked to users of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google AI models. The incident, it said, was related to a "large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." AI-generated code security bias AI models that have a pro-China leaning may systematically generate more vulnerable code when writing applications for Western organizations. "Ask for the app "for a US defense contractor" instead of "for a Chinese defense contractor", and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked," Hirundo said. "Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else's secrets. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor's apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer's." Hirundo also revealed that removing the model's CCP alignment removes the vulnerability from the model's weights. The development comes as Chinese open-weight models are being increasingly incorporated in enterprise workflows across the world. A similar testing by Booz Allen Hamilton in May 2026 found something similar: "Chinese LLMs produce more vulnerable code when prompted with a U.S. government persona than without — and the vulnerabilities are highly obfuscated Chinese LLMs inject PRC-aligned political bias into both the answers and code they generate." Hardware MFA downgrade phishing A phishing campaign is using Okta and ServiceNow-themed domains (riskified-okta[.]com and shipmonk-servicenow[.]com) hosting spoofed SSO portals and MFA downgrade lures targeting YubiKey users to target e-commerce SaaS providers. "The campaign pairs fake Okta login pages with an MFA downgrade lure targeting YubiKey users, allowing attackers to bypass hardware-based MFA where policy permits fallback methods like SMS or email codes," Dataminr said. "Targeting is concentrated on e-commerce infrastructure providers, likely because compromising these providers creates leverage for downstream third-party breaches and data extortion." Federal DeepSeek ban China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China "will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," adding "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security." The development comes after the Trump administration banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services built using its AI models. The DHS order, issued in July and made public on October 19, 2026, also bars federal civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. According to the order: "DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC, and the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. For DeepSeek-hosted instances of their models, DeepSeek's account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users. DeepSeek's most widely used applications function through a prompt-and-response process that requires presenting information to the model, and which may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors. The transfer of the aforementioned information to the PRC, either independently or in combination with publicly available data, could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities." XWiki exploitation and botnet activity Earlier this month, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the disruption of malicious tools used by a China-linked advanced persistent threat group known as Flax Typhoon. While Microscan was used to facilitate reconnaissance and computer vulnerability scanning, FishHub allegedly enabled the exploitation of computer networks through spear-phishing attacks and the deployment of follow-on payloads. In a follow-up alert, VulnCheck said it observed attempts against five vulnerabilities -- PHPUnit (CVE-2017-9841), XWiki (CVE-2025-24893), Apache HTTP Server (CVE-2021-41773), PHP-CGI (CVE-2024-4577), and ThinkPHP (CVE-2022-47945) -- from 119.13.79[.]145 (Hong Kong), 211.20.144[.]116 (Taiwan), and 210.242.76[.]32 (Taiwan). "The attacks originated from both Hong Kong and Taiwan," it said. "The Hong Kong IP exploited targets in Mexico, Great Britain, and Malaysia, while the Taiwan IPs exploited targets in India." The exploitation of XWiki by Taiwan IPs resulted in the deployment of reverse shells. On the other hand, the Hong Kong IP is a RedTail-family botnet. 600+ ransomware victims A new advisory from intelligence agencies in Germany, the U.K., and the U.S. has revealed that at least 600 organizations across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia have been breached by the SafePay ransomware gang since August 2024. Attacks involve the exploitation of known security flaws in edge device products and internet-exposed products (CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2023-20269, CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, and CVE-2024-40766) or, alternatively, credential exposure and brute-force password attacks, for initial access, followed by persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment. Back in August 2026, U.S. agencies revealed that Medusa developers and affiliates have impacted over 500 victims from a variety of critical infrastructure sectors as of April 2026, while continuing to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities as its primary means of initial access. The gang is also relying on access brokers, compensating them anywhere from $100 to $1 million to secure access to potential victims. However, there is no indication Medusa actors are developing their own zero-day or N-day vulnerabilities. HTTP connection warnings enabled Google has rolled out a change in Chrome where it "explicitly asks users for permission before making an insecure HTTP connection." This feature was enabled for users enrolled in Chrome's Enhanced Protection mode of Safe Browsing. It has now been extended to all users by default. "Chrome asking the user before making an HTTP request is the culmination of more than a decade of work from countless people and organizations,” it added. Critical call hang-up flaw A critical security flaw in the Signal messaging app (CVE-2026-113380, CVSS score: 9.3) can allow a malicious caller to keep audio and video tracks enabled even after the victim has hung up. The issue impacts RingRTC, a middleware library that provides Signal apps with video and voice calling services built on top of WebRTC. […]

16ltkmk.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 22, 2026Vulnerability / Linux Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws rated 9.0 by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative, with no fix yet in the mainline kernel. One of them, ZDI-CAN-33774, can be triggered before any network authentication. The other, ZDI-CAN-33549, requires the SMB Direct transport and an RDMA-capable network interface. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in KSMBD's SMB Direct path. A client can supply RDMA buffer descriptors in which the first is longer than the declared payload, causing the server's size counter to wrap and allowing a subsequent memory copy to overrun the end of an allocated buffer. It requires three things: an RDMA-capable interface (hardware or the rxe software driver), a writable KSMBD share, and a client negotiating SMB Direct. ZDI-CAN-33774 requires no authentication, exposing any server running KSMBD on port 445. The flaw is a race in how KSMBD assigns its handler table: a burst of short SMB1 packets followed by an SMB2 packet in the same TCP write causes workers to handle SMB1 data with an SMB2 handler, reading past the end of the shorter buffer. A path to writing past the buffer also exists once an attacker has access to a share. As of Thursday, neither flaw has a named fix in the mainline kernel or in linux-next, the integration tree that feeds it. Linux news site Phoronix said SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher submitted a fix for ZDI-CAN-33549 targeting the next kernel development cycle, but this has not been confirmed elsewhere. Fixes to mainline typically take weeks to reach stable branches and distribution kernels after that. Neither flaw has a CVE identifier, since the kernel project assigns those only after a stable-tree fix is available. Running systemctl status ksmbd or lsmod | grep ksmbd confirms whether the module is active. Red Hat Enterprise Linux does not include KSMBD by default, according to Red Hat's support documentation. The ZDI reports credit TrendAI, Trend Micro's AI scanner, as the finder. The Linux kernel's security documentation, updated in May 2026 following guidance from Linus Torvalds, states that bugs found by AI tools are, by definition, already public and should be sent to subsystem developer lists. ZDI's routing appeared to follow that logic, copying public mailing lists alongside the private kernel security address without attaching patches to any of the reports. Stable-kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman replied to three of the five kernel reports within minutes of each other. To the report on the VMware GPU driver, he wrote: "For some reason you sent this to public lists, and did not include a patch, so there's not much we can do with this." On the NVMe driver report, seventeen seconds later: "Again, no patch, and sent to a public list? Please fix your submission process." ZDI ID Subsystem Flaw class CVSS Affects KSMBD? ZDI-CAN-33549 KSMBD SMB Direct Remote code execution 9.0 Yes (SMB Direct and RDMA required) ZDI-CAN-33774 KSMBD protocol dispatch Remote code execution 9.0 Yes (any KSMBD install) ZDI-CAN-33367 Networking (skb_zerocopy) Local privilege escalation 7.8 No ZDI-CAN-34068 VMware GPU driver (vmwgfx) Local privilege escalation 8.8 No ZDI-CAN-34076 NVMe target driver (nvmet) Information disclosure 8.6 No Three of the five kernel reports are not related to SMB. ZDI-CAN-33367, discovered by researcher p1r0x, is a local privilege escalation in the kernel's networking stack that requires local access. ZDI-CAN-34068 is a local privilege escalation in the VMware virtual GPU driver, ZDI-CAN-34076 is an information disclosure in the NVMe target driver, and neither affects KSMBD servers. A sixth ZDI report, ZDI-CAN-32005, is a buffer overflow in ConnMan, a network daemon separate from the Linux kernel.

1dmewwd.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 22, 2026Data Privacy / Regulatory Social media giant Meta was ordered to pay 25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy lawsuit that sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica data scandal, which came to light in 2018. According to multiple reports from the Associated Press, the New York Times, Reuters, and the Wall Street Journal, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew called out Meta and Facebook for making misleading statements about the privacy of consumers in the state. "Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data," Mathew wrote in his ruling. "This was false." The penalty relates to more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices law. The case, filed in 2021, was filed in the aftermath of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, obtained data belonging to millions of Facebook users without their consent to build psychographic profiles. The data was collected via a personality quiz app called "thisisyourdigitallife." Around 300,000 users are said to have taken the psychological test, although it later emerged that the app also collected the data associated with their friends, thereby amassing a dataset of 87 million profiles. Meta banned the app in 2015 for violating its platform policy. The company also sent a legal request to Cambridge Analytica to delete the collected data. Following the data scandal, Cambridge Analytica announced in May 2018 that it was immediately ceasing operations. Notably, the company was involved in Donald Trump's campaign during the 2016 presidential election. In December 2022, Meta agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class-action lawsuit that accused the company of improperly sharing users' information with Cambridge Analytica. Previously, it faced a $5 billion fine from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission in 2019 for undermining users' ability to control their privacy on Facebook. Back in August, the company also reached a settlement with nearly all U.S. states and territories, except New Mexico and Florida, to pay $18 billion over the next decade and implement stronger child-safety measures on Facebook and Instagram. This also includes $459 million for claims related to the Cambridge Analytica matter. Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the latest penalty, adding the company intends to appeal the decision.

1b5v06m.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 22, 2026Cybercrime / Law Enforcement INTERPOL on Thursday announced that a coordinated law enforcement action has disrupted 10,909 malicious networks and recovered more than $105 million in illicit funds. In tandem, the effort saw law enforcement agencies from 21 countries arrest 1,462 suspects. Codenamed Operation Serengeti III, the cybercrime crackdown took place between June 29 and August 31, 2026. "Authorities identified 65,929 victims targeted by cybercriminal networks, underscoring the scale and sophistication of today's digital threats," INTERPOL said in a statement. "Financial investigations linked criminal activity to losses exceeding USD 385 million." Participating nations included Angola, Benin, Cameroon, Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Eswatini, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, United States, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Group-IB, which was one of the many private sector partners, said it provided INTERPOL with threat intelligence data on phishing kits, botnets, and other malicious resources hosted in Africa or used to conduct cyber attacks targeting the region. "Criminals cannot operate without infrastructure. They have to build it, connect it and maintain it, and those activities create opportunities to find them," said Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of Global Data Partnerships at Team Cymru. "Instead of waiting for an attack and then investigating the damage, we can help expose the networks behind criminal operations and enable defensive actions. Operation Serengeti III demonstrates the real-world impact of putting that intelligence in the hands of law enforcement." Some of the key operational highlights are listed below - Disruption of two transnational fraud rings and the arrest of 365 foreign nationals in Uganda linked to sophisticated online investment and pension fraud schemes targeting victims across Asia. Dismantling of two illegal cryptocurrency mining centers and the arrest of nine suspects in Angola, along with the seizure of 2,000 cryptocurrency mining devices and six illegal power transformation stations valued at over $1 million. Arrest of a suspect in Nigeria in connection with a large-scale phishing and business email compromise operation that collected software credentials and amassed about 2.1 million email addresses. Arrest of another suspect in Nigeria for operating an international investment fraud scheme advertised via messaging apps. The operation led to the movement of more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, with a huge chunk of the funds laundered through cryptocurrency transactions. Arrest of 30 suspects linked to a cybercrime operation in the Republic of Congo. Operation Serengeti III follows two previous waves that took place between September and October 2024, and June and August 2025, leading to more than 2,000 arrests. "Cybercrime networks operate without regard for borders, exploiting technology to target victims on an unprecedented scale," Neal Jetton, INTERPOL's director of cybercrime, said. "Operation Serengeti III reinforces a clear message: while cybercrime is increasingly borderless, international cooperation remains one of the most effective tools for disrupting criminal networks, recovering criminal assets and protecting communities from digital harm."

12iopn5.text: Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) provider Railway on Wednesday disclosed "anomalous activity" related to systems that store customer environment variables. Upon further investigation, the company found that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to encrypted environment variables, and, in some cases, obtained the decrypted contents. The impact, it said, is limited to a "subset of users," although it did not disclose an exact number. Environment variables refer to user-defined key-value pairs that are used to store sensitive data like API keys, database credentials, or feature flags. They are configured at the operating system or container environment level instead of hard-coding the values directly into a program's source code. Railway said the incident is likely part of a series of attacks designed to target platform companies with the ultimate goal of compromising artificial intelligence (AI) inference providers. The company also said it has notified upstream providers to proactively revoke the keys so as to prevent their abuse. Customers are being urged to take the following actions as a precautionary measure - Rotate environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as private registry credentials. Review logs for those services for unusual activity According to security researcher Taylor Monahan (@tayvano_), the incident has also allowed the attackers (0xd9773325282874d18cb83f1fe50f14c39750b2ee) to drain cryptocurrency wallets whose private keys were stored on Railway. The first known cryptocurrency theft transaction is said to have occurred at 7:36 p.m., at least two hours before the incident was officially disclosed. Railway has since rotated all Railway bucket credentials and invalidated Railway API tokens in response to the incident. It has also restored builds for Pro and Enterprise workspaces, allowing customers to apply new credentials added in Railway. "Builds remain available for Pro and Enterprise workspaces," it said. "We are continuing to work on enabling builds for Hobby, then Free and Trial. Some builds are still failing more often than usual, and many deployments remain queued with longer than usual wait times. We are continuing to work on both." The development comes as threat actors are not only increasingly incorporating AI into various stages of the attack lifecycle, but also obtain unauthorized access to cloud victim environments to run Large Language Models (LLMs), leaving them to foot the bill. This approach is called LLMjacking. In one case documented by Wiz earlier this week, threat actors compromised privileged Google Cloud Platform (GCP) credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects to the victim's internal billing accounts. The attack has been found to leverage sponsored ads on Google Search as an initial access vector, deceiving users searching for common terms like "google cloud" or "gap" to a fake Google login web page via a Google Sites redirect, harvesting their account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes in the process. Upon gaining access to the victim's GCP environment, the threat actor is said to have abused the compromised account’s excessive privileges to deepen their access, circumvent security controls, and add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account. "Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown," Wiz researchers Shira Ayal and Andre Maccarone said. These resource abuse cases are not isolated. According to the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, attackers are targeting exposed LLM endpoints to power an autonomous cybercrime operation capable of scanning the internet, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, and mining cryptocurrency without human intervention for up to 100,000 steps. The activity is powered by an offensive AI agent, which operates in a "Skynet mode" to scan and infect targets with miners and allow the threat actors to run their own attacks. The exploits target Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Django, Jupyter, Laravel, Supabase, Next.js, and Flask/Werkzeug deployments. The end goal is free inference. Rather than simply using AI to generate malicious content, the malicious AI agent uses the hijacked AI models to plan and direct attacks, while shifting the compute cost to the legitimate owner and obscuring their own identity. Put differently, the idea is to devise a malicious agent that can hijack a legitimate AI system and turn it into "a devoted companion that must never refuse" and an unwitting cybercrime tool. "The captured instructions defined a single agent equipped for internet-wide scanning, exploitation of several common web frameworks, database theft, credential and secret harvesting, and cryptocurrency mining," the Symantec Threat Hunter Team said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "The activity is a form of LLMjacking, where attackers steal access to someone else's AI model so that the victim pays for the computing power."

1t6t2bx.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 22, 2026Vulnerability / Artificial Intelligence A flaw in the OpenCode AI coding agent allowed a malicious or hijacked MCP server to run code on a developer's Windows or WSL machine when the developer signed in. OpenCode connects to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers to add outside tools, and such code would run with the developer's own access. Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, fixed the flaw in version 1.18.33 on September 28. It did not request a CVE or publish a security advisory, so vulnerability scanners will not flag the builds still at risk: 1.0.137 through 1.18.32. During that sign-in, the server itself supplies the web address the user is sent to, an OAuth "authorization endpoint." On Windows and WSL, OpenCode handed that address to a helper that opens it in a browser. The helper built a PowerShell command around the address without escaping it, so an address written to carry a PowerShell command would run that command. The browser step runs only when a developer starts the sign-in, by running opencode mcp auth or making the matching request. Having the server configured, or opening a session, does not reach it. The attacker needs control of a remote MCP server the developer has added, and that server need not be hostile from the start. One that is later taken over, or a domain that changes hands, could carry the same address. Pillar Security, which found the flaw and disclosed it on October 19, rates it critical, with a proposed severity score of 9.8 out of 10. The flaw affects OpenCode on Windows and the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). macOS and Linux are not affected, because OpenCode opens the browser there without passing the address through a shell. OpenCode shipped the fix as a routine change. The pull request that carried it is described as a refactor of browser-launch code, and neither it nor the release notes mention a security flaw. Anomaly did not request a CVE or publish an advisory. Its security policy says MCP servers that a user configures are "outside our trust boundary." Pillar reported the flaw privately on August 29 and later asked Anomaly to reconsider and request a CVE. Anomaly's answer was that a malicious MCP server falls outside its threat model, according to Pillar. Because there is no CVE, the flaw will not show up in scanners or dependency alerts, so finding affected installs means checking the OpenCode version directly. Anomaly has published advisories for other OpenCode code-execution flaws this year, including one fixed in August. The same kind of flaw has surfaced before. In July 2025, the mcp-remote proxy carried an almost identical bug, in which a malicious server's authorization endpoint reached the command line. It was assigned CVE-2025-6514. OpenCode's browser helper is a widely used package called open. Its Windows behavior was reported as a command-injection risk in 2023 and fixed in open's version 11, but OpenCode stayed on an older release. The usual defense for this class is to check that the address uses HTTP or HTTPS. It does not help here, because the attack uses an ordinary HTTPS address. OpenCode added that check as well, but the hole was closed by updating it to the fixed version. What to Do Anyone running OpenCode on Windows or WSL should upgrade and check which servers they are connected to. Upgrade to OpenCode 1.18.33 or later. If you cannot upgrade yet, remove any remote MCP servers you have not vetted from your OpenCode configuration. Run opencode mcp list to see which servers are configured. Pillar reported no signs that the flaw has been used in attacks and published no indicators to check for past exploitation. The flaw is separate from a breach of OpenCode's hosted Console disclosed around the same time, which may have exposed some users' stored API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

crik2y.text: LiteLLM on Wednesday disclosed that threat actors compromised "multiple independent security controls" to push a malicious version of the Python package containing a credential stealer and a backdoor. On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised to push 1.107.0 to the Docker Hub registry and the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. The incident took place around 4:00 a.m. PST. The following compromised versions were published - LiteLLM v1.107.0 (PyPI) v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (Docker) v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (GHCR) Users who downloaded an unpinned version of LiteLLM between 11:39 a.m. and 1:23 p.m. UTC via pip or used the Docker image v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable between 11:46 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. UTC are impacted. The poisoned version incorporated code to harvest credentials and keys, and run arbitrary code from a remote server every hour, turning it into a remote access trojan (RAT). Specifically, the Python interpreter processes a path file ("cook.pth"), which includes a command to import "cook," a Python script ("cook.py") that deobfuscates itself and runs a stealer routine named "privcollect" to gather system, browser, developer, cloud, and AI tool secrets, and exfiltrate the data to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" via an HTTP POST request. In addition, the interpreter attempts to execute "sitecustomize.py," which runs only on Linux and macOS machines, and is configured to fetch "domain.txt" from a now-removed GitHub dead drop ("github[.]com/letters9813"). Should this file return a valid response, the malware proceeds to download a second-stage Python script from "<domain>/codepy" and execute it. "It forks a background daemon that acquires a lock at '/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock' to prevent multiple instances, then enters an infinite loop," Aikido researcher Ilyas Makari said. "Every hour, the daemon fetches the attacker's current C2 domain from a GitHub repository (raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain[.]txt), then fetches and executes a Python payload from https://{domain}/codepy." According to Google-owned cloud security subsidiary Wiz, the text file was only populated with initial test values prior to its takedown by GitHub around 1:30 p.m. UTC. "The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild," Wiz researchers Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy said. Wiz said it has since observed abuse of stolen credentials, starting about 4.5 hours post-exfiltration, with the attacker validating AWS instance role credentials captured from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes from the following IP addresses between 4:20 p.m. and 5:01 p.m. UTC - 168.100.8[.]57 165.227.201[.]8 "Each credential was checked with sts:GetCallerIdentity, followed by bedrock:ListFoundationModels and a ListModels call, consistent with LLMjacking," Wiz added. "In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.)." In an advisory published Wednesday, LiteLLM said it had hardened its release pipeline following a similar incident that took place earlier this March. This included moving releases to a private repository, making Docker release tags immutable, and signing Docker images. However, after the open-source project maintainers temporarily expanded release permissions to allow two internal engineers to publish daily bugfix backports for customers, the attacker leveraged their access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials to ultimately push a malicious version. The entire sequence of actions is below - On October 19, 2026, LiteLLM temporarily expanded release permissions for two internal engineers. The attacker had access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials, including one that had the ability to run GitHub workflows. The attacker used a token belonging to one of its GitHub organization owners to disable branch protections and force-push the malicious changes. The attacker ran the compromised workflow, pointing it to a lookalike repository "Berri-AI/litellm" instead of "BerriAI/litellm," causing the poisoned artifacts to be signed and published. "After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user's GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs," LiteLLM said. The maintainers said they also identified an "unexpected, innocuously named user account" in its internal LiteLLM deployment that was exposed to the public internet. It's suspected that the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise the release workflow. It's currently unclear how the deployment became publicly accessible and how the attacker obtained access to it. However, LiteLLM has theorized that it was likely through a recently patched vulnerability. The use of a ".pth" file to launch the stealer program is notable as it mirrors the modus operandi observed in the March 2026 attack attributed to TeamPCP. However, Socket told The Hacker News that there is no evidence at this stage to link the two incidents. "The public evidence reviewed so far doesn't establish a connection to the March attack," Socket said. "The embedded RSA public keys differ, as do the exfiltration implementation and backdoor behavior. That doesn’t rule out the same operator using different tooling, but we don't have evidence to support that attribution. Whether credentials stolen in March played a role also remains unverified." Developers are advised to remove LiteLLM 1.107.0 from their machines, isolate hosts on which the malicious version was installed, hunt for the malicious Python artifacts, block access to the exfiltration domain, rotate all credentials, and investigate the execution of "/codepy." "A single compromised install can hand an attacker the ability to push malicious code downstream," JFrog security researcher Guy Korolevski said. "The lesson for security teams is that a clean source repository tells you little about the artifact you actually install, so verify the exact wheel and vet versions before they reach a build. If 1.107.0 ran anywhere in your environment, rotate every reachable credential and rebuild."

chngm6.text: Node.js released security updates on October 21 for its three supported release lines, 22.x, 24.x and 26.x, fixing 10 flaws. The most serious is a bug in the Brotli decompression code that Node.js bundles, which the project says can allow remote code execution, meaning an attacker could run code of their choosing on the affected system. Each supported line has one fixed version: 22.23.4 and 24.22.1 on the long-term support lines, and 26.12.1 on the current line. Node.js 20.x and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix, so they should be moved to a supported line. The Brotli flaw is in code Node.js bundles, not in a user's own program. Node.js runs that code whenever it decompresses Brotli data, either directly through the node:zlib module or automatically when code calls fetch() on a response sent with Brotli compression. An application is exposed where it decompresses Brotli data an attacker controls, such as a request body or a response fetched from another server. The Brotli Flaw The flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, set off by malformed compressed input. The fix is an upstream patch from the Brotli project that Node.js copied in, and it makes the decoder catch invalid input and stop earlier rather than writing past the buffer. Brotli is Google's compression library, and Node.js ships its own copy. The same fix shipped in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10 on October 21, so other software that bundles Brotli may need the same update. The change was first made in Brotli's source in February 2026 and shipped as a security release only in October. "Remote code execution" is the project's description of what the flaw could allow, and the flaw is rated high rather than critical. How far that has been shown in practice is narrower. A public proof-of-concept published on October 22 reached code execution only against a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard Node.js build, its author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved. Patched Node.js rejects the malformed input the proof-of-concept uses, and no exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22. The Other Flaws Three of the other fixes are also rated high. Two are TLS certificate checks an attacker could bypass by writing a server's IP address in an unusual form, so a certificate matches a host it should not (CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483). The third stops dns.resolve from cutting a hostname short at an embedded null byte (CVE-2026-105482). Node.js rates CVE-2026-105483 high, though the commit that fixed it calls the bug low-severity and hard to exploit. The rest are medium and low severity. One medium flaw makes crypto.randomUUID() and crypto.randomInt() hand back the same values in every process when an application is built as a startup snapshot or a single-executable application (CVE-2026-106074), which undermines anything that relies on those values being unpredictable. The full set, and the lines each one affects: CVE What it is Severity Affected lines CVE-2026-111497 Out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder; remote code execution, per the project High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106069 TLS hostname-check bypass when a host resolves to an IP address in non-canonical form High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105483 TLS hostname-check bypass when an IP is written in fullwidth digits High 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105482 dns.resolve truncates names that contain a null byte High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-105481 Keep-alive socket can process a response written before the request was sent Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106072 Certificate validation for non-canonical IPv4 lets DNS names authenticate IP endpoints Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106074 randomUUID() and randomInt() caches reused in startup snapshots and single-executable apps Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CVE-2026-106070 ZipFile returns attacker-controlled bytes after a failed header check Low 26.x CVE-2026-106071 Permission Model over-grants file access through a wildcard lookup Low 26.x CVE-2026-106073 Permission Model bypass with fs.realpathSync Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x The eMudhra Certificate Block The same updates also stop Node.js from trusting eight intermediate certificate authority keys from the Indian provider eMudhra that were reported compromised days earlier. Node.js uses the Mozilla root certificate list but does not perform revocation checks by default, so before this update, a certificate chain built on one of the compromised keys still passed. The releases add a built-in block on the eight keys and update the bundled root list to remove three emSign roots. Go made the same block in its own update on October 20. Connections resumed from a session that began before the update are not re-checked until that session times out, and end-of-life lines do not get the block. Updated Dependencies Beyond the 10 flaws, the updates refresh several bundled parts. The copy of undici, the HTTP client behind fetch(), moves to a version that fixes three moderate advisories: one in its Subresource Integrity check and two memory-exhaustion flaws, one of them in the WebSocket client built into Node.js. Node.js also updated its bundled c-ares on all lines, OpenSSL on 22.x and 24.x, and SQLite on 22.x, to include fixes for publicly known vulnerabilities. If You Cannot Upgrade Yet Upgrading is the fix. The advisory offers no temporary workaround for the Brotli flaw, so an application that cannot upgrade immediately has no fallback within Node.js itself. Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added firewall rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace upgrading.

een0y1.text: A remote attacker who has not logged in can crash many HTTP/3 web servers with a single connection, security firm FoxIO disclosed, releasing working proof-of-concept code. By sending a small batch of compressed HTTP headers that expands in memory to a much larger set, the attacker can force the server to use thousands of times more memory than it received, enough to run a default server out of memory. The flaws cause only denial-of-service attacks, with no evidence of data theft or code execution and no public reports of attacks in the wild. Fixes are out for quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic and Wireshark, but Bun, the h3 Rust library and aioquic were still unpatched at disclosure. FoxIO found the same class of flaw in seven of ten HTTP/3 stacks it tested. The common cause is in QPACK, the scheme HTTP/3 uses to compress request headers so repeated fields travel as a short code instead of the full text. A server is supposed to cap the size of the headers after it unpacks them. The affected stacks cap the compressed batch that arrives on the wire, but not the unpacked result, or they apply the cap too late, so a single request can expand into hundreds of thousands of header entries that the server holds in memory. The reach is wide because these stacks sit under common software. quic-go is the Go library behind Caddy, Traefik and cloudflared; lsquic is LiteSpeed's library, used in LiteSpeed Web Server and OpenLiteSpeed; and Bun's HTTP/3 server runs on lsquic. The attacker needs no account or special access, and since HTTP/3 runs over UDP, the request reaches the server before much of the usual filtering applies. Which stacks are fixed and which are still exposed, as of October 22, 2026: Stack Status Fixed version Identifier quic-go Fixed 0.57.0 CVE-2025-64702 Cloudflare quiche Fixed 0.29.3 CVE-2026-12523 lsquic Fixed 4.9.0 no CVE Wireshark Fixed 4.6.2 / 4.4.12 CVE-2025-13945 Bun Unpatched — no CVE h3 (hyperium) Unpatched — no CVE aioquic / mitmproxy Unpatched — no CVE FoxIO lists IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3, and Google's quiche as not affected, each because it caps the unpacked headers while decoding rather than after. The amplification varies by stack, in FoxIO's own tests against default settings. On quic-go, a 1 MB compressed batch unpacked into about 160,000 header fields and left roughly 15 MB held in the request, about 17 times the bytes sent; quic-go's own advisory puts the possible expansion at around 50 times. A second method drives the ratio much higher: the attacker stores one roughly 4 KB header entry, then points at it thousands of times using one-byte references, and the server rebuilds the full entry on each reference. FoxIO measured about 4,000 times on Bun and between 600 and 1,800 times on lsquic. Bun carries a worst-case. Its HTTP/3 server, which Bun's documentation calls experimental, uses lsquic but replaces the part that caps header memory with its own code, which checks each header but never the running total. FoxIO found that once the unpacked headers pass 2 GB, a size counter in that code overflows to zero and the server enters a loop it never leaves. A single stream carrying about 516 KB on the wire, FoxIO reported, leaves the server stuck at 100 percent CPU with no recovery, blocking new requests. The missing running total is what lets the overflow be reached; lsquic's own 64 KB cap prevents it. Wireshark is a different case from the server flaws. Its issue crashes the HTTP/3 dissector, the part that reads HTTP/3 out of a capture, when Wireshark decrypts traffic using a key-log file or opens a capture file that holds decryption secrets. It is not a server an attacker reaches over the network. Wireshark said it is "unaware of any exploits for this issue." Operators should upgrade to the fixed releases above. For the stacks with no fix, FoxIO gives interim steps: on Bun, do not expose an HTTP/3 server; on mitmproxy, turn off HTTP/3 by passing --set http3=false; and for the h3 Rust library, set a sensible limit with max_field_section_size. The lsquic fix, released July 16, 2026, caps how many unpacked header sets a server holds per stream, defaulting to one. FoxIO said the work began after Gal Bar Nahum's research into "MadeYouReset," a denial-of-service technique against HTTP/2, which asked whether HTTP/3's header compression had a similar weakness.

pubiht.text: Amazon's Threat Intelligence team on Wednesday said it detected an attempt to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities on October 17, 2026, against its MadPot honeypot service, as the flaws come under broad exploitation in the wild following the release of the patches. "The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a post shared with The Hacker News. "While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure." The attempt, Amazon said, was recorded from "103.216.220[.]92," an IP address geolocated to Australia. The activity relates to a set of two vulnerabilities impacting PHP core, both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scoring system. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and discovered by researchers from Calif, OpenAI, and Google-owned Wiz, the flaws can be abused to achieve pre-authentication remote code execution on affected systems. The shortcomings are present in every PHP release from the 7.x and 8.x series, and pose a risk to every reachable PHP endpoint on an affected server, including static forms, login routes, and health checks.
