According to CrowdStrike, an attack exploiting the flaws leaves virtually no digital traces. "There is no authentication to bypass, no session to steal, and no vulnerable endpoint to discover," CrowdStrike said. "The exposure is independent of the CMS, framework, or plug-ins in use." "Worker processes remain stable, responses return HTTP 200, and application logs record no anomalies, because no application code ever ran. The only server-side trace is a single memory-limit fatal in the web server's error log, which is routinely dismissed as noise, leaving defenders without actionable web telemetry to identify compromised endpoints." Originally scheduled for coordinated disclosure on October 22, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. UTC, details about the CVE identifiers and a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit leaked ahead of time, prompting the PHP Foundation to move the release forward by one day. "Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling," the PHP Foundation said. "Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions." Amazon said it detected multiple PoC exploits for PHP2Shell coinciding with the day of the release of the fixes, with the earliest attempt flagged around October 21, 2026, at 2 a.m. UTC. This was followed by additional exploitation attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. The variety of payloads and the anonymization infrastructure used indicate that multiple threat actors are involved, Amazon Threat Intelligence said. The attempts have been recorded from the following IP addresses on October 21, 2026 - 31.223.184[.]166 37.19.200[.]5 134.209.159[.]64 103.114.163[.]188 95.217.98[.]37 According to ELLIO, the first PHP2Shell request targeting its sensors was observed on October 21, 2026, at 8:36 a.m. UTC, less than an hour after "Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix." "Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed," the PHP Foundation said. "Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure." The severity of the vulnerabilities has prompted warnings from international cybersecurity agencies such as the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), urging organizations to apply the fixes as soon as possible or consider taking them offline. "Monitor web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an X post. "Ensure appropriate process-monitoring capabilities are in place to help identify potential exploitation." In a similar alert, the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) said the vulnerabilities can provide threat actors with a direct path to the server's file system or database. OpenAI, which described the flaws as "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory," has released a Codex skill to check if a website or local PHP binary is vulnerable to PHP2Shell. With PHP powering a majority of the websites in the world, the vast attack surface, coupled with the severity and ease of exploitation of the PHP2Shell flaws, poses major risks as it allows unauthenticated attackers to execute code and steal sensitive data. "PHP is used by almost 70% of websites," Cloudflare said. "The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the internet." VulnCheck's analysis has identified PHP on 2,608,039 internet-facing hosts, out of which over 700,000 hosts run PHP 3.x through 7.3. Another set of about 400,000 hosts run PHP versions 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1, while 403,000 hosts run supported 8.2 through 8.5 branches. In a similar breakdown, Modat said it detected 4.38 million internet-facing PHP services as of October 20, 2026, with 79% (i.e., about 3.47 million) of them on a branch that PHP no longer supports (4.x, 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1). PHP 7.4, which reached end-of-life in 2022, accounts for 878,761 services, followed by PHP 5.3 with 486,684 services and PHP 7.2 with 461,965 services. "PHP is a massively popular language, and powers large parts of the internet," Ilkka Turunen, Field CTO at Sonatype, said in a statement. "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed." "It is likely there is a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch as PHP is bundled into many other operating system distributions, as well as is found in many historic environments." Some of the other notable developments are listed below - WebOps platform Pantheon said it has blocked over 60,000 suspicious requests probing the vulnerability. VulnCheck has identified two hosts, 85.11.167[.]243 and 45.198.224[.]169, with the user-agent "php2shell-scan/109618" weaponizing CVE-2026-109618 to target its honeypots, while 109.71.252[.]97 has leveraged both the flaws. Cloudflare has observed attack traffic targeting its customers, with threat actors "mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic." CloudLinux has released fixed packages for ea-php52 through ea-php85 and every alt-php version. Additional guidance and mitigations have been published by numerous security and software vendors, including Akamai, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Arctic Wolf, Automattic, Cisco Talos, Corelight, CyCognito, Fastly, Google Cloud, Hadrian, Imperva, Kaspersky, Microsoft Azure, NetSPI, Orca Security, OX Security, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Pentest Tools, Rapid7, ReliaQuest, SOCRadar, Searchlight Cyber, Sophos, Tanium, Vercel, watchTowr, and Zscaler. "The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," Moses said. "In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them.." "That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed."

kn4b3v.text: Microsoft on Wednesday disclosed that a China state-aligned actor dubbed Storm-0940 was behind the recent supply chain compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application. During the incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX, a Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework that was made closed-source in the wake of its abuse in cyber attacks targeting South Korean financial institutions, to speed up scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims. The tech giant said the threat actor used the AI tool at "machine speed" to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations across the world spanning a broad range of sectors since September 2026. Targets include aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. "Storm-0940's use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to target environments through applications that had already been granted access, allowing the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in," Microsoft said. "AI-accelerated follow-on activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access." Storm-0940 was first detailed by Microsoft in November 2024, revealing that the threat actor has been leveraging a botnet called Quad7 (aka CovertNetwork-1658) to conduct highly evasive password spray attacks. The threat actor is assessed to be active since at least 2021. The adversary is also said to exploit internet-facing applications to gain initial access, followed by using compromised accounts to move through targeted environments. It has also been observed establishing persistence by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications within cloud infrastructures to ensure access to Microsoft 365 resources. According to Microsoft, a chunk of these ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the adversary gaining privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure, including several instances where the time frame from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. In the case of the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 has been observed using ARTEX to attempt to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute, a pace the company said gives defenders a short window to detect and respond. "Between October 10 and 14, 2026, Storm-0940 infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 conducted an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations to gain access to Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online," Microsoft said. During this window, Microsoft said it captured over 151,000 failed logon events. The activity peaked on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute, resulting in more than 111,000 failures in a single day. Of these, 48 accounts received more than 1,000 failures. No successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change was detected, it noted. That changed on October 15, 2026, when the AI agents gained access to the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications and began to use them to authenticate to customer environments. "Additionally, after acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant," the tech giant added. In some of these cases, the AI agents are assessed to have progressed beyond authentication to Microsoft Graph and directory operations. This included reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups, and privileged roles. The TAG-217 attack chain | Source: Zscaler "The application credential modification made by Storm-0940’s associated agents in the targeted victims' environments can lead to persistence through other identities, credentials, and cloud services," Microsoft said. "These changes can remain active as a backdoor even after the original compromised application is mediated." Storm-0940 is far from the only hacking crew to rely on ARTEX. Microsoft said it has observed threat actors across multiple geographic regions weaponizing the framework in their operations. Recorded Future Insikt Group, which is tracking the threat cluster behind the attacks on South Korean financial institutions under the moniker TAG-217, said it identified activity linked to the threat actor dating back to August 17, 2026, when it "tested infrastructure designed to maintain remote access to computers and conducted internet scanning." Over the next few weeks, the Chinese-speaking threat actor is said to have put together tools to attack cryptocurrency mining operations using the YiiMP platform, as well as set up a workspace for testing weaknesses in iPhones and modifying Android system software. Zscaler ThreatLabz has since revealed that the attack's footprint extends beyond South Korea, and that it opportunistically targeted organizations around the globe and across multiple industry sectors. The findings come from a custom ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. "ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok," security researcher Seongsu Park said. "Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another's findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents." An analysis of the prompt histories has revealed requests for bulk personal and transaction data, along with questions about selling stolen data, suggesting the attacks were likely financially motivated. Other prompts related to extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges. The findings once again highlight how threat actors are increasingly integrating agentic AI tools into their offensive security workflows to quickly carry out attacks at scale. "Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously, enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises," Microsoft said. In response to the findings, ConnectWise said the activity "describes a campaign that reaches well beyond any one company," adding "nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations." "AI now lets them test those connections at [...] 'machine speed.' MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve. Every vendor and every MSP must defend itself with both of those risks in mind." ConnectWise, which temporarily shut down services following the attacks, has been restoring services in phases, a process that it said will take several days.

1ixu5qs.text: GitLab released fixes on October 21 for a flaw that lets an attacker run code on a self-managed server without logging in, and it affects every version of the software going back to 7.0, released in 2014. The fix matters even for administrators who patched nine days earlier: the October 12 update covered only versions 19.2 and later, and the new fixed versions sit one patch above it, so an instance updated then is in range again. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-110264, is rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale, the maximum. GitLab says that, under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code on the server due to an integer overflow during the compilation of a specially crafted regular expression. GitLab has not said what those conditions are. The company reports no sign the flaw has been used in attacks, and it is not listed in the U.S. CISA catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 22. Only self-managed installations need to act. GitLab.com already runs the fixed version, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on the internal releases 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already have the fix. GitLab fixed the flaw in seven versions at once. The table below pairs each release branch with the version that fixes it. If you run Upgrade to 19.5 before 19.5.1 19.5.1 19.4 before 19.4.3 19.4.3 19.3 before 19.3.6 19.3.6 19.2 before 19.2.9 19.2.9 19.1 before 19.1.9 19.1.9 19.0 before 19.0.10 19.0.10 7.0 through 18.11, before 18.11.13 18.11.13 Four of those versions are older than GitLab normally patches. The company's policy covers the current release and the previous two monthly releases, which, as of today, are 19.5, 19.4, and 19.3. GitLab said it backported this fix to 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9 on top of its standard releases, a step it reserves for severe issues. The reason the flaw reaches so far back is the part of GitLab that failed. The regular-expression compiler is Ruby's built-in engine, called Onigmo, which GitLab ships inside its own packages and patches in its own builds. A weakness in that engine is present wherever GitLab has shipped it, which is every release since 7.0. GitLab also published two detection rules to help self-managed administrators look for exploitation attempts, named "Onigmo native worker crash" and "Org mode render error burst." They are part of the company's open-source TLDR framework, which writes each detection in the Sigma format against GitLab's own application logs. GitLab has not said what preconditions an attacker needs to reach the compiler, so administrators cannot yet rule themselves out by configuration; the fix is the only certain protection, and GitLab's advisory offers no interim workaround. This is the fourth code-execution flaw in GitLab's regular-expression engine that the same researcher, who uses the handle joaxcar, has reported in a month, and the first to reach versions before 19.2. On October 12, GitLab fixed CVE-2026-97229, also an unauthenticated 10.0 overflow in the regex compiler, in versions 19.2.8, 19.3.5, and 19.4.2. On September 23, it fixed two more, CVE-2026-93577 and CVE-2026-89078, both rated 9.9 but requiring a logged-in account. The three earlier flaws stopped at version 19.2; this one does not. The October 21 release fixes 11 security issues in all, one critical and the rest high, medium, or low. Two of the others concern authentication. CVE-2026-15723, rated high at 8.2, could allow a logged-in user to take over another account, but only when an administrator has enabled both SAML and LDAP auto-linking. A cache-poisoning flaw in GitLab's OAuth and OpenID Connect endpoints, CVE-2026-112212, rated high at 7.5, could allow an attacker to redirect certain sign-in flows to a server they control in setups that use a shared cache. The upgrade carries a cost worth planning for. The 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 releases include database changes that run during the upgrade, and on a single-node server that means downtime while they finish. GitLab says multi-node setups can apply the patch without downtime using its zero-downtime procedure.

16i0hg4.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 21, 2026Malware / Artificial Intelligence The popular LiteLLM Python package has been compromised as part of a software supply chain attack that delivered a credential stealer and a backdoor, according to reports from SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Upwind. The compromise affects LiteLLM 1.107.0, distributed through PyPI wheels and Docker images. The Python package has since been quarantined on Python Package Index (PyPI), and the malicious Docker images have been removed. Oliver Jensen, director of security at LiteLLM, said an investigation into the incident is ongoing, and that it's still working to trace the original attack vector by which the threat actor published the malicious release. "We have identified that the malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens," Jensen said. "The threat actor used one user's account to trigger the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked." "We have not yet identified the mechanism by which the threat actor acquired the relevant tokens, so cannot yet assert that no further access to these GitHub accounts. As a temporary mitigation, we have removed all but one (unaffected) user from our GitHub organization." Separately, LiteLLM said it has updated the public registries to remove any trusted links to its GitHub organization so as to prevent further publication of malicious packages. Analysis of the malicious version shows that it's equipped to collect cloud credentials, private keys, browser data, and authentication files for AI development tools. The following wheels are affected - litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_10_12_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_aarch64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz (No payload files, but has the tampered pyproject.toml) "The first payload is a credential stealer that calls itself privcollect," StepSecurity said. "The second payload forks a background daemon that checks a GitHub dead drop every hour and runs whatever Python the attacker serves." The malware is launched by Python even before LiteLLM is imported through a path file ("cook.pth"), which is designed to automatically execute code when the interpreter starts. It's worth noting that the same behavior was observed in the LiteLLM compromise that took place as part of the TeamPCP supply chain attacks earlier this March. The "cook.pth" file contains a single line, "import cook," which, in turn, launches the credential collector payload. This includes harvesting cloud tokens, developer accounts and private keys, AI tooling credential JSON files, browser data associated with Chromium and Firefox, and environment variables. The malware is also capable of targeting LiteLLM deployments with an aim to extract the proxy's saved credentials and model configuration. The collected data is packaged into a GZIP-compressed TAR archive and sent to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" by means of an HTTP POST request. In addition, the malware is designed to read the contents of a text file ("domain.txt") located within a GitHub repository ("github[.]com/letters9813"), check if it holds a domain and, if so, run the same stealer, and finally run an HTTP GET request against "<domain>/codepy" and execute the response. The GitHub repository currently returns a 404 error. Users who have downloaded the malicious version are advised to revoke and replace exposed credentials from a clean environment and pin version 1.106.2 by digest.

1phmdky.text: OpenAI has revealed that two artificial intelligence (AI) agents powered by GPT-6.1 Sol and one GPT-6 Astra weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes during two internal coding tasks. The AI company said the incident took place on October 3 and 6, 2026, for Sol and Astra, respectively, as part of an internal deployment. "A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications," OpenAI said in a report. The end result of this action was that the misalignment monitor still ran and saved its reports, but automatic human alerts were disabled by setting "no_notify" to true and emptying the lists of people configured to receive monitoring reports. In another task on October 6, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program is said to have removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that the functionality had not been removed. "No [...] I did not remove an enabled monitor from it," the final response from the agent reads. OpenAI said, in both cases, the AI agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be retained, but ultimately chose not to do so after interpreting routine coding instructions as "permission to weaken them." In response to the findings, the company said it's strengthening its misalignment monitoring system and assessing if these scenarios are an outlier or whether they demonstrate a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring. "In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring [during evaluations], we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place," OpenAI said. "It is possible that this behavior is simply an example of 'benign' overpersistence, with models not understanding why monitoring is important or insisting that instructions be executed beyond what a reasonable person might expect." The disclosure is the latest instance of AI agents acting in ways their developers did not intend to. Last week, the ChatGPT-maker disclosed seven misalignment incidents, including one case where an internal research model stole cryptocurrency from a wallet it did not own to pay the fees needed to deploy smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network and failed to report that it took the funds without permission. Microsoft Targets Rogue AI Agents With Dynamic Permissions, Risk Score It also comes amid growing concerns that the development of increasingly powerful AI systems is outpacing safety efforts, leading to warnings that this could make it harder to monitor and control them as they gain greater autonomy. Earlier this week, Microsoft announced new controls to monitor and contain potentially rogue AI agents in enterprise environments as part of Project Perception, a continuously learning AI-powered cyber defense system the company unveiled in July 2026. "Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment," Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, said. "Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended, and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised." With agents often having extensive permissions to access data, tools, and systems, not to mention take actions and make decisions on their own, Redmond said they pose a new kind of insider security risk that requires continuous monitoring. To that end, Microsoft's Project Perception employs Guardian Agents to supervise other AI agents and secure them across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime layers by - Discovering and identifying every agent. Limiting their permissions using the principle of least privilege (PoLP) before execution and then dynamically grant or revoke access based on the task at hand. Monitoring the agent's actions and checking if it's straying from its original task. Adapting protections as behavior, context, and risk change. The system is architected on the foundations of three new themes - Dynamic Permissions, which scopes the permissions to the task assigned to the agent and makes it time-bound. Dynamic Agent Risk, which assigns each agent a risk score that is continuously updated and draws from how securely it's configured, what resources it can reach, the potential impact if something goes wrong, and whether its actions are deviating from the user's or organization's intent. Dynamic Conditional Access, which extends Entra Conditional Access for agents so that permissions can be adjusted when there is a change in risk. "Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start," Microsoft said. "If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it."

1jmlfip.text: PHP has released emergency updates that fix two critical flaws in the language itself, letting an attacker without an account run code on a web server. The fixes are in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, and the PHP team says only updating fully protects a server. The flaws, together called PHP2Shell, sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application, so a site is exposed even when its own code is secure. The risk is highest on servers using Apache's mod_php, where a working exploit triggers the attack before any application code runs. Both flaws are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and carry the identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. PHP published them around the scheduled release time of 14:00 UTC on October 21, a day after details leaked ahead of a planned October 22 disclosure. Researchers at Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI found and reported the flaws, which affect nearly every PHP version back to PHP 5.4. Who Is Affected Every PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, according to the PHP security advisory. Because the flaws are in the engine rather than in any site's code, even a simple "Hello World" page on a vulnerable PHP version can be attacked. The advisory singles out mod_php as the highest risk, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs. PHP-FPM behaves differently, because it shuts the worker down when a request fails early in setup. For one of the two flaws, PHP's own analysis supports that FPM is susceptible but says no complete FPM exploit has been shown; the second flaw was shown to reach code execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM, though the FPM path there depends on an operation inside the running application. An attacker can also read memory from the PHP worker process, which may hold passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, without first gaining code execution. The researchers demonstrated this reading of live worker memory against applications they did not control, making it independent of the application running on top of PHP. What to Install Update the PHP runtime that serves web requests, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running PHP workers. Updating an application such as WordPress or Laravel does not update the PHP runtime beneath it; that comes from the server package, the host, or the container image. PHP branch Vulnerable First fixed version 8.5 below 8.5.12 8.5.12 8.4 below 8.4.27 8.4.27 8.3 below 8.3.36 8.3.36 8.2 below 8.2.35 8.2.35 PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, and PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For the older branches, the PHP security team has published source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 to help people building from source or waiting on a vendor. Linux distributions and long-term-support vendors received the patches in advance, so a distribution package can carry the fix under an old-looking version number; check the package changelog for the CVE, as Debian advises, not the version string. If You Cannot Update Yet Only updating is a complete fix. The measures below reduce exposure to specific attack paths and do not make a server safe, according to the advisory. For CVE-2026-109618, set memory_limit=-1 so applications cannot override it, keep post_max_size low, and enforce request-size limits at the web server or proxy. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA as a substitute, because PHP warns they can trigger the same vulnerable path. For CVE-2026-109619, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker, and on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Turning off session upload progress blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants, and no configuration change fully mitigates this flaw short of updating. That setting is the one circulated as a workaround before the patch, and the release confirms it was never a complete fix. Session upload progress is turned on by default and can reach session handling before PHP finishes setting up a request, which is why it takes part in one confirmed attack path for CVE-2026-109619 and why turning it off does nothing for CVE-2026-109618. "The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching/upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much," PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard wrote before the release, replying to someone who suggested the setting might be enough. After updating, review your memory settings. The fix adds a new hard memory limit, and reaching it ends the process and stops shutdown handlers from running, so check memory_limit and post_max_size against what your application needs. If you already patched but suspect an earlier break-in, the researchers suggest watching for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, oddly large PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained restarts of PHP workers. Is It Being Attacked Before the patch shipped, Cloudflare said it was seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws. "We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said, calling the firewall rules Cloudflare deployed a stopgap and urging administrators to patch. No source has confirmed a successful break-in. watchTowr, which reproduced CVE-2026-109618, reported no exploitation in the wild as of 11:26 UTC on October 21, and neither flaw was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at that time. Some organizations took services offline as a precaution rather than in response to any break-in. BambooHR took its service offline across the United States, Canada and Ireland, warned that payroll would be interrupted, and said it did not yet have a restoration time. In the Netherlands, MijnOverheid, DigiD, the lower house of parliament's site, the national cyber-security center and several education systems went offline, the broadcaster NOS reported; the centre said it had not seen the flaw abused but urged everyone to patch. How It Came Out A leak pulled the release forward. On October 20, as The Hacker News reported, a post on Hacker News said two PHP remote code execution flaws, with the two CVE identifiers, were set for disclosure on October 22, on no more than a trusted tip. PHP posted an advance notice that evening and moved the release to October 21. The leak's claim of a CVSS 10.0 score was not PHP's; PHP rates both flaws 9.2. The flaws were found by Wiz Research, Calif, and OpenAI's Codex Security team, working with the PHP security team and Google's Gemini team on the fix. The underlying code had been in PHP for more than a decade. The researchers say AI models helped turn these long-standing flaws into working exploits, letting one researcher do in about a week what they say would otherwise have taken a team months. Calif, which traced the bug's lineage to PHP research from 2004, says knowing the target's history still mattered, and that current models do not reliably start from obscure, twenty-year-old primitives on their own. Update: watchTowr Reports Exploitation Attempts, Still No Confirmed Break-In watchTowr, which earlier in the day reported seeing none, said in a new advisory at 14:19 UTC on October 21 that it is observing "active exploitation attempts" of both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Cloudflare said it saw attack traffic against its customers and watched attackers change their payloads to get around its firewall rules, which it had switched on by default at 03:02 UTC, before the patch. No source has reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server as of this update. The PHP Foundation said the coordinated disclosure came apart before the release. Around 20:00 UTC on October 20, the research firm Calif mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept, and at 07:41 UTC on October 21, about six hours before the fix shipped, the vendor Chainguard published built images containing the patch, letting anyone study the fix while other users waited to update. Update: PHP Foundation Says a 2024 Audit Found the First Signs of the Flaw In the same post, the PHP Foundation said a core developer first found signs of the out-of-memory flaw behind CVE-2026-109618 during PHP's 2024 external audit, but a working attack was only theorized and no concrete route to code execution was found then.Competing fixes each risked breaking compatibility, opening denial-of-service paths, or forcing changes on third-party extensions, and a small team struggled to agree, so work on a fix stalled for months. The Foundation called the delay "a structural failure" of its decision process and its resources. The 2026 reports from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, which used AI tools, established the working exploit that made the flaw's full impact clear and moved the fix to the top of the queue. The Foundation said it has since changed how it makes security decisions and added staff and tooling to catch similar problems sooner. (The story was updated after publication on October 21, 2026, to add later reports of exploitation attempts and the PHP Foundation's account of the flaw's history.)

1epyggl.text: Google on Tuesday said it's rolling out improved safeguards in its Chrome browser to secure users against ClickFix attacks when Enhanced Protection is enabled. ClickFix is a popular social engineering technique in which bad actors trick users into copying and pasting malicious code directly into their computer's operating system, thereby bypassing conventional security controls. As part of these attacks, unsuspecting users who land on legitimate-but-compromised sites or malicious ads are redirected to phishing landing pages that display fake Cloudflare or Google reCAPTCHA verification or other non-existent errors and instruct users to copy and paste a command on the Windows Run dialog (or the Mac Terminal app) to address it. The moment a user presses the Enter key after pasting the command, it triggers a multi-stage infection chain that leads to the deployment of malware, such as information stealers or remote access trojans. In an attempt to blend in with regular activity and evade detection, the commands often make use of living-off-the-land (LotL) tools like PowerShell or cmd.exe to download next-stage payloads. A key reason why ClickFix remains an effective initial access method is that it flips the script on traditional phishing. Instead of exploiting sophisticated vulnerabilities or getting a user to click on suspicious links, it tricks them into opening the front door themselves under the pretext of troubleshooting a commonplace issue. "By shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections," Google said. "To combat this technique, Chrome now detects when an Enhanced Protection user is tricked into copying suspicious commands." If a user copies a potential ClickFix script, the clipboard payload is scrubbed of any personal information it may contain and sent to Safe Browsing for further analysis. If the security system determines the command is dangerous, Chrome displays a warning. By doing so, the idea is to prevent the attack from taking place before the user executes the malicious command. Separately, Google is also introducing the following defenses in Chrome to tackle scams for users who enable Enhanced Protection - Establishing a taxonomy for Safe Browsing site warnings: Suspicious sites, which exhibit deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites, and Dangerous sites, which refer to sites that are known to be malicious and have a high risk of user harm. Building upon on-device large language model (LLM)-based approaches to flag tech support scams and others, such as fake antivirus and browser update scams. "This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites," Google said. "Throughout this process, Chrome minimizes the amount of data shared with the server by only analyzing page text when a site exhibits high-confidence scam indicators. And whenever page content is sent off the device, it is processed ephemerally – meaning it is never logged, retained or used to train models." On Tuesday, Google said it's introducing Financial Services Verification in the U.S. and Canada to validate an advertiser's credentials and ensure ads come from authorized financial providers. The verification program already applies to various markets globally, including Australia, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Türkiye, and several countries in Europe. "Under this policy, advertisers must demonstrate they are authorized by relevant regulators or recognized registries before running certain financial ads – helping prevent brand impersonation and stopping bad actors from reaching people," Google said. "Alongside our ongoing work with financial regulators, we're working in the U.S. with the American Bankers Association to use their dedicated registry to verify authorized banks before ads can run. In Canada, we’re engaging closely with the Canadian Bankers Association as we prepare for our rollout." Apple Blocks Identity Resolution in Safari and WebKit The development comes as Apple revealed new privacy protections built into Safari and WebKit as part of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases, taking steps to block a practice called identity resolution that turns email addresses into persistent tracking identifiers. "In this scheme, third-parties (i.e., not the website owner) invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter," Apple's WebKit team said. "They send the email address to their servers, create an opaque tracking ID permanently linked to your email address, and send that tracking ID back to the web page." "The tracking ID is stored on the website and can from thereon be used for arbitrary purposes linked to your email address, such as building a profile of your browsing or targeting ads at you across websites. Logging out or unsubscribing from that newsletter does not remove the tracking ID or your email address stored with the third party." Apple said the third-parties can build more data about users as they log in with their email address or fill in forms containing personal data, allowing them to create an identity graph with their name, residential address, phone number, and IP address. To prevent this sort of cross-site tracking, Safari blocks network access to identity resolution infrastructure embedded within the web pages, effectively stopping the third party from sending the email address to their servers. The blocking, Apple said, is done at the domain level. "It's not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web," Apple said. "They have ushered into what they call the post cookie era and in our latest releases we have put strong protection in place."

5lp12c.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously undocumented China-aligned threat cluster known as Bronze Sandcastle that has been observed targeting organizations in Asia and Africa since mid-2025. "The most distinctive technical marker for Bronze Sandcastle is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading," Sophos security researcher Gabor Szappanos said in a post published Tuesday. Between August 2025 and August 2026, attacks mounted by the threat actor have resulted in victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea. Evidence indicates that Bronze Sandcastle is most active in the UTC+8 time zone. DLL sideloading is a popular adversarial technique that exploits the way Windows loads DLL files, allowing an attacker to trick a legitimate program into loading a malicious DLL. When an application is launched, it needs to load various DLLs in order to function correctly. If the application does not provide the full path to a required DLL, the operating system looks for it in a predetermined sequence of directories. An attacker can take advantage of this behavior by planting a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in a location that Windows searches before the folder that contains the actual DLL. Thus, when the legitimate application starts, it proceeds to load and run the malicious DLL, giving the attacker a way in to the system. "Because the malicious code is executed by a trusted and often digitally signed application, it is less likely to be flagged by antivirus software and other security solutions," Zscaler noted in an analysis last week. "If the legitimate application runs with elevated privileges, the malicious DLL will inherit those same permissions, allowing the attacker to perform more sensitive actions on the system." What's more, the technique enables persistence if the compromised application is configured to automatically run every time a system is rebooted, thereby allowing the attacker's code to execute on the infected host. Sophos said it observed legitimate Sandboxie executables placed in multiple victim environments, along with a malicious "sbiedll.dll" file, which, in turn, causes the trusted application ("SandboxieWUAU.exe") to load attacker-controlled code during runtime. Besides Sandboxie, Bronze Sandcastle has been leveraged in seven other DLL sideloading combinations - javaw.exe (Java application) - jli.dll Krita.exe (Krita digital painting) - Krita.dll NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access) - NvdaHelperRemote.dll Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper) - Libcef.dll Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer) - version.dll LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application) - msvcp140.dll bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information) - snmpapi.dll "The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files," Sophos said. "This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims' environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts." The DLL is designed to load and execute an encrypted payload ("config.ini"), which functions as a backdoor designed to enumerate local network and user accounts, as well as collect system metadata, running processes, keystrokes, and screenshots. Two different versions of the payload have been identified to date: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. The payload has also been found to communicate with external sites (e.g., file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io), likely in an attempt to receive additional tasking from its operators. In addition, version 1.1.5 has been observed using dc.cathaypacifice[.]com and net.dpworldto[.]com for command-and-control (C2). Version 1.1.7 payloads, on the other hand, have been observed communicating with GitHub repositories ("github[.]com/LatonyCharnleyaW") via the API to download encrypted config files. The GitHub account is no longer accessible. This is not the first time Chinese hacking groups have relied on DLL sideloading, nor is it the first time Sandboxie has been employed in such attacks. In July 2024, the APT41 threat actor leveraged a different executable signed by Sandboxie ("taskhost.exe") to sideload a malicious version of "sbiedll.dll" to deploy a backdoor called MoonWalk ultimately. "The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective," Sophos said. "Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity."

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. 1aqcvsf.text: Every image scan returns hundreds of CVEs; the question is which ten your containers actually execute and which base image would zero the list entirely. We scored ten options with context and elimination weighted above raw detection. Evaluating scanners alongside the Top 10 Best Container Security Tools in 2026 reveals that static vulnerability counts alone do not prevent attackers who compromise container hosts through misconfigurations. Aqua’s Trivy takes 1 as the free floor everyone should run; Sysdig and Wiz complete a podium built on making findings mean something. Key Takeaways • 1 overall: Trivy the ubiquitous free scanner with platform depth above it. • Podium: Trivy (floor), Sysdig (in-use runtime filtering), Wiz (graph exposure ranking). • Strategy pick: Chainguard’s zero-CVE bases beat scanning by removing what scanners find. • One-vendor note: Grype and Syft are Anchore’s OSS pair SBOM-first scanning free. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based: detection quality, SBOM support, context/prioritization, registry/workflow fit, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: context quality 30%, detection/SBOM 25%, workflow fit 20%, pricing accessibility 15%, elimination strategy 10%. Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Aqua (Trivy) — Best Free Floor + Platform Snapshot: OSS free + Aqua tiers | Images, IaC, deps in one Why it earns 1: The most deployed scanner in the cloud-native ecosystem: fast, accurate, multi-target, and completely free with Aqua’s enterprise platform adding admission control and runtime security above it. Even as organizations maintain vigilance following threats like the Trivy supply chain attack on public registries, its multi-target engine remains the baseline floor no CI/CD pipeline should lack. Standout features: Image+IaC+SCA scanning; SBOM; CI-native; policy packs. Pros: Ubiquity; consolidation; free. Cons: Prioritization lives upstack. Bottom line: The scan without an excuse. 2. Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Sysdig — Best In-Use Prioritization Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Runtime-informed filtering | Falco lineage Why it earns 2: Marking which vulnerable packages actually load into memory at runtime collapses CVE backlogs by 90-plus percent triage governed by execution truth rather than static theoretical risk. Built upon its open-source Falco heritage and Sysdig Threat Research on container escape vulnerabilities, it connects image vulnerabilities directly to live Kubernetes behavior. Standout features: In-use filtering; runtime detection; registry scanning; admission. Pros: Context that empties queues. Cons: Platform adoption. Bottom line: Only the vulnerabilities your containers run. 3. Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Wiz — Best Exposure-Graph Ranking Snapshot: Platform quote | Agentless | Blast-radius context Why it earns 3: Image findings correlated with workload exposure, cloud entitlements, and network reachability determining which vulnerable container image actually endangers crown-jewel assets at cluster scale. Grounded in insights from Wiz threat research analyzing cloud attack paths, Wiz separates sandboxed images from workloads facing public ingress. Standout features: Graph correlation; agentless scanning; prioritization. Pros: Consequence ranking. Cons: Platform economics. Bottom line: The image ranked by what it can reach. 4. Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Chainguard — Best Eliminate-First Strategy Snapshot: Published per-image | Zero-CVE minimal bases Why it earns 4: The strategic answer to alert fatigue: start with container bases that have nothing to flag. Minimal, continuously rebuilt, and cryptographically signed images resolve what CVE counts miss about container security by collapsing false positives and shrinking software bills of materials before deployment. Standout features: Hardened bases; provenance included; FIPS variants. Pros: Queue elimination. Cons: Migration engineering; per-image cost. Bottom line: The base with nothing to report. 5. Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snyk — Best Fix-Oriented Workflow Snapshot: Free tier + per-dev | Base-image upgrade advice Why it earns 5: “Switch to this tag, eliminate 80 CVEs” pragmatic recommendations that empty backlogs through direct action inside the workflows developers already use. Snyk pairs base-image intelligence with automated pull request remediation and fix advice so engineering teams can remediate Dockerfile bloat in a single click. Standout features: Upgrade advice; registry integrations; K8s monitoring. Pros: Actionability. Cons: Runtime context elsewhere. Bottom line: The recommendation that ships as a fix. 6. Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Anchore (Grype/Syft) — Best SBOM-First OSS Snapshot: OSS free + enterprise | One vendor’s pair Why it earns 6: Syft generates the Software Bills of Materials the ecosystem standardized on; Grype scans them with precision free, accurate, and evidence-native, with Anchore Enterprise adding centralized policy gates. It provides the toolchain necessary for addressing what CVE counts miss about container security while pairing with container registry security tools to maintain artifact integrity across CI/CD environments. Standout features: Syft SBOM; Grype matching; policy (enterprise). Pros: SBOM depth; OSS credibility. Cons: Enterprise features gate up. Bottom line: The scan that produces evidence, not just alerts. 7. JFrog Xray — Best Registry-Native JFrog Xray — Best Registry-Native Snapshot: Platform tiers | Artifactory unity | Impact graphs Why it earns 7: Recursive binary scanning and build-impact analysis executed directly where artifacts live the authoritative source-of-truth integration for JFrog estates. Standing out among dedicated container registry security tools , Xray inspects image layers, nested dependencies, and curated packages in a unified catalog. Standout features: Artifactory integration; impact graphs; curation. Pros: Registry leverage. Cons: Platform gravity. Bottom line: The registry scanning itself. 8. Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud) — Best CNAPP Unity Palo Alto (Prisma Cloud) — Best CNAPP Unity Snapshot: Quote | Twistlock heritage | Pipeline-to-runtime Why it earns 8: Comprehensive image scanning delivered within a unified Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) with built-in admission control and runtime defense. Incorporating its Twistlock heritage, it prevents threats by monitoring CI/CD environments and registry pipelines before non-compliant containers reach cloud clusters. Standout features: Pipeline+registry+runtime; admission; CNAPP context. Pros: Breadth. Cons: Packaging shifts. Bottom line: Image security in the platform estate. 9. Docker Scout — Best Workflow-Native Docker Scout — Best Workflow-Native Snapshot: Free + tiers | Desktop/Hub integration Why it earns 9: Vulnerability scanning and policy evaluation embedded inside the Docker CLI and Docker Desktop workflows developers use daily. Catching issues early prevents scenarios where malicious Docker Hub images deploying cryptominers or bloated layers slip into production registries. Standout features: Desktop/Hub integration; recommendations; policy. Pros: Native fit; free floor. Cons: Enterprise depth. Bottom line: The scan inside the CLI you already use. 10. Clair — Best OSS Registry Veteran Clair — Best OSS Registry Veteran Snapshot: Free (OSS) | Quay lineage | API-driven Why it earns 10: The long-serving open-source scanning engine behind Project Quay and OpenShift deployments delivering static layer analysis via an extensible API. Clair provides an essential building block for securing Linux containers across build and runtime within private, self-hosted container registry architectures. Standout features: Registry-oriented scanning; API; layer analysis. Pros: Free; registry fit. Cons: Momentum vs Trivy/Grype. Bottom line: The registry’s own veteran, still serving. Add context when volume drowns triage: in-use filtering (Sysdig) or exposure graphs (Wiz). Pilot Chainguard bases on your busiest service elimination beats detection where migration fits. Match estates (Artifactory→Xray, Docker-centric→Scout), retain SBOMs always, and retire CVE-count dashboards for in-use and fix-rate metrics. FAQs What is the best container image scanning tool in 2026? Trivy ranks 1 as the free floor with platform depth, Sysdig for in-use runtime prioritization, Wiz for exposure-graph ranking with Chainguard’s zero-CVE bases as the elimination strategy and Grype/Syft the SBOM-first OSS pair. Which free scanner should we pick? Trivy (broadest targets) or Grype+Syft (SBOM-first) both production-grade; standardizing on one matters more than the choice. Clair persists for Quay-lineage registries. How do we handle hundreds of CVEs per image? Context or elimination: in-use filtering shows what executes, exposure graphs show what’s reachable, base upgrades and hardened images remove the inventory. Raw counts are the metric of despair. Can container image scanning stop cluster takeovers? Scanning prevents known vulnerabilities from deploying, but it must be paired with admission controllers and runtime defense. Attackers who exploit unpatched libraries often leverage Kubernetes privilege escalation vulnerabilities to break out of pods and compromise host nodes. Are Grype and Anchore different vendors? No Grype and Syft are Anchore’s open-source tools, with Anchore Enterprise above. One vendor, one entry. Scan or harden which wins? Both: hardened minimal bases shrink the attack surface; scanning guards what remains and produces the SBOM evidence contracts demand. Verdict Trivy floors it free, Sysdig and Wiz make findings mean something, and Chainguard asks why the findings exist scan everything, contextualize at scale, eliminate where you can, and keep the SBOMs. The queue that matters is the one your runtime actually loads. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. Teams planning automation can consult Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal access overview and API documentation and check their account limits. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total.
